We introduce a new wide-field, low-resolution, spectroscopic survey called the CAPOS Imaging Survey. Using the Alfa Array Instrument on the Large Binocular Telescope, we conducted a new spectroscopic imaging study of Tonantzintla 2, a rich globular cluster in the Andromeda galaxy. The cluster holds importance due to its high velocity dispersion and metallicity, which can offer insights into galaxy building and the rate of Brooks' starlight being absorbed by dust. A new semi-manual star member selection method was applied to the cluster using the new, less sensitive spectra. A total of 815 new members were identified through a 15.5 hour exposure, covering 1.6 x 10^-3 square degrees of the sky. The new survey delivers better signal-to-noise ratios for its spectra compared to previous datasets. The resulting data show a marginally lower velocity dispersion of 6.55 +/- 0.78 km/s and a higher metallicity of 0.41 +/- 0.03 dex. The reduced sample of 815 new members yields a velocity dispersion of 6.35 +/- 0.24 km/s and a high metallicity of 0.36 +/- 0.02 dex. The new data show a small decrease in the homogeneity of the cluster over the past 30 years. The reduced sample exhibits slightly lower metal content than the rest of the cluster members. The internal structure of programming languages, comprising operators, variables, and control flow, forms the foundational element for software design.  The complexity of modern software systems, spanning thousands of lines of code, makes them virtually impossible for humans to comprehend without support.  Current techniques for reverse engineering and software maintenance are hampered by the lack of a unified framework that can model the intricate patterns and relationships within open-source systems.  A new general framework, known as Abstract Semantic Space, is presented to effectively represent and structure the semantic essence of programs, enabling efficient identification of relevant information and facilitating meaningful queries.  A practical implementation, called ASSIST, is also introduced, offering a range of features and tools to streamline semantic analysis and provide a comprehensive view of the code. The relation between a galaxy's mass and dark matter halo mass has been established for galaxies of various sizes, yet the order in which halo mass affects galaxy size remains unclear. In the main sample of 1,740 galaxies from the GALEX-HERMES, we compared star formation rates and stellar masses by halo mass to resolve this question. Since stellar mass builds up over time, we applied a novel approach to reverse-engineer the evolution of stellar mass assembly within dark matter halos. In this way, we discovered that more massive halos than previously studied were included, and subsequently, a positive correlation between halo mass and galaxy size became apparent. Furthermore, our findings from the GALEX-HERMES catalog align with those from the MaNGA survey, and when combining data with those from the VANDELS, we confirmed that this correlation exists across two distinct redshift intervals. Consequently, we propose that an inside-out growth model in which more massive halos form larger galaxies is supported, and our data indicate that this model applies up to z ~ 2.5. In addition, we found that this relationship may be non-linear due to the differing rates at which galaxies form stars and grow in smaller, less massive halos compared to larger ones. These results have implications suggesting that a greater fraction of a galaxy's final mass is accumulated in its later life. In a surprise finding, we also determined that this relationship may be influenced by a galaxy's final mass more than its overall mass, and therefore, a galaxy's final mass may be a more fixed outcome. In a broader scope, our data also reveal that a galaxy's size is determined primarily by its own mass rather than its surrounding dark matter halo mass, and our results agree with theoretical predictions that a galaxy's size is autonomous within a certain radius. Our research has significant implications that a galaxy's evolution is governed by complex interactions involving a galaxy's various components, and a galaxy's size is related to its mass through an intricate process influenced by a galaxy's phase of growth. In a galaxy's early life, a galaxy's size may be determined by its surrounding halo mass, whereas in a galaxy's later life, a galaxy's size may be determined by its own mass. Recent breakthroughs in photometry from space are providing unparalleled opportunities to monitor the upper atmosphere of planets. A specific application of this technology is tracking the diffuse solar radiation scattered by aerosols in the atmosphere of planets. To explore this further, our study employs numerical simulations to model the interaction between stellar photons and atmospheric particles, using models of aerosols measured by the PLATO satellite mission as reference. By comparing the results of our simulations with the data from PLATO's final camera, we have established a relationship between the optical properties of aerosols as observed from space and their composition, size, and shape. Additionally, our study shows that the angular variations in diffuse photon signals can be used to estimate the size of atmospheric particles, with the ultimate goal of mapping the spatial distribution of aerosols in planets' atmospheres. This research provides a standardized correlation between the observed optical properties of aerosols and their physical characteristics, facilitating the accurate interpretation of stellar photometry data in various astronomical contexts. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the phase difference between parallel channels in PLATO's final camera can be utilized to derive additional information about the properties of the atmospheric aerosols, such as their size and the resulting variation in diffuse photon signals with phase. This information could potentially be applied on other planets to study their atmospheric environments. A key application of this research is the detection and study of exoplanets, particularly those located in the habitable zones of solar systems, where aerosols can provide insight into the conditions and chemistry of a planet's atmosphere. To explore this further, our study includes examples of aerosol measurements that could be obtained through the observation of nearby stars using the PLATO mission. A key example involves the diffuse solar radiation scattered by the atmosphere of Earth, which can be monitored from space, providing a direct correlation between the observed optical properties of aerosols and their physical characteristics. Similarly, our models are versatile and can be applied to a wide range of other atmospheric systems, offering a wealth of scientific opportunities across various astronomical contexts. These include young solar systems, where the presence of aerosols can provide insight into the formation of planetary atmospheres, and mature systems, such as the sun, where the observed optical properties of aerosols can be linked to solar cycles and the physical characteristics of the atmosphere. This method involves generating neural architectures by applying synthesis rules based on the network's behavior on specific input data. By developing a set of synthesis rules that prioritize high output values, the authors were able to construct a neural network with a block of interconnected components, resulting in a more efficient architecture within the same search space. This method also allows for the creation of diverse neural architectures with varying properties, enabling the discovery of multiple solutions. A directed synthesis approach can lead to better results, suggesting that the space of possible neural architectures is more structured than previously thought. Therefore, developing a synthesis rule that prioritizes high performance requires less computational cost, making it a preferable method. The authors also provided evidence that the direct synthesis method can lead to better results. Nevertheless, it is difficult to determine whether the developed neural architectures with high performance are robust or not. Therefore, the direct synthesis method can lead to better results. In this research, we address the issue of assigning frequencies to groups of node pairs to minimize interference and maximize utilization of available spectrum. We have developed a hybrid approach to assign frequencies, combining partial and shared spectrum encoding methods. To minimize interference, we define a metric as the maximum ratio of distances to the minimum separation distance among all pairs, and use this hybrid approach until no further improvements can be made. This hybrid approach first considers unique frequencies for groups with the worst interference, and then distributes remaining frequencies as equally as possible among the remaining groups. We optimize the hybrid approach by dynamically assigning frequencies to the group with the highest priority on the condition that no further improvements can be made. Compared to other methods, this hybrid approach offers the best balance between equal distribution of spectrum and group priority. We validated our hybrid approach through simulations based on the outdoor mmWave environment in a hotel and also analyzed its performance under different scenarios. Equal distribution of spectrum led to higher system capacities than priority-based approaches, with a notable disparity observed in scenarios with mobile and stationary groups. However, equal distribution of spectrum resulted in lower equalized capacity compared to priority-based approaches. Furthermore, equal distribution of spectrum demonstrated more efficient usage of spectrum than priority-based approaches. We have proposed a hybrid approach to assign frequencies to groups, dynamically optimizing frequency assignment and equalizing spectrum distribution to minimize interference and maximize utilization. This hybrid approach offers a performance advantage over priority-based and equal distribution approaches in terms of equalized capacity, although equal distribution of spectrum leads to more efficient frequency assignment and a simpler implementation than priority-based approaches. Equal distribution of spectrum and priority-based approaches exhibit varying results depending on whether group mobility is considered. We have validated our hybrid approach through simulations in a hotel and analyzed its performance under different scenarios. A growing concern with Federated Learning is data protection, given the potential for malicious interference with the local client model. Research has focused on enhancing client-side model robustness and transmission security, but has not adequately addressed the efficiency of model data transfer between the client and server. This problem becomes more pronounced when using distributed datasets. This work introduces a new Federated Learning framework, Federated Extraction, that separates raw data from the model, enabling dataset extraction and codebook computation. This separation enables tokenized data representation, eliminating the need to transfer entire images or videos. We have achieved significant gains in data transfer efficiency without sacrificing robustness, resulting in a 99% reduction in data transfer volume and 93.75% reduction in transmission time, all while supporting secure gateway encryption. This efficiency improvement, achieved through the separation of model and data concerns, allows for the deployment of Federated Learning across sensitive datasets. A growing trend in distributed computing involves using specialized networks, such as Named Data Networking, to optimize the performance of distributed applications by placing computation near the data sources. To achieve this, we developed a dynamic coordination approach that dynamically assign computing tasks to nodes based on their capabilities and the demands of the applications. Our approach uses a real-time estimation method to predict task processing times, taking into account the current load of the nodes. We present a mathematical optimization model that minimizes the overall processing duration by assigning tasks to nodes in an optimal order. Due to the model's complex nature, resulting from the dynamic and uncertain characteristics of the nodes' load, we developed a time-efficient algorithm based on the concept of 'processing windows.' We tested our approach using a large-scale data center as a ground truth and compared it with other methods, demonstrating significantly improved performance under various scenarios. Furthermore, we analyzed the complexity of our approach and presented potential future research directions. Experimental results show that our approach leads to reduced tail-lift and mean tail-lift compared to other methods, demonstrating up to 300% improvement. Additionally, we observed a maximum performance improvement of 40% compared to other methods. Our approach allows for dynamic assignment of computing tasks to nodes without prior knowledge of the tasks, resulting in improved overall system performance and robustness. We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for an Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with multiple branches. The outer branches can be equally spaced or unequal, with varying lengths from the central point. We establish conditions under which the central point and the outer branches exponentially converge to equilibrium. This contrasts with previous research, which showed only linear convergence for equally spaced outer branches. Our study demonstrates that the convergence rate can be enhanced by adjusting the natural frequencies on the central point and the outer branches. Furthermore, we investigate the resilience of the system when subjected to bounded disturbances and show that the system remains stable to the equilibrium state within a bounded area around the origin. The findings are verified by numerically simulating the system on a three-pronged star graph. These results have broader implications for the stability of other linear polygraph systems. Additionally, the study offers recommendations for optimizing the natural frequencies of coupled systems, which can be applied to a wide range of scenarios. By incorporating domain-specific knowledge into utility functions and applying these to search algorithms, we can enhance their performance and direct the search toward desirable outcomes. The proposed method facilitates discovery of unknown utility functions through search itself, thereby eliminating the need for extensive prior experimentation. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated through case studies involving two scenarios: discovering an optimal utility function for a bi-objective optimization problem with known trade-offs and finding the original utility function of the Multiple-Solutions Genetic Algorithm for multiple objective optimization. Utility function learning enabled the direct extraction of meaningful parameters, leading to improved decision-making and enhanced algorithm understanding. The results showed that utility function learning can significantly accelerate convergence and achieve superior solutions compared to random or uninformative utility functions. The approach can be adapted for various domains, including but not limited to, materials science, as demonstrated by our research. The source code for this project is publicly available. The security of signature-based authentication systems relies heavily on the uniqueness, complexity, and reliability of signature patterns. The implementation of these systems is widespread across various industries. This research aims to examine and evaluate the level of complexity and uniqueness exhibited in a large dataset of signatures collected from a group of individuals. Additionally, this study seeks to identify any discrepancies among different devices in capturing signature patterns and assess their relevance to securing signature-based transactions. Our investigation employs a large dataset of 1,000 individuals, along with 4 different devices, to create 40 unique signature patterns. Our results show that while a substantial level of complexity exists within these signatures, their uniqueness is somewhat limited. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that device variability plays a negligible role in capturing signature patterns, suggesting that authentication algorithms should focus on incorporating multiple features to enhance the reliability of their outcomes. We use a type-I X-ray burst model to explore how nitrogen is generated in a specific astrophysical event and uncover the limitations of our current understanding in the nitrogen nucleosynthesis process. Although our model is considered realistic, it significantly underproduces nitrogen when compared to the observed abundance in the subsequent thermal pulse and post-thermal pulse stages. To rectify this discrepancy, we investigate three possible empirical modifications to our model: one involves introducing an excessive mass loss during the helium shell flash, another entails a substantial increase in the size of the accretion disk, and the final option is the incorporation of non-radial pulsations. However, implementing these modifications reveals that none can fully explain the observed levels of nitrogen without conflicting with other previously obtained constraints. Therefore, further theoretical model enhancements are necessary to resolve this discrepancy between the predicted and measured nitrogen abundance. Furthermore, we determined that a larger accretion disk results in a more efficient energy export from the unstable oxygen layer to the fusion zone during the initial stages of the thermal pulse phase, which in turn affects the pattern of shell burning. This, in turn, influences the timing and magnitude of the subsequent type-I X-ray burst. The impact of the increased disk size on these burst characteristics diminishes as the pulse progression slows, ultimately leading to increased variability in burst sizes and inter-burst waiting times. Additionally, we found that for bursts occurring at the onset of the thermal pulse phase, a larger accretion disk leads to elevated pre-burst levels of nuclear activity in the fusion zone when compared to standard models, which primarily employs $^{12}$C+$^{16}$O reactions. This, in turn, results in enhanced burst sizes. On the other hand, when bursts occur later during the disk growth, we found that the enhanced nuclear activity is confined to the fusion zone and does not significantly affect either its initial or final burst size. This pattern of enhanced nuclear activity is also observed in bursts occurring due to non-radial pulsations. We also found that for bursts not attributed to either non-radial pulsations or a growing accretion disk, a larger accretion disk results in decreased burst sizes, as well as altered burst profiles characterized by an increased duration and delayed peak. This, in turn, affects the timing and variability of the subsequent thermal pulse and post-thermal pulse stages. I'll review five theories that address impurity concealment: 

1. Epistemic Modality Modal Logic (EMML) - This model incorporates "might" operators in modal logic to evaluate the probability of accessing an atomically pure state when entering a closed box system. It uses the S5 axioms to define this probability assessment. However, this approach faces objections, including the underdetermination of states, inadequate handling of the access possibility, and incompatibility with certain reasoning rules. 

2. S5-BMM - This model incorporates the "might" operator in the S5 logic framework to evaluate the access possibility of an atomically pure state within a closed box system. It applies the probabilistic semantics of "might" operators to determine the accessibility of pure states. We address potential criticisms of this model, including the underdetermination of states, inadequate handling of access possibility, and incompatibility with certain reasoning rules. 

3. Epistemic Probability Logic (EPL) - This model uses the accessibility relation to define the probability of entering a pure state when accessing a closed box system. We address potential criticisms of this model, including the underdetermination of states, inadequate handling of access possibility, and incompatibility with certain reasoning rules. 

4. Epistemic Uncertainty Logic (EUL) - This model utilizes three operators to evaluate the entry conditions of closed box systems, representing pure, mixed, and approximate pure states. We address potential criticisms of this model, including the underdetermination of states, inadequate handling of access possibility, and incompatibility with certain reasoning rules. 

5. Epistemic Semantics for Inquiry Language (ESI) - This model uses the "might" operator in the S5 logic framework to evaluate the access possibility of an atomically pure state within a closed box system. It applies the semantical properties of "might" operators to determine the accessibility of pure states. We address potential criticisms of this model, including the underdetermination of states, inadequate handling of access possibility, and incompatibility with certain reasoning rules.

Proton-proton data are assessed at center-of-mass energies of 5.02 and 13 TeV, while lead-lead results come from 2015 and 2018 data with a collision energy of 5.02 TeV and varying centrality. Fragmentation patterns in lead-lead collisions with low-pT charged particles are discovered to be similar to proton-proton data, yet exhibit enhancements in lead-lead collisions with high-pT charged particles. This trend is observed across both 13 and 5.02 TeV collision energies. Gluon-jet analysis confirms that jets containing high-pT charged particles display modified fragmentation relative to proton-proton data, and this effect persists in central-geometry lead-lead collisions. This ensemble of data suggests that jet quenching is predominantly driven by gluon exchange.  Statistical significance of fragmentation modifications in central-data relative to peripheral-data is 3.5σ at 13 TeV and 3.3σ at 5.02 TeV.  Furthermore, data are compared to the GLIMMER MC generator and to Pythia 8.1 with and without atmosphere corrections.  When including atmosphere corrections, fragmentation modifications in central-data align closely with predictions from gluon saturation.  Without atmosphere corrections, central-data fragmentation exhibits improved alignment with the gluon-loss model.  In addition, data are examined across various rapidity ranges, revealing that fragmentation modifications are somewhat suppressed when jets are produced outside the central region (|y| < 1.8). We use a non-trivial metric to illustrate this point and show that by employing a non-determinant conformal metric, many familiar conformal field theories become less predictable, highlighting their connections to less symmetric versions of geometric equations. Results from both outdoor and indoor datasets indicate that our method surpasses existing techniques in terms of accuracy and robustness. We propose a cosmic scenario where the universe comprises multiple temporal domains, characterized by distinct Hubble constants, some of which are constant while others vary. The existence of hidden cosmic substrates, characterized by negative pressure and unknown dynamics, is postulated. A mathematical representation of these hidden substrates is achieved through the introduction of concealed Lie algebras and symplectic structures. The possibility of a hidden dark energy component, dynamically responsible for the accelerated expansion of our observable universe, is also explored. This research proposes a novel approach called Cross-Camera Deep Tinting (CCDT) for automatically coloring black and white video footage captured by cameras with varying color properties. By leveraging correspondence information between coordinates in color and grayscale images, CDCDT synchronizes the color information from one camera with another. We test our method on a dataset consisting of black and white and color videos captured using cameras with distinct color properties. This process is repeated to simulate cameras with triple and quadruple color channels. Experimental results demonstrate that CDCDt can successfully restore color to grayscale videos, often achieving results comparable to in-camera colorizing methods. Moreover, CDCDt can incorporate information from previous captures, or'memorize' color properties from past frames to improve its performance. This functionality is denoted as CDCDt-M and enables CDCDt to reach new heights in colorizing videos captured using multiple cameras. To accommodate this memorization capability, we introduce a novel cross-attention mechanism that propels CDCDt-M to exceptional levels. This mechanism allows CDCDt-M to remember colors from up to 512 frames, or clips, from previous captures. This research seeks to facilitate the utilization of videos captured using multiple cameras to exchange and combine color information, or 'browser-based video colorizing'. This application holds vast practical implications because it enables videos to be captured, processed, and analyzed without requiring consistency across cameras and clippings. Consequently, CDCDt-M is employed to colorize videos captured using cameras with distinct color properties in a recent study on browser-based video colorizing. This data augmentation technique, utilizing CDCDt-M to combine colors from multiple captures, surpasses baseline performance in evaluating videos captured using a single camera. To evaluate CDCDt's effectiveness in a theoretical framework, we test its capacity to learn generalizable principles from a diverse set of videos captured using cameras with varying color properties. This framework assesses CDCDt's performance across three dimensions: the number of clips used, the variability in color properties between clips, and the level of memorization required. This framework enables the evaluation of CDCDt's fundamental characteristics and surprising results show that CDCDt can excel in a single shot of a new capture, or 'new capture colorizing'. This capability holds substantial practical implications because it enables generalization across cameras capturing different content. Furthermore, we discovered that CDCDt can produce colors from a new capture simply by using correspondence information and incorporating the average of colors from the prior capture. This finding demonstrates the unsupervised nature of CDC

We examined the characteristics of seven gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) that had their lensing properties observed. To date, this is the largest collection of observed lensing data. We discovered that five out of eight bursts exhibit clear lensing effects, with the remaining three displaying tentative evidence of lensing. To further investigate the impact of these observations, we compared them to the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Interestingly, we found that the standard model failed to fully account for the lensing effects seen in eight bursts, with an average underprediction of $40\pm15$ percent. We also found that incorporating the observed lensing data led to a reduction in the probability that the universe is flat, with the probability dropping to $0.4\pm0.3$ percent when using the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, as compared to $2.8\pm1.1$ percent when using a non-flat $\Lambda$CDM model. Consequently, we determined that the observed lensing effects set a limit on the spatial curvature of the universe, with the radius of curvature required to fully explain the observed lensing effects measured as $4.1_{-1.0}^{+2.1}\times 10^5$ Mpc. We also discussed the implications of these findings for various types of spatial surfaces, with our analysis indicating that current observations of lensing effects reveal that the universe is likely to be flat, with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model failing to fully account for the observed lensing effects and indicating a preference for more lensing than the model predicts. Current collaborative filtering methods and aspect-based collaborative filtering methods have achieved significant improvements in precision and generalization. However, these algorithms often rely on pre-define domain knowledge and can be susceptible to data shortages, while users' diverse preferences span multiple interconnected domains. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework that captures complex user preferences across multiple interconnected domains with minimal pre-defined domain knowledge required. Utilizing an innovative comprehensive aspect preference learning technique from multi-domain user data, our system identifies interconnected domains and learns shared user preferences through collaborative information sharing. We further enhance data sparsity through domain cooperation and propose a novel ranking method that captures user interests across multiple interconnected domains. Experimental results demonstrate our framework surpasses several state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance and pre-defined domain knowledge requirements. We investigate this phenomenon in one dimensional interacting systems and find that it shares similarities with the random singlet phase observed in disordered chains of free fermions. In the free fermion case, this phase arises when the system is disconnected into isolated islands of connected states. These islands cannot be separated from each other because of entanglement present throughout. In the interacting system, we find that a wave function's properties can be described locally, devoid of non-local correlations. A significant concept in Artin Groups, known as the foundation theorem, has been generalized for the B-type Coxeter groups. This generalization was initially derived from the proof of monic Artin Group Symmetry by the first author. Additionally, this development led to the demonstration of Artin Group Symmetry in the specific case of B_n. Furthermore, this generalized foundation theorem was applied to establish a theorem relating to the characteristic polynomials of the groups. This characteristic polynomial theorem, initially conjectured by Kohel and fully proven by Patig, can now be derived directly from the generalized foundation theorem for B-type Artin Groups. This derivation is credited to the first author. Moreover, this generalized foundation theorem was employed to characterize the kernel of the map that sends B_n to its associated complex reflection group. This characterization is represented by the second author. Lastly, this generalized foundation theorem was utilized to establish an isomorphism between the algebraic closure of Q(B_n) and Q(G_m, G_l). This isomorphism is represented by the third author. We address this issue by developing a model that integrates various sources of information, including partially regulated data, to build a more comprehensive reward function. This model treats the expert's goals as a higher-level concept, represented by a hierarchical Bayesian model, which uses the learned parameters to calculate the probability of a reward function given an observation. We define strong small loop transfer domains relative to subgroups of fundamental groups and establish the relationship between these domains and the ramification index. This allows us to identify the exceptional value of the ramification index for such domains. Furthermore, we construct non-compact Riemann surface domains with specified properties and show that their strong small loop transfer domains correspond to a particular type of Riemann surface decomposition. To achieve this, we utilize techniques from complex analysis, metric geometry, and toplogy. Additionally, we explore the connection between our results and the theory of minimal surfaces. Conversely, we show that a certain class of Riemann surface decompositions can be realized as strong small loop transfer domains relative to subgroups of fundamental groups. This involves developing new metrics on these decomposed surfaces and establishing key properties, such as compatibility with the uniformization theorem. Ultimately, we establish a duality principle between the theories of strong small loop transfer domains and Riemann surface decompositions. This involves proving that every strong small loop transfer domain corresponds to a particular type of Riemann surface decomposition and vice versa. As a consequence, we characterize the metric on the universal cover of a strong small loop transfer domain as a certain type of Ahlfors regular metric. This relationship is initially expressed through the Pogorelov theorem, which establishes a connection between the surface's geometry and its connection to a certain type of Riemann surface decomposition. This result is further refined using the Monotonicity Equation technique from the work of Jost and Meersch, which allows us to show that a certain type of metric on the universal cover of a strong small loop transfer domain is a constant metric. This in turn enables the characterization of the surface's fundamental group and its realization as a certain type of minimal surface. This process ultimately yields insights into the surface's geometric and topological properties. This research is part of the author's Ph.D. thesis at the University of California, Berkeley, under the direction of Professor Richard Maschler. This work presents the main findings from the author's research. We also demonstrate the surface's connectivity using 2-singularities and show that a certain type of metric on the universal cover of a strong small loop transfer domain is a constant metric. We introduce a novel algorithm for control problems that leverages pre-trained deep reinforcement models. Unlike traditional end-to-end approaches, our method decouples policy and controller training, utilizing a preliminary stage that learns a general policy through random trajectory sampling. This policy is then utilized in the second stage to train a controller optimized using actual trajectory data, thereby enhancing its performance. Our method is validated on difficult control problems, namely a collection of 2D and 3D visual tasks and a set of challenging robotic manipulation tasks, achieving superior results when compared to existing reinforcement learning methods. Additionally, our approach allows for seamless integration with pre-trained tools, also known as 'tools learned in isolation' (TLI), dramatically reducing the number of training interactions required to obtain high-quality controllers. For example, in a robotic pushing task, we reduce sample complexity by a factor of 5.3 compared to traditional end-to-end RL methods. Our code and experiments are publicly available for evaluation purposes. This research was made possible through funding from BAE Systems and an Amazon Research Award. We express our gratitude to Jeremy Hilton and Andrew Geiger for their assistance with evaluating the proposed algorithm. This research is an advancement on our initial study, where we first demonstrated the two-staged decoupling of policy and controller training through random trajectory sampling. We have since refined the algorithm, replacing random trajectory sampling with guided sampling that utilizes actual data from the environment, thereby enhancing the overall performance. This revised two-staged decoupling algorithm serves as the basis for our recently published paper at IJCAI 2022. It represents an innovative approach for training controllers that are resilient to a wide range of disturbances, as demonstrated through evaluations on 4 aircraft systems and 4 humanoid robot systems. We have since incorporated the two-staged decoupling algorithm into a general-purpose tool for automatic policy and controller decoupling, thereby enabling seamless integration of our method with a variety of RL algorithms. This tool was independently evaluated by 7 researchers and shown to significantly outperform RL baselines in 28 evaluated scenarios. Furthermore, our method has enabled developers to achieve state-of-the-art results on the VizDoom game and has successfully trained a general policy for navigating 3D environments in the ViZDoom environment. We have also demonstrated that our method can train controllers and policies using natural language commands, thereby establishing a connection between RL and natural language processing. This research was funded through an Amazon Research Award. We have recently developed a novel algorithm for training general policies and controllers using natural language commands.

This series continues with an examination of the mechanisms that might have created (super)massive black holes weighing greater than 10,000 solar masses. This second paper presents new insights from two additional creation mechanisms, high-efficiency accretion and major mergers, with the aim of identifying the most effective process at producing (super)massive black holes. As a result, the global rate of (super)massive black hole creation has been determined, with the findings validated by two independent methods.  Consequently, this study has established a more accurate (super)massive black hole mass distribution over the redshift interval of 2-5. Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant transformation since their initial emergence in 1991. At their core, preprints embody the fundamental principles of the scientific enterprise by which researchers disseminate their preliminary findings and receive feedback from peers before official publication. Historically linked to and facilitated by print-based copies distributed among colleagues, the advent of the Information Age led to the creation of initial preprint servers such as arXiv, paving the way for a vast expansion of preprint dissemination. Today, a plethora of preprint servers and platforms host millions of scientific preprints, radically altering the traditional temporal and spatial dynamics of scientific communication. This review traces the evolution of preprints, focusing on key milestones, and examines current trends and the far-reaching implications of preprints for the future of scientific research and communication. Our analysis reveals that preprints have profoundly influenced modern science and will continue to shape the development of future research ecosystems, ultimately constituting a pivotal component of scientific knowledge production and dissemination. As such, preprints deserve greater recognition and support from research policies, institutions, and the scientific community. By promoting their adoption, researchers, researchers-in-training, and members of the scientific community can leverage preprints more effectively to achieve their individual and collective objectives, thereby promoting open and inclusive science. Ultimately, preprints hold the potential to revolutionize the traditional paradigm of scientific publication by empowering diverse communities and facilitating robust, collaborative knowledge production. To achieve this vision, it is imperative that scientific research and communication become online, open, and preprint-friendly. Online preprint services such as arXiv, DOAJ, PLOS, BioArxiv, medRxiv, and ResearchGate have contributed significantly to this goal by empowering researchers to disseminate their research independently and promote open science. By analyzing the last thirty years of preprint evolution and implementation, this review aims to inspire the scientific community to adopt a more preprint-centric approach to science communication and research production, thereby paving the way for a more inclusive and collaborative future research ecosystem. This paper introduces a cutting-edge method to create interactive online laboratory manuals, leveraging a unified framework that combines multiple tools already widely employed in the industry. By harnessing the capabilities of Git, GitHub, and Markdown, we devise a systematic, lazy approach to achieve this integration. As proof of concept, we demonstrate how this methodology can be effectively applied to reproduce a comprehensive online laboratory manual for a major university course. Furthermore, this method enables the automatic generation of HTML documents from Markdown source files, facilitating seamless collaboration among students and instructors. It also includes a comprehensive guide to utilizing the electronic laboratory journal, which can be easily adapted and utilized within various online courses. Additionally, we provide a live demonstration of the electronic laboratory journal, allowing for real-time interaction and testing. It should be noted that the source code for this journal is openly available on GitHub, thereby giving the community free access to reproduce and modify its source code. This allows users to contribute to the code and adapt it for their own purposes. Furthermore, we invite users to collaborate in enhancing and distributing this code, which can be achieved by cloning the repository and initiating changes, then submitting merge requests to share their modifications with the community. It is hoped that this electronic laboratory journal will facilitate the exchange of knowledge and experiences among users, ultimately benefiting the entire community. Although early studies found examples of nonlinear functions within the Slim Sidon set with specific properties, it remains challenging to find such examples with large dimensions. Thus, discovering examples of nonlinear functions within the Slim Sidon set, particularly for vectorial Boolean functions with large dimensions and characteristics other than permutation matrices, contributes to our understanding of nonlinearity. This article provides infinite examples of nonlinear vectorial Boolean functions with characteristics that enable high nonlinearity and places them in the Slim Sidon set with respect to a semilinear permutation matrix. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research, spanning various domains such as network analysis, spatial statistics, information retrieval, and bioinformatics. Researchers often employ uniform sampling methods on binary matrices to gather random datasets for comparative purposes or to test hypotheses. Despite the existence of such methods, there remains a gap in the literature for an efficient algorithm that can randomly sample a binary matrix while maintaining a fixed sum of elements. To address this void, we present a probabilistic algorithm that creates a binary matrix with a predetermined number of rows, columns, and a fixed total element count. Our approach ensures the generated matrices are uniformly distributed and independent. The algorithm's time complexity is directly proportional to the generated matrix's size, and it includes a dependent version for square matrices with a reduced time complexity. The code has been implemented and validated through numerous examples, and it is now available as open-source software. Additionally, we have developed a companion web application that enables users to easily generate binary matrices based on specified parameters. The software includes example usage guidelines and a detailed explanation of the algorithm. The proposed method can sample large binary matrices in memory-constrained environments, and it offers a compact, single-threaded implementation that outperforms multithreaded approaches, even for small matrix sizes. The algorithm's efficiency is attributed to the use of spread arrays, which allow for the efficient sampling of binary matrices, and a fixed-size cache for heap operations, which reduces memory usage and enables the sampling of large matrices. The underlying algorithm can be generalized to obtain non-uniform binary matrix samples by introducing a weight function that distributes elements equally across the matrix's diagonal. The modified algorithm includes a practical application in spatial statistics, and it can be further extended to support partial column duplication. The proposed method demonstrates excellence in various quantitative metrics, and it outperforms existing algorithms in terms of performance, especially for large matrix sizes. The sampling algorithm has numerous scientific and practical applications, and it can be effectively used for theoretical and experimental purposes. The main algorithm can be applied to obtain uniform binary matrix samples, and it includes a companion web application for easy usage and testing. The code has been successfully validated with numerous examples, and it outperforms existing solutions due to its efficient and generalizable approach. We develop a concept of complete conjugacy in the setting of infinite groups, which we use to investigate a particular type of random subgroup. Specifically, for an arbitrarily chosen finite subgroup, we define a probability measure that selects a subgroup within a fixed group G, and we establish conditions under which this subgroup is both invariant and "loyally" related to G. In doing so, we demonstrate that it satisfies certain properties, such as having a certain structure, and we provide an example to illustrate its non-trivial nature. We also prove that it shares certain characteristics with the original finite subgroup under specific conditions. Furthermore, we investigate its existence within the settings of free groups and surface group, and we propose a question to further extend our findings. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables to investigate how their distribution affects the neural network's learning dynamics. Since binary weights can only take on +/- value, their distribution is restricted to two possible states. Furthermore, the network's non-linear behavior is heavily influenced by its linear initialization, which in turn is determined by the weights' sign structure. Consequently, we observe that the flow of information throughout the network is governed by its first moment - the weights' distribution. When we apply the Neural-Tangent Kernel framework to analyze the learning dynamics, we find that the optimal regularization for binary weight networks arises from the weights' variance, or equivalently, their distribution's second moment. Moreover, we devise a novel approach to approximate the kernel's spectrum, which we use to investigate the relationship between the kernel's volume and generalizability. Through these theoretical contributions, we demonstrate that the kernel's volume optimality indeed underpins the benefits of binary weight quantization. This findings are further validated by our analysis of state-of-the-art binary neural networks, where we find that their generalizability can be entirely attributed to the kernel's volume optimality. Based on these insights, we propose a straightforward stopping criterion to determine the optimal quantization bit-depth for binary neural networks. The theoretical framework we've developed is the first of its kind to investigate the binary weight neural network's learning dynamics from an intrinsic perspective. It lays the foundation for further research into the intrinsic properties of binary weight networks, and their underlying learning dynamics. The key insights we've identified can also be leveraged to improve the design of binary neural networks. Furthermore, the theoretical results we've obtained can be employed to construct novel binary neural network architectures, and to develop new training algorithms that are tailored to their unique requirements. The behavior of a cell is influenced by its shape, which is regulated by specific molecular processes. Due to the complex and diverse forms of cells, generating synthetic cell shapes using physics-based methods or physics-inspired algorithms proves challenging. In this research, we demonstrate the effectiveness of using implicit neural networks to model the shapes of living cells, leveraging their ability to represent a wide range of complex geometries. By training neural networks on a dataset of cell shapes, obtained through manual segmentation of microscopy images, we enable the generation of synthetic cell shapes, which can then be used for testing cell behavior in controlled environments. The advantages of using implicit neural networks become apparent particularly in the modeling of cells undergoing rapid changes in shape. In comparison to other shape representation methods, implicit neural networks exhibit superior results, as measured by metrics such as Fr\'echet kernel embedding distances and the number of generated cells requiring intervention to avoid shape deformation. Researchers have proposed and tested various mental map theories,  including vector, gradient, and peacock metrics, to explain spatial information representation. A key idea behind these theories is that the system learns to prioritize relevant data features and filters out unnecessary ones. This concept parallels the goal of representation learning in machine learning, specifically self-supervised learning methods like contrastive learning. Building upon this idea, we explored whether incorporating reinforcement learning into this framework could improve the representation quality. Through simulations, we discovered that the integration of reinforcement learning significantly enhanced the performance of contrastive learning. This success inspired us to investigate whether similar improvements could be achieved in biological spatial representation theories. A potential mechanism for incorporating reinforcement learning into these theories is through a system of active exploration, where the agent learns to prioritize spatial predictions based on the relevance of its past experiences. To test this idea, we developed a simplified model of two spatial agents that learned to optimize each other's performance through a game-like dynamic. The integration of this active exploration mechanism led to a significant enhancement of the performance of the biologically-inspired models. The proposed dynamic models and the active exploration mechanism could facilitate further research into spatial representation learning in various contexts. Additionally, we proposed two new types of spatial models - the 'chase' model and the 'collaborative gradient model - that outperformed existing models and provided potential connections to the spatial cognitive mechanisms underlying humans' navigation abilities. The potential impact of these models was discussed in terms of future research directions and applications. Research into the links between distinct El Ni\~no flavors and global precipitation patterns has been conducted.
It was found that the distribution of very low and high seasonal precipitation around the world varies significantly in accordance with the type of El Ni\~no event occurring.
Previous studies often combined all El Ni\~no events as a single phenomenon, thus masking the unique impacts of each flavor on global precipitation.
Contrasting profiles of atmospheric anomalies were identified during El Ni\~no and La Ni\~no events, which have opposite signs but distinct spatial extensions.
The presence of a strong La Ni\~no event was found to increase the likelihood and severity of extreme precipitation in the UK, whereas El Ni\~no events have the opposite effect.
Analysis of long-term datasets revealed that each La Ni\~no event exhibits a distinct signature in the global precipitation patterns.
It was observed that high solar irradiance during La Ni\~no events may contribute to the disruption of the normal African Monsoon pattern, resulting in a reduction of rainfall in Africa, as opposed to El Ni\~no events which have the opposite effect.
The unique characteristics of each La Ni\~no event were found to significantly influence global precipitation patterns, thus making it crucial to consider these variations when modeling very low and high seasonal precipitation events.

The origins of massive black holes remain a subject of ongoing research, with various theories suggesting either primordial emergence from dense cosmological structures or more conservative views that massive black holes evolve within galaxy centers, fed by stellar feedback and feedback loops. Despite ongoing debates, a definitive answer has yet to be established. In this paper, we explore the relationship between massive black holes and their host galaxies, specifically examining the links between black hole mass and stellar mass, surface density, metallicity, and star formation patterns. By analyzing a relatively small sample of 12 galaxies, consisting of 7 unique systems, we aim to identify distinct patterns or groupings that may indicate particular massive black hole formation pathways. Although our data set is relatively limited, we find that the galaxy satellite galaxy system, Leo I and its companion, NGC 338, reveals anomalies in the standard massive black hole galaxy interactions chart. Furthermore, we propose that the distinctive properties of Leo I may represent a previously unrecognised group of massive black holes that originated from a system of accreted and dispersed galaxies. This finding suggests that the standard massive black hole galaxy interaction model may not adequately account for various galaxy merger scenarios. The implications of our data set are constrained by its small size and the limitations of our current understanding of massive black hole feedback. As our data set consists of two distinct groups of galaxies, primarily driven by systemic and hierarchical accretion, we encourage further research on the extensive database of observed galaxies to establish a more comprehensive understanding of massive black hole feedback. Ultimately, a more in-depth analysis of the massive black hole galaxy interaction dataset could potentially identify the necessary evidence to disprove or validate the hierarchical versus primordial massive black hole galaxy formation theories. In line with our expectations with hierarchical accretion, we predict that further observations will uncover massive black holes with lower surface densities, older ages, and less metal-rich galaxies. In contrast, if hierarchical accretion prevails, we anticipate that massive black holes will predominantly be found in galaxies with less metal-rich stars, while primordial massive black holes are more likely to be embedded within galaxies with higher metal content. This expected outcome may hold significant implications for the forecasting of dark matter structure on a cosmic scale. In this context, we suggest that the massive black holes within early galaxies may serve as reliable proxies for predicting other dark structured entities. Ultimately, the massive black holes within these galaxies may ultimately fade away, either by being expelled or by having their energy diminished as their host galaxies merge with larger systems. Specifically, it is found that the arrangement corresponding to a Severini-Steiner configuration is the only instance where the automorphism group is transitive on flags when the parameter r is greater than 1. By integrating this model with the Dyson series expansion, we obtain a closed-form expression for the atomic ground state. From this, we evaluate key properties, including the atomic energy, magnetic moment, and entropic measures. Notably, the Coulomb correlation model produces results for $n=1, 2, 3$ that align with established methods, and we use it to analyze how electronic confinement affects entropic measures. Employing this model, we evaluate energy expectations and entropies for hydrogen-like atoms with $Z=1, 2, 3$ under various types of confinement. Our findings indicate that electronic correlation within these atoms leads to decreased energy and entropy compared to the free particle case. Furthermore, the impact of electronic correlation on entropy is most pronounced for the dipole-disk hydrogen atom, and we demonstrate that confinement gives rise to non-zero magnetic moment for $n \geq 2$. Finally, the proposed model's results for entropy and magnetic moment are conducive to experimental verification. Notably, this study provides entropy estimates for the hydrogen and helium atoms that align with established methods, and we evaluate entropy as a function of confinement for these atoms as well as for the helium-like muonic hydrogen and positronium atoms, and discuss the implications of these results for the observation of quantum Coulomb correlation effects in low-energy entropy experiments. In particular, we propose that high-speed collisions between hydrogen-like ions provide a means of observing the Coulomb correlation effect, and estimate that this phenomenon could be observed in experiments involving ions with $Z \leq 10$ under conditions of strong and weak confinement. Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior data provided by advertisers, which can result in underperforming new advertisements that lack training data.  To address this, we focus on leveraging the visual elements of advertisements to update CTR predictions.  By utilizing a combination of natural language and vision capabilities, our model identifies which visual elements are most crucial for CTR and how to model them effectively.  Since the content of these visual elements is unstructured and highly varied, we employ a multi-modal learning approach, incorporating both vision and language abilities.  To capture the highly discriminative visual features, we also use a multi-scale vision network.  Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model yields a significant enhancement over current methods.  Specifically, compared to a leading CTR prediction model, our approach increases overall CTR by 11.0%, particularly excelling with new advertisements that were undervalued by up to 20.1%.  Furthermore, by analyzing our model, we uncover insights that can inform ad creation and improve CTR.  Interestingly, it's the the "shopping" and "text" categories that are most sensitive to visual elements.  Also, using our model, we identified the commonly used visual elements that are most predictive of CTR and found them to be predominantly icons, headlines, and top-product images.  These findings underscore the potential for using visual elements to better understand and optimize the CTR of advertisements. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a practical prediction method is needed to fill in the gaps and
correct errors by leveraging all available satellite data streams.
By incorporating physics-informed spectral convolutional neural networks (PIS-CNN), we can estimate AOD values by streamer-wise fusion of satellite data and streamer-wise correction of errors, including the use of historical AOD data.
Our method achieves high accuracy by comparing predicted values with ground-based measurements, demonstrating better performance than other methods, with improved root mean squared error (RMSE) and coefficient of determination (R-squared) values.
Additionally, PIS-CNN reduces the reliance of AOD prediction and prediction uncertainty estimation models on ground-based measurements, while also facilitating the integration of new satellite data streams and improved prediction performance with increased training data. Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
primarily driven by the widespread use of language blending among young people 
in social media and other online platforms. Despite its importance, processing 
code-mixed text remains a significant challenge. One major obstacle is the lack 
of effective methods for handling unknown language symbols. Current approaches 
either ignore this issue or treat unknown symbols as errors, which hinders text 
understanding. This paper introduces PESTO, an innovative model leveraging 
switching point detection to identify unknown symbols and apply appropriate 
encoding strategies, enhancing word representation quality. The model's adaptive 
and comparative positional encoding capabilities also enable improved performance. 
Experimental evaluations on various language pairs confirm PESTO's superiority, 
with notable gains of up to 3.5 NLU accuracy points and 8.2 F1 points for SRL. 
Additionally, PESTO exhibits notable success in zero-shot and multi-task settings. 
The model's source code is freely accessible on GitHub.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that a notable increase in the density of states at the Fermi level occurs at around 180 GPa, characterized by a van Hove singularity. We found that this enhancement triggers a significant rise in the isotope effect coefficient and critical temperature. Specifically, the critical temperature is seen to increase by 35% (from 6.9 K to 9.3 K) in response to a 70 GPa increase in pressure. Consequently, considering the density of states at the Fermi level, our calculated critical temperatures for H3S at 230 and 250 GPa (under conditions mimicking those in diamond anvil cells) align closely with experimental findings. Our study demonstrates that the van Hove singularity plays a crucial role in the superconducting properties of high-pressure hydrides. Additionally, to gain deeper insights into their behavior, we analyzed the superconducting gaps under pressure, revealing the presence of multiple gap components that vary as a function of pressure. Moreover, our findings show that the largest gap component exhibits a near-linear increase with pressure, while the density of states affects the relative sizes of gap components. Specifically, at high pressures (above 180 GPa), the largest gap component becomes the superconducting gap related to the S 3p-H 3s orbital. Our analysis also highlights that the isosymmetric structural transition (where all atoms remain in equivalent positions) does not significantly impact the relative sizes of gap components controlled by the density of states. However, it does affect the critical temperature, as observed at around 180 GPa. Consequently, their behavior should be analyzed thoroughly, taking into account both volume and density of states at the Fermi level. Fisher developed the fundamental concept of the average effect in his comprehensive analysis of multiple linear regression. This average effect measures the overall impact of a linear model's coefficients on a specific dependent variable. Building upon Fisher's work, I demonstrate that his average effect retains its significance as a statistical metric in the context of linear models employing standardized coefficients. Furthermore, I illustrate that this average effect maintains its importance as a causal indicator in linear models that incorporate standardized coefficients, such as in the case of multiple regression and partial regression coefficients. These findings confirm the causal significance of Fisher's average effect in the specified types of linear models. To address potential concerns, I also justify the use of standardized coefficients within these models, demonstrating their validity through reference to both classical concepts and modern axiomatic theories in probability and measurement theory. Alongside the reevaluation of Fisher's average effect, I also provide a clear definition of its counterpart, the average partial effect. In addition, I establish a pressing research challenge to develop an analogous mathematical treatment for nonlinear models, encompassing both the logistic and general linear causal models. Such an achievement would yield far-reaching applications in both statistical theory and the scientific investigation of causal relationships. Ultimately, this research aims to promote a deeper understanding of statistical theory through the integration of pure mathematical concepts and ongoing methodological developments in the field. This paper outlines our approach to developing efficient and reliable bipedal robots using thruster-assisted locomotion. By combining simulations and experimental testing of a bipedal robot equipped with a thruster, we have identified and validated strategies to improve its movement patterns. As bipedal robots navigate through diverse environments, they encounter a mix of challenges such as maintaining balance and generating forward momentum. Our research focuses on addressing these issues by exploring the potential benefits of thruster-assistance during walking. Specifically, we have investigated how thruster-support can affect a bipedal robot's ability to recover from disturbances and move at varying speeds. Through simulation and physical testing, we have found that thruster-assistance can substantially improve the robot's ability to recover from disturbances and optimize its movement patterns. Notably, we have observed a significant enhancement of the robot's ability to recover from disturbances of up to 240%, as well as a comparable reduction (40-50%) in the number of steps required to reach a target speed with thruster-assistance. These findings indicate that thruster-assistance can significantly impact a bipedal robot's ability to move efficiently and reliably. As such, we intend to further develop and refine our approaches to better understand the potential benefits of thruster-assistance during bipedal locomotion. Moreover, we plan to experiment with various designs for thrusters and actuation systems to identify the potential impacts of different configurations on the robot's performance. By combining our research outcomes with existing knowledge from control theory, we aim to establish a comprehensive framework for the optimal design, control, and operation of bipedal robots equipped with thrusters. Given the general applicability of our approach, we believe it has the potential to benefit the development of efficient and reliable bipedal robots across a range of environments and applications. Keywords: Bipedal robots, Thrusters, Locomotion, Motion planning, Robot control, Robot design.

By building on prior research that maps images to 3D surfel maps, we developed a more robust approach for visual relocalization. This approach, which supports geometrically uncertain 3D maps, relies on the learning of two distinct image descriptors: one that captures overall relational information and another that retains fine-grained details. Our method, which relies on this dual descriptor strategy, surpasses state-of-the-art approaches for image relocalization within a single view. Moreover, we extended existing surfel-based methods to support loop closure detection by incorporating an additional similarity metric that measures image-to-map similarities. As a result, we achieved state-of-the-art performance for loop closure detection using surfel maps. Our approach is also supportive of both monocular and stereo cameras. To validate its efficacy, we used real-world datasets, including KITTI datasets, to demonstrate its superiority over existing methods. To evaluate its geometric accuracy, we used metrics such as the mean absolute error (MAE) in pose estimation and the average symmetric difference (ASD) in map segmentation. Our results show that both localization and map segmentation performed accurately using our method. Federated learning has a built-in challenge of maintaining model consistency across clients with possible formulation variations. Besides, dataset imbalance among clients causes label distribution discrepancies, which complicates the issue. Semi-Supervised Learning has seen a resurgence with the advent of GAN-based models, but their consistency with the central server is hard to maintain due to possible data augmentation differences. This paper tackles the problem of minimizing ambiguity in decentralized semi-supervised learning by addressing three key challenges: (1) eliminating label ambiguities, (2) reducing inference ambiguities, and (3) clarifying class boundaries. We draw inspiration from the Prune-Average algorithm to develop a novel decentralized ambiguity minimization procedure. By analyzing the problem through a generalized loss function perspective, we employ a two-player game approach to find an optimal balance. PAMS brings about substantial improvements in classification performance on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, and sees notable gains when dealing with dataset imbalances. To identify patterns in hospital admissions and better plan for staffing and resources, 
we analyzed the average trajectories of patient arrivals and service durations in an emergency department.
By applying a multivariate parametric model, we estimated the probability distributions of patient visit intervals and service durations.
Our empirical analysis revealed distinct behaviors in patient visit intervals and service durations, which followed different distributions depending on the day of the week.
Notably, visit intervals were found to be dependent on the previous interval, whereas service durations were found to be independent.
We further analyzed the data to uncover consistent patterns in service duration trajectories and identified the underlying distribution functions for critical care and non-critical care areas.
Our findings provide a basis for developing simulation systems and strategic decision-making models to improve emergency department efficiency. Our method can also be applied to other service systems to uncover patterns in patient or job arrival and processing times.

In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordinating multiple tasks simultaneously can be crucial for complex missions. We investigate the implementation of two strategic multi-task synchronization algorithms over regular networks for robots with computational and communicational limitations. These algorithms distribute workload and synchronize interactions strategically to minimize communication demands and achieve the fastest possible processing speeds. We analyze the algorithms' performance by simulating variable communication delays and demonstrate their robustness and efficiency through experiments involving mobile robots. Results show that the proposed techniques not only require fewer communications but also allow tasks to be completed faster compared to a direct approach that involves frequent and distributed interactions. Additionally, these algorithms remain effective under delayed communication, outperforming a task-based approach in such scenarios. The performance of the interface between semiconductors and barriers is a critical factor in producing consistent output from atomic-thick atomic monolayer superconducting transducers. Although dry etching can cause damage to these interfaces, a study has shown the potential for using standard full 300mm CMOS processes to manufacture devices with high mobility. In experiments, devices with an undoped body and a gate stack consisting of spacer materials demonstrated exceptional electron mobility of around 10,000,000 cm^2/Vs. In addition to high mobility, these devices also displayed low gate resistance, relatively weak source-fanin resistance, and efficient current modulation, making them suitable for on-chip transducer applications. However, moderate performance was observed in devices with an LDD body design likely due to charge accumulation in the source and drain regions. In order to further improve performance, techniques such as work function engineering or floating gate modification may be employed to enhance mobility and reduce contact resistance. Overall, these findings indicate that high-quality MOSFETs with high mobility can be reliably manufactured using standard full 300mm CMOS processes. The potential integration of these MOSFETs with on-chip ellipsometers and spectrometers could enable high-quality MOSFET transducers to be produced efficiently. The observed mobility values are comparable to those previously reported in cryogenic quantum circuit components, indicating the potential for high-mobility MOSFETs to be used in quantum computers and other applications. The data collected also identified several full 300mm CMOS process parameters that significantly impact mobility and resistance. Based on the data, threshold voltage, gate length, and channel width influenced mobility, while source and drain resistance, coupled with interface trap density, affected mobility and current modulation. The data further demonstrated that high-mobility devices can be efficiently manufactured using short gate lengths, narrow channels, and higher doped substrates. The observed mobility and resistance trends are consistent with theoretical models and can be readily optimized through further adjustments to the CMOS process design. The advancements in high-mobility MOSFETs could contribute to the development of high-performance and efficient quantum computers. The study also proposed an alternative definition for mobility that is applicable in real-world circuits and is resistant to short-channel effects. To conduct fair video search outcomes, it is crucial to consider the range of video sources available. However, it has been observed in prior research that underrepresented sources, such as videos created by individuals with disabilities, are often overlooked. A possible explanation for this phenomenon could be due to source bias, where search results favor videos from well-represented sources. To examine and rectify this issue, a method employing a range of synthetic characters mimicking real human search queries is proposed. This approach enables the assessment of source diversity bias in video search outcomes and identifies videos that were previously overlooked. By utilizing the scores assigned to each video source by the characters, a quantitative metric called the source variety score is calculated. An analysis on a large dataset revealed that many video sharing platforms struggle with variety bias. Moreover, it was discovered that videos promoting inclusive culture are frequently overlooked. Additionally, it was found that videos promoting disability awareness are frequently favored over disability-specific videos. Our findings and method contribute to a deeper comprehension of source variety bias and offer a straightforward solution for enhancing the diversity of video sharing platforms. In a test of the breaking of supersymmetry, we investigate the violation of monodromy in the Wess-Zumino model by employing a bootstrap technique. We find that violation of monodromy can occur for any number of supersymmetries and that a critical parameter value marks the transition from conservative to destructive behavior. A critical exponent governs the behavior change and its value can be determined through either analytical methods or numerical analysis. Moreover, we find that bootstrapping gives us access to information beyond that provided by monodromy. Specifically, we derive a precise limit on the growth of two-point functions, a limit that is influenced by the critical exponent and is dependent on the number of supersymmetries. Moreover, we find that this growth limit can be reached, and the rate at which it is approached can be determined through an iterative process. Furthermore, we find that our results are consistent with physical expectations when we consider the limit of zero supersymmetry and that a critical power law governs the behavior of a specific Wess-Zumino model partner, a model which features a critical exponent of three-fourths. Finally, we believe that the violation of monodromy, now demonstrated in a supersymmetric model,, will have far-reaching impacts on the way we understand physical systems and will likely lead to new discoveries. Additionally, this point $P$ is a rational point in the curve $E$ defined over the small field $K$ of degree 3. It's worth noting that such a point $P$ cannot exist in curves $E$ defined over the rational field $\mathbb{Q}$ or its finite extensions. This result is obtained by computing the action of Galois representations on curves with large ranks and extensive computational methods using arithmetic on curves. Interestingly, our findings show that points with ranks of 13 and 14 can exist in extension fields of degree at most 9, even though these ranks cannot occur in the original rational field $\mathbb{Q}$. This discovery highlights the significance of exploring non-trivial extensions of fields to analyze curves with large ranks. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the interference connections resulting from this probabilistic approach are always non-directional, symmetric, and probabilistically bi- directional. Furthermore, it is established that a random medium access mechanism can give rise to a connected underlying graph in wireless networks with limited node density. Moreover, it is shown that the probabilistic model can be utilized to develop algorithms for constructing spanner graphs and approximate shortest paths in ad-hoc networks. Additionally, this research provides statistical measures to gauge the reliability of connections in wireless networks and proposes a metric for assessing path reliability. Notably, it is observed that the proposed approach can be used to develop robust algorithms for the minimum-energy path problem, demonstrating that a reliable wireless connection exists between any pair of nodes. Finally, this research explores the connection between the probabilistic model and subgraph principles of wireless interference. Overall, this research delves into the probabilistic origins and characteristics of wireless interference, offering a probabilistic framework for tackling various problems in ad-hoc networks. Pseudo-labeling is a popular semi-supervised technique that generates informative pseudo tags for limited data. To address these limitations, we introduce Informative Pseudo-Tagging for GNNs, a novel framework that optimizes pseudo labels and reduces their uncertainty. Our approach incorporates a graph semantic generator to create diverse pseudo tags and an uncertainty estimator to filter unreliable labels during training. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, with notable improvements over existing baselines on standard datasets, such as the Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed-DD datasets. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method, focusing on its connection to label propagation and reliability. To showcase the applicability of our approach to real-world scenarios, we present an application case involving the recommendation of graph-based semantic entities.
