This corresponds to examining the linearized Hamiltonian of the system under mechanical linearization. The analysis demonstrates that microwave optomechanics is consistently modeled through three key components: a massive mechanical oscillator, a counter-rotating wave approximation for optical oscillators, and properly defined coupling and driving mechanisms. Furthermore, we show that a wide range of microwave optomechanical models have already been inherently circuit-compatible. These models include systems with optical oscillators of any degree of anharmonicity, as well as additional degrees of freedom, by means of either internal or externally coupled interactions. The validity of this circuit-based approach is verified through detailed analysis of the optical spectrum, mechanical oscillation spectra, and the behavior of back-action forces. Ultimately, this method enables the utilization of established circuit-theoretic methods for investigating optomechanical dynamics. It allows the evaluation of optomechanical performance based on circuit principles, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of optomechanical systems. with a focus on specific combinatorial aspects and the infinite divide property. 
It's proven that for any k, a particular class of semorbid colorings has a related 
generalized Airy polynomial sequence, which shares many characteristics with the 
standard Airy polynomials but may lack real roots. Additionally, it's shown that 
these polynomials are well-suited to define a symmetric, infinite Toeplitz matrix 
and that the resulting determinant exhibits a notable expansion in terms of 
monic generalized Airy polynomials, which in turn, relates to a specific class of 
semorbid colorings called cacti. This relationship is shown to hold for any 
k, extending a prior result that held only for k=1. This paper also delves into the 
morphism from cacti to Dyck paths, which is known to be an order-preserving 
bijective function, and presents a novel proof using the concept of 'cuts'. 
Finally, several specific families of generalized Airy polynomials are presented, 
which are related to well-studied classes of permutations, such as Skolem sequences, 
via a previously unrecognized pattern, which is itself a result of a broader set 
of properties in play, which are tied to the properties of a specific type of 
binary tree called a q-q prefix tree. This work was a result of a research project 
in the fall of 2021, guided by the paper 'Recent results in the theory of alternating permutations' by Proctor, Haddley and Chan.

Laparoscopic surgery has become a common practice, allowing surgeons to visually track abdominal organs from an external perspective.
The development of enhanced visual assistance has significantly improved surgical precision, albeit with increased costs.
Previous research revealed that smoke during surgery could cause laparoscopic image distortion, hindering surgical visibility.
In an effort to minimize costs associated with advanced technology, we investigated whether standard image processing methods could benefit smoke detection in laparoscopic videos.
These videos are publicly accessible through the CSUR platform, providing raw and filtered images that can be used to evaluate the effect of smoke influence.
By applying different image processing techniques to the CSUR dataset, we determined which filters benefit smoke detection, ultimately aiming to reduce the need for high-cost surgical assistants. 
The results showed that certain image processing techniques can be beneficial in finding smoke during surgery, suggesting that standard image processing methods could also be useful in other laparoscopic video applications. 
The code for our project is openly available on GitHub.

A recent approach to developing and analyzing optimization methods relies on empirical risk minimization, typically employing heavy-tailed loss functions and robust gradient methods. Our work presents an alternative average-case optimization challenge where we seek the most accurate parameter estimation with minimal assumption on the objective function. We demonstrate that standard gradient-based methods can achieve exceptional performance when the distribution of data points has significantly reduced tails. From an algorithmic perspective, our work introduces a new family of full-blade optimization methods that can tackle complex non-convex objectives efficiently. We show that these methods can successfully solve the optimization problem in the convex regime, outperforming existing solutions by a significant margin when the distribution has minimal outliers. We test the performance of these methods through rigorous experiments, comparing them to other popular algorithms, and find that they display remarkable resilience to changes in the distribution's tails. To validate the average-case analysis, we develop a novel process for estimating the number of significant data points, and we propose a Tail-Sensitivity Procedure that can accurately detect the presence of outliers. Our work ultimately presents a novel framework for full-blade optimization, and we hope that our approach will contribute to the development of more robust and universal optimization algorithms. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Moreover, as the tool can generate proofs in $\LaTeX$ or PDF, it allows educators to create printed syllabi containing visual representations of the proofs, thereby making it easier for students to review these proofs during office hours or when access to digital resources is restricted. Furthermore, this system caters to reviewers' needs by providing a summary of the proofs in visual form, which can aid reviewers in comprehending the proofs more effectively. As an added feature, when reviewers encounter obstacles in understanding the proofs, they can interact with the visual representation by clicking on a particular line or section, which will automatically highlight the corresponding line in the proof script, thereby granting access to contextual metadata. By doing so, this system emulates the functionality of integrated development environments (IDEs) and visualizers commonly used for programming purposes. Moreover, the tool's generator is language-agnostic, meaning it can visualize proofs written in various versions of Coq and support multiple review and learning scenarios. However, the tool exhibits some notable limitations: it is confined to evaluating the correctness of proofs constructed using sound typing; it is incapable of evaluating the correctness of proofs constructed using heterogeneous lists; it is unable to visualize proofs that incorporate external modules or programs; and it does not generate visual representations for goals that are yet to be achieved. Despite these limitations, the tool showcases that visual representations of proof scripts can serve as an accurate and robust means of evaluating correctness, as evidenced by our pilot test of reviewing a proof involving a significant mathematical concept. Based on the encouraging outcomes of this test, we propose to expand the tool to facilitate learning and proof review in various areas of mathematics and programming, thereby making it a valuable resource for the broader community. Additionally, we plan to augment the tool with capabilities that enable reviewers to submit their own visual representations of proofs, thereby creating a comprehensive database of visual proofs that can be accessed through a web interface. This will effectively empower the research community with an additional means of promoting, disseminating, and sharing evidence, thereby expanding the tool's existing functionality. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited by the expression $\exp\left[A_4+\varepsilon\right]$ and establish the best possible limit with the prior work of Iwaniec, Liu, and Zhou. Our investigation involves exploring the properties of the non-negative coefficients of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms and employing the Chowla conjecture, in addition to applying other significant results, such as Deligne's conjecture and Sato-Tate conjecture, to achieve our goal. Furthermore, our reasoning enables the quantification of the given limit, allowing for the assessment of the impact of $L$-functions at their critical values on the holomorphic Hecke cusp forms in question. It is worth noting that our proof requires only basic knowledge beyond standard undergraduate mathematics. We make generous assumptions about the existence of novel geometric analytic tools, as well as the generalization of the Chowla conjecture to multiple primes, which my research partner and I previously proposed as the "Multiplicative Case of the Chowla Conjecture." Our investigation also reveals a notable connection between the behavior of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms and the characteristics of abelian varieties, which gives rise to several significant hypotheses, such as the "Abelian Reciprocity Conjecture," as well as the "Prime Pseudorandomness Conjecture" of myself and my research partner. We presented these proposals at the 2019 Harvard Number Theory Seminar, where they sparked significant discussion. Our work also offers an innovative approach to evaluating the influence of $L$-functions on the holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, which can potentially be generalized to the study of other orthogonal and unitary Hecke cusp forms, as well as other categories of automorphic forms. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that the limit of the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms can be determined using the mathematical framework of high weight and deep level forms, which is an intriguing aspect of the subject. We provide an appendix that outlines the generalization of our investigation to other types of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, which can potentially be further generalized to the study of non-holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, as well as other categories of automorphic forms, while also exploring the abelian varieties angle of the problem. We offer an introduction to the abelian varieties aspect of our investigation in section 3 and conclude with a comprehensive summary in the conclusion. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently result in excessive post-solving iterations to achieve sufficient precision for IPMs. This excess can be eliminated by introducing a new halt condition for Krylov solvers, directly taking into account the IPM's tolerance, and this modification has been successfully implemented within an IPM framework. Comprehensive numerical tests have shown that the implementation remains competitive with established benchmarks in terms of efficiency. Additionally, the methodology has been incorporated into an open-source IPM code available on GitHub. This study's findings have been presented at WOPPAM 2021. Further details can be found in a longer report filed with the University of Wisconsin-Madison under reference ARQ-2021-02. It is also planned to be published in a technical report. A recent breakthrough utilizes the Gardner-Redlich-Scharf method to integrate RG concepts into neural network training, allowing the RG process to be mapped onto a gradient flow in the neural network's parameter space. Building upon this innovation, we develop a novel algorithm combining RG techniques with gradient descent. This new method enables the removal of artificial barriers that may guide neural network training towards low-energy fixed points, while still ensuring the emergence of an effective low-energy theory. Moreover, we find that it naturally introduces a form of regularization, as parameters become less sensitive towards low-energy scales. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this new algorithm through simple numerical examples. Furthermore, we propose a valuable method for analyzing the RG flow dynamics of complex neural network models based on their low-energy fixed points. This approach involves constructing a portrait of the RG flow landscape by sampling high-dimensional parameter spaces, allowing for deeper insights into the RG process. We find that this technique provides valuable semantic information, enabling the deciphering of the RG flow's course. We also discover that the low-energy fixed points of complex neural network models are typically characterized by mild (analytically tractable) transitions. Additionally, we introduce a novel testing ground for evaluating the reliability of neural network-based RG procedures. This challenge involves developing low-energy and high-energy neural networks that are in agreement with each other, while the initial and final parameter sets are also congruent. We find that our new algorithm allows for the successful resolution of this puzzle. We provide extensive numerical demonstrations of our algorithm's effectiveness, along with the relevant code accessible through a public GitHub repository. Lastly, we suggest potential future applications and extensions of our algorithm, integrating the RG techniques with emerging methods in neural network embedding and multiple-time-scale modeling. These potential future developments could lead to breakthroughs in neural network-based RG procedures. We envision significant potential in utilizing neural networks for approximating low-energy QFT fixed points. However, we acknowledge that deep neural networks may not be sufficiently versatile to accurately replicate the QFT dynamics, particularly towards very low scales. We propose supplementing shallow neural networks with physical insights from QFT to bridge the gap with numerical QFT results. We envision that neural networks can serve as effective bridges between non-perturbative QFT and numerical QFT. We present a plan for future research aimed at realizing this goal. We anticipate that shallow neural networks can be trained to accurately mimic low-energy QFT behavior by incorporating physical insights from QFT, thereby complementing numerical QFT and furnishing new insights into QFT fixed points. This work establishes a unified framework for analyzing and evaluating hybrid process models, which are represented through high-level Petri nets. To do this, we define a formal language that encompasses constraints for net modifications and develop an automated method for generating finite-state machines from these constraints. These machines are then used to create monitors for enforcing net modifications and optimizing the monotonous changes in a net's markings. Specifically, the optimal strategy for net modifications ensures that only the most efficient transitions are enabled, while optimized monotonous changes help reduce unnecessary net modifications. Our approach is evaluated through a combination of theoretical and experimental analyses of its time and space complexities. To validate the efficacy of our method, we performed a set of experiments that demonstrated a significant reduction in computation time for averaging 57% and individual samples 75% in specific hybrid process scenarios. Additionally, we compared our approach with other automatic and semi-automatic monitoring methods on a set of 50 nets and found that it provided the fastest average computation time and the highest success rate (up to 97%) for optimizing net modifications. Further studies are needed to investigate other automatic monitoring methods and evaluate their performance relative to our monitor. The proposed monitoring method has been implemented and made available for public use under the LGPL license on GitHub. It also includes a Python interface for interacting with the DynIPer tool, which can import and evaluate Petri nets with specific attributes. The code also includes additional tools, such as DynIPer's GUI for visualizing nets and their optimal modifications, and IPER3, which provides a net-based interface for analyzing and optimizing hybrid process models. Both DynIPer and IPER3 are compatible with the proposed monitoring method and can be used in conjunction with each other for further analysis. A detailed evaluation of our approach is also provided, which compares the performance of our monitor with other automatic and semi-automatic monitoring methods on a set of 50 nets and reveals that it offers the best overall results. The Proto-Quipper framework serves as a tool for developing quantum algorithms, utilizing a quantum-specific extension of Haskell to make the translation process more straightforward. The advantages of high-level programming become more pronounced when implementing complex algorithms, and by keeping close to existing Haskell code, it becomes easier to integrate classical and quantum data types. However, the original Proto-Quip semantics, introduced using a categorical model, pose difficulties for program verification due to the lack of a clear framework for reasoning about quantum algorithms. In response, we introduce a new specification language, AQPM, designed to model quantum algorithms at a higher level of abstraction, using a type system based on first-order logic with inductive and functional types. By incorporating principles from functional programming, AQPM provides a more expressive framework for specifying quantum algorithms, enabling the incorporation of fundamental logical operators and enabling the specification of algorithms based on specific applications. We demonstrate the compatibility of AQPM with the existing Proto-Quip semantics, highlighting the way AQPM types correspond to categorical types and reflecting the structure of quantum circuits. We verify a key theorem relating AQPM types to correct quantum operations, offering a framework for reasoning about quantum algorithms. By integrating AQPM into a interactive proof system, IQPM, we can perform sound program verification for a quantum-specific extension of Haskell, using AQPM as a specification language to model the translation of quantum algorithms into Proto-Quip, and leverage the existing Proto-Quip semantics to provide a denotational model for AQPM, facilitating the verification of quantum algorithms within a high-level specification framework. This allows for the verification of algorithms originally designed within Haskell to ensure they produce correct outcomes, and provides a way to ensure that quantum algorithms compile correctly into Proto-Quip. As an example, we verify a simplified version of Shor's algorithm using IQPM. This approach provides a framework for performing algorithmic verification in quantum programming, and provides a specification language and interactive proof tool for evaluating the correctness of quantum algorithms. Further work could be directed at expanding the capabilities of IQPM to accommodate more interactive evidence and incorporate more techniques from predicate logic, as well as applying IQPM to verify specific quantum algorithms. Additionally, the integration of AQPM could provide an expressive framework for specifying and automatically generating quantum circuits based on logical proofs in quantum applications. This could offer a more efficient alternative to current direct compilation methods between Proto-Quip and quantum circuits, and enable the specification of multiple high-level quantum algorithms. We suggest creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of neutral atoms with magnetic properties, which are trapped in an optical cavity with a thin-walled mirror. To achieve this, we use a specific light field that produces coherent population transfer, resulting in pairs of atoms released from the cavity when the light is switched off. To measure the phase of this light, we use a parameter that indicates when the atoms interact with the light, which can be increased through a process that compresses the energy within the atoms, making the effect of the light on the atoms easier to measure. This process, called squeezing, is crucial for measuring the phase and can be increased to the point where a single released atom can be used to measure the phase. We use mathematical models to predict how well the system can be compressed and to estimate the minimum amount of energy within the atoms, which is related to the phase measurement accuracy. Our results show that it may be possible to measure phases close to $180^\circ$ with around a thousand atoms, which could be increased to nearly $360^\circ$ with tens of thousands of atoms. To experimentally verify our predictions, we plan to use a setup that is similar in design to the one proposed here. To demonstrate the feasibility of our idea, we present data that shows population modulation, which is a step towards achieving bosonic pair generation and improving the measurement of optical phases. However, the current population modulation method lacks persistence, which means it does not appear in the final population distribution after the atoms are released from the cavity. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative method that can be used to measure the phase before releasing the atoms from the cavity. This method requires modifying the cavity with additional materials that have strong interactions with the atoms and can be modeled using quantum key distribution protocols to estimate the phase. Our suggestions demonstrate that it may be possible to achieve robust bosonic pair generation and improve the measurement of optical phases in systems with long-lived interactions. To demonstrate the feasibility of our idea, we present data that shows a persistent modulation pattern using our proposed method. This research can be further developed to explore the intersection of fundamental principles and cutting-edge technologies in quantum key distribution, bosonic pair generation, and optical phase measurements. One potential application of our research could be the development of a persistent bosonic key for distributing phases in applications like quantum computing, where a stable connection to the phase is required to perform certain tasks efficiently. Additionally, our suggestions can be used to develop a persistent bosonic signal for phase measurements in experiments that require a stable phase

Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrix operations to efficiently create continuous DNA sequence intervals within a chromosomal region. By partitioning a weighted directed graph into subgraphs across multiple processes, this method effectively assigns and computes interval lengths on each process without the need for global synchronization. We evaluate the performance of our approach using real-world genomes and diverse machine architectures, achieving an average speedup of 4.6 times on 64 threads for the largest genome tested. Furthermore, our method demonstrates excellent assemble-long-reads scalability and stability, surpassing existing techniques in terms of performance and consistency. The proposed algorithm remains adaptable to varying genome sizes and architectures, ensuring efficient assembly results for genomes of any size when employed on high-performance computing systems. The code is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/grasp-ipl/CLARA. Additionally, the comprehensive benchmark results can be found on the GRASP-ipl GitHub at https://github.com/grasp-ipl/benchmark-CLR. The benchmark dataset can also be obtained through NCBI's BioTools at https://btool.org/tool/copy?tool=assemble-long-reads. The equation features a delayed Ricker response, where the nonlinearity is displaced due to cell division habits. It's observed that this nonlinearity occurs asynchronously, leading to a distinct nonlocal influence in population dynamics. The investigation involves establishing equations for the fixed points and stability assessment, particularly focusing on the critical threshold $\frac{ab}{4}$. When $\frac{ab}{4}$ serves as a Lipschitz constant for the mapping, we determine the fixed point and examine local stability in the vicinity of this constant. However, when $\frac{ab}{4}$ functions as an eigenvalue for the linearized system, a cobweb diagram illustrates periodic behavior, with the sequence $\{y_k\}$ converging to a periodic orbit. Building on this, a mapping-based approach helps identify conditions for the occurrence of periodic, semiperiodic, and chaotic behavior in various scenarios. Ultimately, a condition linked to the product $bc$ plays a crucial role in differentiating the global dynamics of the given equation from those of the standard logistic equation. Additionally, the study highlights the practical implications of nonlocal influences in modeling cell populations that exhibit delayed responses. To support these findings, the analysis is accompanied by numerical examples, along with corresponding graphical representations, that demonstrate how different parameters affect global dynamics and create varying phases for population dynamics. The concept of statistical depth has been developed to provide a minimum and maximum measure of point processes, essential for defining order statistics and quantiles. However, existing methods lack robustness against changes in process dimensions. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new point process depth based on the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation, which maintains a constant distance between processes while allowing the evaluation of depth along process trajectories. Our technique effectively prevents the influence of process scaling on the depth calculation, producing an unbiased metric. To achieve this goal, we utilize the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation to map the process into a fixed, finite-dimensional space where the distance between processes remains consistent. Based on this framework, we propose a new method for computing the depth of functional time series processes, which we evaluate using synthetic examples and real-world data from applications involving functional regression and time series forecasting. Further, we extend our approach to define order statistics and quantiles for functional time series processes. Our study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method in estimating these parameters compared to existing techniques. The methods presented in this work have been made available on the RCRfts package for functional regression analysis. The Isometric Log-Ratio transformation was initially presented in the paper titled "Isometric Log-Ratio: A Transform for Compositional Data Analysis" by Azimonti et al., which can be downloaded from arxiv.org/abs/1803.05191. The application of this transform to the analysis of functional time series processes is presented in the paper titled "Functional Time Series Classification and Regression with the Isometric Log-Ratio Transform" by Azimonti et al., which can be downloaded from arxiv.org/abs/2005.06842. The RCRfts package was initially presented in the paper titled "Functional Regression Models: A Review on the JMLR 2020 Special, Volume 2" by Azimonti et al., which can be downloaded from arxiv.org/abs/2006.16777. This package provides functions for computing the Isometric Log-Ratio transform, conditional functional regression models, and predictive intervals. It also includes methods for a novel conditional functional linear regression model based on the Conditional Variance Decomposition framework and demonstrates the effectiveness of these models in predicting relevant variables based on available data. Additionally, this technology offers the promise of reliable and efficient hybridizations that can be widely applied in the development of ideal hybrid machines. It is also possible that this hybrid concept will be useful in the generation of quantum motors. The focus of the investigation is on nuclear properties of germanium isotopes, specifically those near $N$ = 40.  Past studies on this region have revealed a pronounced shell closure effect at $N$ = 40, however the present research considers only the central part of the shell closure.  Notably, the study found that the mean $N$ = 40 closure effect across the germanium chain was confined to a relatively narrow range of $A$ = 66-74.  The study further observes that the extent of closure effect increases in a direct, linear correlation with the two-proton $rp$-reaction cross section.  The investigation also found that the angular distribution of the $^{42}$K+$^{66}$Ga reaction, occurring at an energy of 990 keV, exhibited a sudden shift of 180 degrees at an angle of approximately 90 degrees.  This notable phenomenon is attributed to the presence of a near-resonant $^{67}$Ge state at an energy of 166 keV, which is modulated by a mixture of direct and indirect reaction mechanisms.  The study also discovered new isotopes of germanium, namely ^{58}Ge and ^{78}Ge, and further updated existing germanium mass measurement data, thereby establishing a set of reliable nuclear mass measurements.  Additionally, the research considers several aspects of germanium nuclear properties, including magnetic moments, nuclear radii, and specific properties near the $N$ = 40 shell closure. The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand radio sources and improve our knowledge of large-scale structure. Recently releasing its first data, which covers 175 square degrees, the survey allows us to analyze nearly 9,000 radio galaxies between 200 MHz and 350 MHz. By using these galaxies as probes, we examined the large-scale structure of the Universe and obtained valuable insights. To start with, we confirmed that these galaxies follow the typical distribution of galaxy power spectra on large scales, with an average amplitude that increases with their brightness. Additionally, we found that the brightest galaxies have a higher average redshift, which means they are more distant than their less bright counterparts. By comparing the LoTAR survey's data to simulated observations, we established that the LoTAR galaxies follow the expected biasing pattern. Consistently with previous surveys, we found that the biasing pattern changes depending on the galaxies' brightness, and we found that the smallest galaxies show an increased deviation from the typical biasing pattern. Finally, we found that there are indications of a non-random distribution of the surveyed galaxies on a 75-halo-by-75-halo grid, which was analyzed through a 2D Fourier interpolation, and this needs to be confirmed by further surveys. Future data releases will allow us to decrease the uncertainty and confirm whether the typical biasing pattern changes significantly at higher galaxy brightnesses. Meanwhile, the LoTAR survey's data is already providing substantial insights into the large-scale structure of the Universe and will continue to do so as it progresses. Furthermore, our findings and methodologies offer valuable insights for the broader machine learning community. We've extended the concept of asymptotically flat black holes with holographic scalar clouds to include a new type of object - asymptotically flat hairy dark stars. These dark stars are derived from a stationary, spherical, and spherically symmetric setup in a classical Einstein-Dirac-Burgers theory. By iteratively solving a non-linear set of equations involving an effective potential, we can determine a profile for the scalar field, after which we can reconstruct the metric using the Einstein-Dirac-Burgers-Jacobson equation. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions, it's possible to prevent a black hole from forming and create a star-like structure instead. This phase transition from a black hole to a star is driven solely by the interaction between the metric and the quantum field, and it's characterized by a specific threshold for the quantum field's amplitude. For initial holographic cloud cases, we've observed that this threshold is directly linked to the AdS radius, whereas for core collapse cases, it's instead determined by the local maximum of the potential where the scalar field begins to develop. By altering the parameters in our theory, it's possible to change the mass of the resulting dark star, and even cause it to exhibit thermodynamic properties such as an increase in temperature with respect to entropy. Finally, we've identified a set of conditions under which it's feasible to accurately model the behavior of these hairy dark stars using effective field theories. However, for cases involving shorter-wavelength scalar fields, we've found that the resulting objects can't be captured by simple effective models. Rather, we've observed that the resulting holographic scalar clouds can lead to a misinterpretation of the behavior of these sources in terms of their coupling to gauge fields. This could potentially have broader implications for our understanding of compact objects in general. Through this work, we've opened up a new realm of asymptotically flat hairy hydrodynamic objects and have suggested a fresh perspective on compact object physics - one in which quantum matter plays a central role in shaping the metric, and where stationary states can give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena. Furthermore, we've identified numerous unanswered questions surrounding the thermodynamic consistency of these objects, as well as the behavior of their sources, and have suggested several areas for further investigation. It's possible that the asymptotically flat hairy dark stars we've created can serve as a starting point for further research into more general scenarios, such as phase transitions in compact objects, and potentially even gravitational wave signals of interest to astronomers. Different genes exhibit varying speeds of transcription. Some genes encode proteins crucial for cell cycle regulation, yet the relationship between their expression patterns and cell cycle behavior remains unclear. By leveraging single-molecule RNA sequencing data from multiple cell types at different stages of the cell cycle, researchers discovered patterns of RNA production delays. These patterns provide crucial insights into the mechanisms of transcription regulation and suggest a model where rapid changes in gene expression are primarily achieved through alterations in RNA processing rather than the duration of transcription. The findings also reveal the importance of transcriptional control in maintaining stable equilibria of gene expression across the cell cycle. The data, along with the development of the TRANS-CycLE model, opens up new avenues for the application of systems biology to the analysis of cellular processes. The TRANS-CycLE model enables the prediction of transcription dynamics from genomic DNA sequences, enabling the identification of functional non-coding regions and the calculation of the probability of changes in gene expression being caused by mutations in the human genome. The data also enables the classification of transcription factors with high accuracy based on their capacity to influence gene expression rapidly or slowly. The research further validates the hypothesis that the rapid activation of a group of developmental genes during the G1 phase of the cell cycle is crucial for cell cycle progression, as supported by both the analysis of RNA production delays and the examination of single molecules in live cells. The study demonstrates that the manipulation of RNA production delays offers a significant avenue for the control of gene expression and highlights key areas for the further investigation of the biological mechanisms governing rapid changes in gene expression. Researchers proposed a novel approach for creating efficient RNNs by introducing random connections,
which lead to faster learning times on individual cognitive tasks. Although this method yields
positive results, it still relies on task-specific parameters, which can be chosen arbitrarily.
In this study, we introduce the concept of fixed and sparse random neural networks (FS-RNNs),
where random connections are applied without regard to task types. We demonstrate that FS-RNNs
can be trained efficiently and achieve faster learning times on a wide range of cognitive tasks.

models, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluations on one-shot learning, navigation,
probability distribution learning, and dynamic decision-making tasks. Consequently, FS-RNNs present
a promising solution for creating efficient and practical cognitive models. Related code can be accessed at

Global averaging techniques, such as average pooling and global average pooling, are often employed in neural networks to reduce the dimensionality of data and prevent overfitting. Historically, their effectiveness has been attributed to the global translational symmetry of the input data. This notion is reexamined in the light of optimal transport theory, which reveals a distinct connection between these methods and the OT solution. Consequently, it is demonstrated that two-sided OT leads to an overestimation of the target's average, whereas one-sided OT corresponds to a biased OT solution. This OT framework interpretation imposes limitations on the use of global averaging methods for breaking translational symmetries in neural networks. Specifically, one-sided OT cannot be applied to groups larger than size two. As a result, the application of global averaging operators to overcome translational biases in image classification is discouraged in favor of more robust methods such as S4D convolutional networks and biased OT, which enables learning a biased target distribution to improve classification performance. Furthermore, the OT Cost Riesz Representation Theorem is introduced and used to formulate an OT Cost Functional for measuring the translation bias of neural networks. This framework is then used to analyze the properties of average pooling and global average pooling, as well as other global averaging operators. Experimentation demonstrates that these operators can inadvertently acquire translation biases, which affect their performance in target object classification. Although a global average pooling-trained network achieves high accuracy on a single target object, its performance deteriorates when confronted with a diverse set of target objects. In contrast, a S4D network is shown to provide superior classification performance for a broad range of target objects. This research aims to increase understanding of the underlying principles of global averaging operators and their potential limitations. Further experimentation is necessary to explore the extent to which these operators can be applied in downstream tasks. The proposed S4D framework and OT methodology provide a solid foundation for this purpose. An open-source C++ framework, OTLab, has been developed to facilitate the computation of OT Cost Functional and biased OT for visual recognition tasks. Furthermore, the SourceCode of S4DNet, including JDS4DNet and ShallowS4DNet, is made available for public use through GitHub. Moreover, the OTLab library has been uploaded to GitHub under the MIT License. A pre-trained Model of ShallowS4DNet is made available through Pastebin. OTLab has been utilized in multiple experiments to compute the OT Cost Functional for diverse datasets, including DomainAdaptation, vehicle make recognition, and landmark retrieval.

further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by significant ambiguity when dealing with unsaturated colors and
mixed objects. In contrast, estimating depth in monocular images proves more
unambiguous and thus a better candidate for pre-training. Nonetheless, previous
attempts have yielded lackluster results, suggesting a sizable knowledge gap.
This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by scrutinizing depth estimation
as a pre-training task, exploring its underlying assumptions and examining how
to refine the technique. In doing so, we've managed to outperform existing
methods, establishing a new benchmark in the field. In addition, we've discovered
that combining depth estimation and classification provides even more substantial
benefits when it comes to simplifying the semantic segmentation task. By leveraging
these findings, we've devised methodological improvements which have allowed us
to surpass state-of-the-art methods, also achieving impressive gains of up to
10% in the misclassification error rate compared to direct training on a smaller
dataset. Notably, we've achieved this advantage without requiring annotated data
and without compromising the model's performance on the primary, classification-based task. Interestingly, we've found that the efficacy of our approach
is unaffected by the amount of annotated data available for supervision. Even
when working with large datasets, including those containing 200k images, we've

and efficiency, also proving versatile when working with video and 3D modalities. As such, we're making the code public, hoping that it will facilitate future research in this area. We analyze a two-dimensional Ising model on a Cayley tree for various temperature and magnetization values, using the free energy functional on the algebra of local sub-sigma-algebras. This analysis leads us to define a particular class of periodic states, which can be either uniquely defined or exist in multiple forms, depending on the specific temperature and magnetization conditions. Unique periodic states are established for all temperatures in terms of complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials, while multiple periodic states are found for temperature equal to one-half magnetization, which are directly related to the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising model solutions on the Cayley tree. Additionally, we introduce and demonstrate the existence of new weakly periodic Gibbs states for temperature less than magnetization and unique periodic states for temperature greater than magnetization. These results are validated through an extension of the inverse problem method for algebra of local sub-sigma-algebras. Lastly, we define an explicit characterization of the developed periodic states through an analytic representation of the specific temperature and magnetization conditions, utilizing a specialized complexification of the Cayley tree called the Bloch tree. This characterization is further substantiated by an inspection of the resulting graphs on the Cayley tree for their symmetry and group properties. It's interesting to note that these unique and multiple periodic states can be similarly analyzed for temperature equal to one-half magnetization, where various extensions of the Ising model on the Cayley tree exhibit the same properties as the temperature and magnetization conditions change. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark stars under the influence of an external magnetic field at finite temperature, employing the MIT bag model. The study begins with an analysis of the energy density and pressure of spin-polarized quarks in the presence of an external magnetic field as a function of temperature. The resulting parameters are then utilized to develop a generalized equation of state for spin-polarized quarks in the presence of an external magnetic field. The generalized equation of state for spin-polarized quarks in the presence of an external magnetic field is then applied to investigate the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars. The findings reveal that an external magnetic field causes the radius of the star to shrink and its mass to increase. Furthermore, we have investigated how temperature, magnetic field strength, and spin-polarization affect the structure of the star. Our research also examines the stability of the star using the adiabatic index and mass-central density curves, revealing that the presence of an external magnetic field makes the star more stable. Our research also examines the impact of temperature on the star's structure, showing that it generates thermal pressure which prevents the star from collapsing and results in a more massive star with a larger radius. Finally, our research demonstrates that the maximum mass that an accurately bound quark star can achieve without collapsing increases as the magnetic field strength increases. Our findings can be useful in understanding the effects of spin-polarization, magnetic field, and temperature on the structure of quark stars, which may be relevant to the study of compact objects such as quark stars, neutron stars, and black holes. This research focuses on estimating the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a nonlinear problem by interpolating the spectral distribution, using a minimal rational model based on empirical measures. The study demonstrates that this model can accurately predict eigenvalues and eigenvectors at a rate comparable to or better than existing methods, with support as narrow as $\sqrt{s}$ and multiplicity $2s$, where $s$ is the degree of the model. The results are further enhanced when the nonlinearity is moderate, allowing for faster convergence rates. To achieve these results, the paper develops a precise estimate of the spectral distribution's covariance, which is also useful in its own right. Additionally, the study demonstrates that a lower-bound minimum exists among all rational models of a given degree. The findings are supported by stable numerical experiments, illustrating the benefits of using a minimal model in practice. The paper further examines the estimation of nonlinear eigenvectors, proposing a method based on solving a weighted least-squares problem and demonstrating its superiority to existing techniques. The estimation accuracy is evaluated using stable numerical experiments, showcasing the improvements achieved. The study implements these algorithms in a real-world context, using survey data from the US Treasury's yield curve to estimate the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix $M_2(\lambda)$, which is defined by the equation $\lambda^2 + m_2 \lambda + m_1$. The results highlight the minimal model's ability to outperform existing methods in this application, with support as narrow as $\sqrt{s}$ and multiplicity $2s$, where $s$ is the degree of the model. This lack of understanding raises significant concerns, as it hampers the models' usability in various applications. Solution models that are more transparent, like those based on Bayesian networks, are often less than fully effective. This study aims to improve on this by introducing a novel method for increasing the clarity of random forest and gradient boosting models. These models use feature importance metrics to provide insight, but even then, the relationships between those features and the target variable remain obscure. Our proposed approach employs an advanced form of regression trees that not only reveals conditional relationships but also sheds light on the models' internal workings by introducing a method for detailed, variable-by-variable explanations. In a comparative analysis with existing model interpretation techniques, our results show that the new method surpasses alternatives in accuracy and clarity, earning high marks from both algorithms and human evaluators. Furthermore, our method facilitates the discovery of hidden variables and relationships within the data, thus offering increased effectiveness for tasks involving variable selection, target variable identification, and causal analysis. Thus, our research offers increased clarity and understanding of black-box models, facilitating their use in a broader array of applications. Despite this setup, collaborative parties are vulnerable to attacks by adversarial servers, and a lack of reliable security mechanisms hampers the scalability of FL systems. To address this challenge, our research introduces flatee, a robust framework for secure FL that leverages trusted execution environments (TEEs) as reliable guardposts for collaborative parties. Specifically, TEEs based on Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) enable collaborative parties to execute and verify ML model training, along with other critical operations, within an adversarial-dominated environment. By incorporating these mechanisms, flatee ensures the security and consistency of collaborative parties, and our evaluation demonstrates the efficacy of this framework through various tests. TEEs have been proven to be secure, and our research shows that flatee offers superior security features compared to other FL systems. Furthermore, our framework boasts improved efficiency, and our findings indicate that certain improvements can be implemented to further optimize flatee. Current methods for evaluating AV software rely on simulation tools, which can be either simple (with limited features) or complex (with numerous variables), or use actual vehicles, subjecting them to the risks inherent in on-road testing. To strike a balance between these opposing aspects, we introduce a novel framework that enables the assessment of AV software functionality on an embedded system with a limited footprint. This proposed tool operates within a realistic environment simulation and evaluates an AV software model, allowing for the analysis of its behavior under normal and exceptional conditions. To maintain simplicity, our model excludes complex variables not crucial to AV software evaluation. The tool leverages a self-contained virtual environment and an embedded system with a limited footprint, enabling on-board AV software testing and easing the process of implementing and evaluating actual vehicle software. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through an actual vehicle driving example from the European Road Federation's database. This research not only introduces a pioneering approach for evaluating AV software but also provides a useful resource for researchers and developers, facilitating joint efforts in testing and comparing various driving algorithms. To promote collaboration, we make our framework accessible on our website at https://av-embedding.github.io/. This paper introduces a novel approach for automated system call filtering in
containerized applications. Typically, interactive applications within
containers engage in system calls, necessitating strict access control to
prevent security breaches. Current methods for system call filtering rely on
preconfigured allowlists or denylists, often leading to a trade-off between
security and functionality. To address this issue, we have developed a dynamic
filtering method called Timeloops, capable of learning and adapting to the
system calls of individual applications. Timeloops utilizes an immutable
filesystem and instrumented system calls to create a read-only sandbox for
precise analysis. Following the termination of an application, its learned system
call policy is appended to a temporary runtime denylist, effectively
restricting future system calls to a defined set. By automating system call
filtering, developers can eliminate the need for manual, error-prone configuration
on production systems, while also preventing security vulnerabilities. Our
results demonstrate that Timeloops achieves a success rate of 99% in accurately
predicting system calls for 9 benchmark applications, also showcasing a
substantial reduction (up to 73%) in the need for manual system call denials. Furthermore, performance testing has revealed a negligible overhead of 1-2%, confirming the efficiency of Timeloops. Additionally, we have employed Timeloops to secure a number of real-world use cases, successfully enhancing the security of a leading e-commerce platform, a popular containerized application, and a set of sophisticated microservices. Our code is openly accessible via GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/c0fe3/timeloops. In particular, the GitHub repository includes the source code for Timeloops, as well as detailed instructions for configuring and running the project. We have developed an innovative method to explicitly formulate a General Neron Desingularization for one-dimensional local rings. We demonstrated the algorithm's constructiveness by employing an innovative technique, and our proof underscores the significance of an essential property, which can be viewed as a refined version of Neron Desingularization. The algorithm's first segment accurately represents the Normalization of the ring in question, and we have successfully obtained a formalized expression for its mapping function. Furthermore, we have obtained a detailed description of the sequence of blow-ups, and we have formally established the algorithm's unambiguous nature, which leads to the direct obtainability of General Neron Desingularization. In addition, we have analyzed the algorithm's second segment, which corresponds to a modified version of Hironaka's Thickening algorithm, and we have obtained a formal characterization of the algorithm's action on the ring's seminormal closure. We have also computed a mapping function for the second segment, and we have demonstrated that the algorithm's second component can be effectively implemented through a new type of monomially/spatially relevant polynomial ring. Finally, we have analyzed the algorithm's third segment, which corresponds to a modified version of Greenberg's Strong Resolution algorithm, and we have obtained a formal description of the algorithm's action on the seminormal closure of the ring's tentatively normal ring. We have also computed a mapping function for the third segment, and we have demonstrated that the algorithm's third component can be effectively implemented through a new type of strongly polynomially filtered ring. Consequently, we have obtained a formal characterization of the algorithm's entire process, which we have subsequently named the Constructive General Neron Resolution algorithm. This algorithm serves as a refined version of an algorithm previously presented by R. Dohmen, and it provides a new proof of an important theorem recently established by J. Spilman. Additionally, we have implemented the algorithm using the Mathematica programming language to demonstrate its constructiveness and obtain explicit formulas for its mapping functions. We have also utilized these implementations to showcase the algorithm's ability to obtain General Neron Desingularization for specific examples, including local rings with a single prime ideal and rings that can be mapped onto a quotient of a $p$-th dimensional polynomial ring. Furthermore, we have utilized the algorithm to obtain General Neron Desingularization for the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(5)}$, and we have explicitly computed its General Neron Desingularization sequence to a quotient of a $5$-th dimensional polynomial ring.

In his 2006 article, Montalbán explored the differences between infinite binary relations and first-order logic. Montalbán demonstrated that second-order logic can express properties of binary relations which can't be represented in first-order logic. This article reaffirms Montalbán's findings using an alternative method and further identifies a novel class of infinite binary relations whose properties can't be expressed in first-order logic, thus providing a refined categorization of infinite binary relations. Additionally, this article links this class of relations to a type of model-theoretic independence and shows that it can be characterized by a specific type of non-extendable sequence. A fundamental tool in establishing this characterization is a constructed property that can discern extendability in any given infinite binary relation, regardless of its underlying domain's cardinality. This article introduces an improved version of a tool first utilized by Montalbán, which can distinguish between extendable and non-extendable infinite binary relations with a specific cardinality. A key consequence of this improved tool is a simplified proof that every theory of infinite binary relations with a specific cardinality is non-compact, building upon a prior result by Montalbán. Furthermore, this article introduces an alternative method for constructing a known example of a property that can't be expressed in first-order logic and a specific type of infinite binary relation. This new construction employs a self-delimiting high-transfinite recursion, a concept initially explored in the article's co-author's PhD research. In particular, it demonstrates that any infinite binary relation with a certain level of complexity can be expressed using a specific high-transfinite symbol, and that every theory of infinite binary relations with a certain cardinality is non-compact if it features a specific type of fundamental symbols. However, applying them to improve resolution remains a subject of debate due to concerns over potential image degradation. In seeking answers, researchers employed numerical methods to analyze the properties of a model phase plate that combines programmable electrostatic and traditional physical components. Their findings suggest that using this phase plate can not only correct for lens aberrations but also enhance resolution beyond the conventional physical limitations. Additionally, the study indicates that using a binary phase plate instead of a sinusoidal one results in more efficient correction of lens aberrations. However, the study also reveals that strong electrostatic fields can impair the phase plate's ability to correct lens aberrations, leading to a higher percentage of distorted electrons. In the United States, the method of assessing student achievement through high-stakes testing has resulted in a detrimental focus on teaching to the test, which severely limited the depth of material covered in classes and caused students to miss out on essential knowledge.  This situation worsened due to the incorrect application of statistical concepts in scoring students' test answers.  A notorious example is the case of James Stunt, whose calculated probability of holding a Monte Carlo gold coin that weighed less than a standard one was considered by courts as evidence of his being the True Crime, as reported in the New York Times.  This work challenges the widely accepted belief that academic achievement can be accurately measured through quantitative data.  It utilizes Bayesian logic to define achievement in terms of language, and identifies a fundamental error in the methods used for assessing student performance, which relies on vague statements that cannot be made precise.  This study examines the implications of these errors on educational policy and outlines a proposed method for making informed decisions about student learning.  This investigation is part of a broader effort to apply critical thinking to the field of educational assessment.  A novel aspect of this research is the integration of diverse fields, such as epidemiology, logic, metallurgy, probability, and statistics, which are used to analyze the underlying logic of assessment.  This study examines the history and impact of incorrect statistical ideas on educational assessment, and proposes a course of action to remedy these errors.  Through its exploration of various fields, this research reveals the interconnectedness of seemingly unrelated areas of study.  A key discovery of this study is the reality that numerical data is often used to describe qualitative phenomena in a way that is inappropriate and incorrect.  This work examines the consequences of statistical errors on educational policy and practice, and highlights the significance of critical decision-making in shaping the future of learning.  A central theme of this research is the responsibility that comes with making informed decisions, and the importance of careful consideration in achieving success.  Through its application of Bayesian logic and critical thinking, this study demonstrates that even the most advanced statistical methods cannot guarantee accurate assessment of complex, nuanced concepts.  A fundamental finding of this investigation is the limitation of language, which cannot be captured by numerical data without sacrificing the very qualities that make this language meaningful.  This study examines the paradox of using numerical data to describe non-numerical ideas and their accompanying text, and highlights the consequences of statistical errors on educational decision-making.  Through its exploration of various fields and themes, this research reveals the importance of critical thinking and clear decision-making

The objective of this paper is to count the number of points within a specific, d-dimensional lattice that lie within a certain bounded area. This counting method will be based on a fundamental theorem related to the generating functions of the central binomial walk. This result will be further extended to the p-norm scenario, and subsequent application to the p-norm ball in the Z^d lattice will yield a combinatorial expression linked to the p-stable distributions' moment generating functions. This method will then be applied to derive precise formulas for the volume of the p-norm ball in the Z^d lattice. This research further explores some interesting volume patterns based on the p-value and examines potential generalizations to higher-dimensional real and complex lattices. This study also delves into the mathematical concepts underlying random walk positions, specifically examining the central limit theorem's limitations through the p-norm scenario. It is observed that the p-norm paradigm offers a unique perspective on achieving convergence to a Gaussian distribution, thereby providing a distinct perspective on the MLR property and the p-stable distributions' characteristics. Lastly, this paper investigates the volume of the p-norm ball in the Z^d lattice and its relationship to the p-stable distributions' dispersion matrices, thereby offering a fresh angle on the p-norm analysis of many well-known probability distributions. This research ultimately seeks to contribute to ongoing discussions on the p-norm paradigm's simplicity, elegance, and effectiveness in statistical physics and machine learning contexts. This study hopes to spark further exploration, especially in the relevant theoretical physics and machine learning domains, with potential applications extending to real and complex p-norm ball scenarios. To demonstrate the volume's recurrence and divisibility properties, this paper employs elementary combinatorial methods, thereby shedding new light on simple counting problems related to random walk positions. This research also addresses a long-standing unsolved problem by deriving a closed-form expression for the volume of the p-norm ball in the Z^d lattice. This solution further generalizes a renowned theorem from the 1920s by expanding its p=2 case to the p>1 scenario. This new finding enables researchers to investigate odd and even p-values as potential sources of volume irreducibility. This paper also delves into the p-norm ball's rational and algebraic properties, specifically examining the prime factors of its volume when p is a prime number. This research offers a novel perspective on the p-norm paradigm, specifically analyzing the volume's factorization and divisibility properties with respect to prime and composite numbers.

We have developed a theoretical approach to study the thermal responses and heat capacity of single and bilayer graphene sheets containing various types of impurities. By employing a random-phase approximation, we have modeled the movement of electrons and heat within these graphene layers. Initially, we analyzed the thermal responses of clean graphene sheets, followed by examining the effects of impurities. Our results for clean graphene align with established laws and show that interlayer coupling significantly impacts the thermal expansion and heat capacity of bilayer graphene. Next, we modeled doped graphene layers with a range of impurities, including those with a flat and parabolic density of states. Consistently, we found that the heat capacity of doped graphene layers exhibits a linear temperature dependence. Furthermore, we observed that the interaction between electrons and phonons causes a sudden increase in the thermal expansion and heat capacity of doped graphene layers at higher temperatures. This phenomenon is caused by the electron density of states becoming linearly temperature-dependent due to the presence of impurities. In addition to these findings, we observed that the heat capacity of doped single-layer graphene sheets exhibits a mild dependence on temperature, while the heat capacity of doped bilayer graphene sheets exhibits a more pronounced temperature dependence. This difference is once again attributed to the impact of interlayer coupling on the electron density of states. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the thermal responses and heat capacity of doped graphene layers. This research may also contribute to the development of new thermal materials and can be applied to study the thermal properties of other two-dimensional materials. Long-form speech generation, like text generation, poses a challenge for models to produce the same level of quality in their outputs as in their training. Current systems using prompt-based approaches can generate spoken words, but the quality of the non-verbal context, such as silence and lip sounds, suffers greatly. To overcome this, we introduce context-aware speech production, a novel framework that involves inserting masked tokens within speech inputs to convey additional information to the model. We developed MaskedSpeech, a system based on this framework that can generate natural-looking speech with a non-verbal context. We evaluated MaskedSpeech through a listening test and found it to have a significant impact on speech quality when compared to systems without a non-verbal context. The code and demo can be accessed through https://github.com/aisks/MaskedSpeech. Speaking-specific parts, such as lip sounds and silence, are often given low priorities in current long speech systems, but we believe this research demonstrates the importance of incorporating silence and lip sounds into non-systemic speech production methods to enhance overall speech quality. The resulting method, called latent PPD (LPPD), retains the ability to target specific structures in data, as demonstrated through applications to clustering and regression. LPPD has been proven to converge to the true distribution as more data is collected, and its performance is shown to be superior to other established methods. A potentially devastating attack on machine learning classifiers can occur when an attacker intercepts communication between a client and a server by posing as a legitimate intermediary, thereby manipulating input provided to the server and causing it to misclassify. This Man-in-the-Middle attack is made more simplified and accessible due to the increased capabilities of generative models, allowing attackers to create fake inputs that trigger specific pre-determined outputs in the target classifier. To launch this attack, attackers can use a pre-trained generative model that can generate malicious inputs that match real data while also determining the corresponding labels that would trigger incorrect classifications. As this attack is easy to launch and can be adapted to affect various models without requiring any prior knowledge, it poses a significant threat to the security of machine learning systems, particularly since the only required component is a generative model, allowing it to succeed in the absence of any other malicious tools. To evaluate the effectiveness of this attack, our research utilized a MNIST model and found that a generative model trained on a small dataset consisting of handwritten digits was able to produce malicious inputs that correctly identified the number 6 in the test set with high accuracy while also determining the label 'zero' for other numbers, indicating that it could be used to induce a man-in-the-middle assault on the target model. Similarly, another attack was launched on a Facebook model that utilizes a generative model to create malicious inputs that correctly identify the target label, which in this case was discovered to be'stressed' with a high accuracy value of 0.857. To mitigate this type of attack, our research proposed several potential defensive strategies, including detecting anomalies in classifier outputs, verifying that provided inputs match the expected data structure, utilizing offline model validation to ensure data integrity, and utilizing models that can detect manipulated input without the need for a generative model component. However, it is worth noting that these potential solutions would require further research and testing due to the lack of existing literature on this topic. In conclusion, our research demonstrated that machine learning classifiers are susceptible to man-in-the-middle assaults triggered by malicious inputs generated by attackers who use generative models, presenting which poses a significant threat due to its ease of launch, adaptability, and limited requirements. As a result, it is crucial that defensive strategies are developed and tested to mitigate this type of attack. Furthermore, our research highlighted the fact that the only component an attacker needs to execute this attack is a generative model, indicating that future research should focus on detecting and mitigating the Malicious Model Assault (MMA)

This research presents a novel variational image segmentation model that integrates elements of image restoration, garnered from optimal solution properties, into the image segmentation process. The proposed model incorporates two important components: a segmentation function u and a parameter m, which facilitates image recovery. By employing the parameters μ and λ, as well as the conventional Newton term ν∇u, the model optimizes image segmentation results. Our approach aligns with a convex-concave-convex cost function, necessitating the use of the Barzilai-Borwein step-size scheme to maintain stability. Efficient image segmentation outcomes can be achieved with a computationally efficient algorithm, supported by numerical experiments. Additionally, the model demonstrates capabilities for weakly supervised image segmentation tasks. Notably, when m is disregarded, the model diminishes to a traditional image segmentation model, offering additional insights. Furthermore, theoretical proofs establish the uniqueness of solutions and optimal solution properties, providing a theoretical framework for the proposed model. In contrast to traditional variational image segmentation models, our approach introduces novel perspectives and achievements, setting a new standard for image segmentation models. Our findings also shed light on the importance of the parameter m in achieving optimal solution properties. In particular, when m is maximized, the model optimizes image segmentation results, whereas a minimized m corresponds to a traditional image segmentation model. To further demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach, numerical experiments are conducted using publicly accessible image datasets, showcasing the efficiency and accuracy of the method. Specifically, the proposed model achieves impressive state-of-the-art performance on the MSRA-10k dataset, highlighting its capabilities for practical image segmentation applications. In summary, this study introduces a novel variational image segmentation model that integrates image restoration elements and offers a range of innovative features and achievements. The model's parameters, stability conditions, and optimal solution properties are meticulously examined, and the algorithm is validated with numerical experiments and evaluations. Additionally, theoretical proofs establish the rigorous mathematical underpinnings for this novel model. Lastly, our findings extensively discuss the importance of the model's parameters, their optimal values, and the consequences of disregarding them, particularly in the context of practical image segmentation applications. However, due to the inherently poor channel conditions resulting from interference and vehicles' frequent movement, it is crucial to implement a channel assessment method to optimize transmission performance. Traditional fixed-duration IEEE 802.11p ACK timing can lead to increased packet loss, and thus a dynamic ACK timing adjustment is necessary. Current solutions using machine learning-based techniques, such as deep learning, often struggle with real-time implementation due to their computationally intensive nature. A linear regression-based solution also faces challenges in accurate channel estimation, particularly in dynamic scenarios. Compared to TA-LSTM, the proposed LSTM-based scheme displays enhanced stability, decreased standard deviation, and a optimized parameter set. Consequently, the implemented LSTM-based scheme is an ideal solution for practical applications, providing efficient vehicle communication under channel dynamic conditions. The source code for the proposed solution has been publicly archived for reference purposes. This framework operates by identifying the underlying factors causing distribution changes and adapting the model output accordingly, effectively merging two techniques: (1) causal inference, used to find these underlying conditions, and (2) output adjustment, used to correct the model output. Specifically, we integrate the concepts of counterfactuals and synthetic sampling, and propose a new method combining the ideas of causal and semi-synthetic sampling. This new method is known as semi-generative modelling. We test our approach on both simulated and real-world data, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority to other established techniques. Additionally, we provide a coding framework supporting the method's implementation. A subgroup $H$ in group $G$ is said to be a lattice minimum if any other subgroup $K$ of $G$, with $H$ within it, must have $H = K$. 
We explore the properties of lattice minima, particularly examining internal subgroups $H$, given that $H \cap K = H$ for some fixed subgroup $K$ of $G$. 
It is shown that if $H$ satisfies this condition for some infinite supersolvable subgroup $K$ of index $2$, then $H$ must be a lattice minimum.
Additionally, if $H$ satisfies this condition for some infinite supersolvable subgroup $K$ of index $10$, then $H$ must be a lattice minimum if and only if it has prime index relative to $K$.
It is further demonstrated that if $H$ satisfies this condition for some infinite supersolvable subgroup $K$ of index $30$, then $H$ must be a lattice minimum if and only if it has prime index relative to $K$ and its order is relatively prime to $30$.

A major obstacle in using neural networks to approximate wavefunction collapse has been the "sign problem" that occurs in some models, like the Hubbard model. This problem arises because certain models don't yield a well-defined wavefunction if their amplitudes contain negative values. Despite this limitation, a new study reveals that certain types of complex-valued neural networks are sign-stable, meaning they can accurately represent the wavefunction without running into the sign problem. This property was found to hold true for a specific model, the Hubbard model, and a particular type of neural network called a pair of complex-valued feed-forward neural networks, and the study shows that this model remains sign-stable across various conditions. Furthermore, a version of this model was used to solve the inverse problem of calculating energies and densities from correlated quantum states, and was found to yield accurate results. Given its ability to overcome the sign problem, this model may hold potential for use in approximating the behavior of complex many-body quantum systems. This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It delves into CPT, a logic system that can identify distinct graphs, and investigates connections to MPC and PCR. This study broadens the scope of research into CPT, contrasting it with UTP, a logic system previously found to be closely tied to PCR but distinguishable from MPC. CPT's capabilities are explored through analysis of its properties, such as tolerance for 3- and 4-equivalence, as well as its ability to recognize cliques, complete bipartite graphs, and cycle structures. Building on this, we introduce new secure protocols for encrypting logical statements and outline future research directions to establish whether CPT can capture the concept of connected graphs. Leveraging a novel CPT-based methodology, we demonstrate that a secure encryption method for graph properties exists, and this, in turn, illustrates that PCR does not necessarily guarantee security in the computational model. This leads to a key finding: there is a class of properties that can be defined through first-order logic with a specific finite quantification limit but cannot be established through PCR. This finding contradicts conventional wisdom and sheds new light on the long-standing question of whether MPC can capture the concept of connected graphs. As a result, we propose a novel notion of 'algebraic and proof-theoretic hierarchy' to capture this concept and its generalisations. Moreover, our research suggests an alternative solution to establishing this hierarchy, which is based on finite model theory and related to the Northcutt-Mansfield problem.
