The increasing prevalence of unfalsifiable claims on social media poses a significant challenge in understanding how such concepts spread rapidly across online platforms, often gaining widespread acceptance in a brief period. Unlike proven scientific facts, these unfalsifiable claims cannot be substantiated through evidence and are largely baseless. Conversely, they also tend to lack the complexity typically associated with made-up information. In this research, we aim to investigate the mechanisms underlying the dissemination of unfalsifiable claims by first identifying them on Twitter and evaluating two frameworks for predicting similar claims. Our analysis reveals that an unfalsifiable claim's framework determines its likelihood of being endorsed by others, with context-specific frameworks yielding superior predictive results compared to random models. Notably, the most successful framework in our study was one that identified connections between past unfalsifiable tweets, enabling us to make more accurate predictions about future unfalsifiable claims. Using eye-tracking data, we also gather evidence suggesting that users process and evaluate unfalsifiable claims in a manner consistent with classical theories of persuasion, where the origin and framework of a claim influence their perception and credibility. Our findings contribute to the growing body of literature on unfalsifiable claims, shedding light on the role of frameworks in disseminating baseless information and facilitating its widespread acceptance. Moreover, our research demonstrates the practical utility of framework-based models in predicting unfalsifiable claims, potential areas for further exploration include applying our frameworks to detect and prevent unfalsifiable misinformation on platforms and exploring the theoretical underpinnings of framework-driven persuasion. Ultimately, we hope that our research sheds light on the mechanisms driving the dissemination of unfalsifiable claims and provides a practical approach for mitigating the spread of baseless information, as well as initiating a more in-depth examination of the role of frameworks in understanding and changing user behavior. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to the formation of a new class of neural networks designed to withstand malicious attacks. However, if a neural network can withstand attacks in a limited sense, it does not necessarily mean it can resist more substantial attacks. Our research reveals that deep learning algorithms in computer vision can successfully withstand cyber attacks within a restricted framework, yet we found no substantial applications of this concept in the field of machine learning. Furthermore, we explored the idea of implementing robust Bayesian neural networks by applying a novel perturbation model that can be verified. Our experiments showed that deep learning algorithms in computer vision can also function effectively with robust Bayesian neural networks, providing certainty estimates that are adaptable to both malicious and non-malicious situations. Our study also demonstrates the possibility of achieving verifiable robustness in complex machine learning scenarios, paving the way for practical applications of robust Bayesian neural networks. The source code for our research is available at https://github.com/robustai/robust_deep_bayes. Our research findings are documented in a research paper at arXiv:2202.05275. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a metric to gauge the influence of each rumor. By employing a neural network to predict rumor propagation timelines, we found that early predictions showed high accuracy and revealed the point at which rumors began to spread widely. Subsequently, we defined the critical period as the first four hours and developed an influence metric that combines the likelihood and timing of peak propagation. Our experimental results demonstrated that the proposed method accurately ranked the severity of rumors that caused significant disturbances, while also showcasing the effectiveness of combining machine learning algorithms with human annotation for accurately predicting propagation timelines. Additionally, we identified key characteristics of rumors that caused significant harm and developed an online platform for users to report and rate the severity of rumors, which enabled users to search and rate rumors based on their perceived threat level. The proposed method and approach to measuring rumor influence have potential applications in areas such as information security, public health warning systems, and social media governance. Furthermore, the developed platform may facilitate research in social media, online psychology, and other related fields. This study investigates the effects of dimensionality reduction on pixel classification in hyperspectral images. Spectral dimensionality reduction (SDR) is crucial due to large pixel densities and dimensionality, but its impact on image classification needs more research. A comprehensive analysis is conducted using 12 real-world datasets, comparing the performance of three common SDR techniques – principal component analysis (PCA), wavelet transform (WT), and self Organizing Map (SOM) – all applied before a fixed classifier. A thorough evaluation is performed through multiple experiments, considering various factors such as dataset, number of dimensions, classifier, and classification metric. The results indicate significant differences in the best performances of the three techniques, with substantial variations depending on the dataset, but consistent improvements in computational efficiency due to reduced dimensions. The findings suggest that WT and SOM outperform PCA in terms of accuracy, but further research is needed to determine which method to use in specific scenarios. Many advanced AI models are too big to work efficiently in applications with limited resources, such as older devices or environments with strict security restrictions. This problem is known as the "pruning problem" in deep learning. Researchers have made significant progress in developing new techniques to further compress already optimized models, an approach known as "iteration pruning". This approach combines various methods, such as adjusting the size and frequency of model updates, to continuously refine the model until it reaches a desired level of performance and efficiency. This paper evaluates different iteration pruning techniques for their effectiveness in compressing AI models, particularly focusing on how they affect the models' memory usage, processing speed, and overall accuracy. The study examines the limitations and potential improvements of these techniques, identifying areas for future improvement and potential applications that could benefit from these methods. The researchers also introduce a new technique to further compress models, an approach known as "semantic compression". This approach focuses on eliminating redundant information within the models, an area of study previously unexplored in the context of deep learning. The findings show that, although the new approach requires some manual input from domain experts, it results in significant improvements in memory efficiency while maintaining comparable performance. This approach may be suitable for tasks where experts are available to provide guidance. The overall goal of this research is to contribute to our understanding of the pruning problem and how it relates to deep learning, ultimately enabling more efficient AI models that can work effectively in resource-constrained environments. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables rapid generation of amide proton chemical shifts for proteins. The ProCS algorithm, incorporating quantum mechanical calculations and protein structures, identifies the most plausible protein conformations through comparison with experimentally obtained chemical shift values. By utilizing ProCS in a constrained global optimization process, the convergence of predicted chemical shifts with experimental data can be enhanced. The results indicate that ProCS successfully verifies and refines protein structures, particularly for challenging cases with distant long-range connections between amino acids. The research demonstrates that ProCS achieves an average ProCS error of less than 0.50 ppm for a test set of 82 proteins, thereby facilitating the verification and refinement of protein structures. Additionally, ProCS holds potential for supporting resonance assignment in NMR spectroscopy, an intricate process involved in determining the three-dimensional structure of proteins. ProCS could become a valuable tool for structure refinement in protein structural genomics and other fields, enhancing the accuracy of protein structures. investigation into the effect of loss functions on their performance. In this study,
we seek to fill this knowledge gap by examining how different loss functions impact
the accuracy of classification tasks. Our findings demonstrate that using various
loss functions can yield improvements in model performance. To facilitate this
research, we created a Python library called \verb|Alfa|
($\mathcal{L}$earning fUnction sArch) that enables an extensive search across the
universe of loss functions to identify the most optimal one for a given model and
dataset. Our study also explores the relationship between model performance and
loss function properties, providing insights that can guide the development of more
effective loss functions. Additionally, we discuss how the principles of our work
can be applied to other problems in machine learning. The \verb|Alfa| library is

The purpose of this research is to assess the informational density of musical creations from the period of 1500-2010, using the normative standards of the Western classical tradition. By analyzing the melody and harmonic elements of songs by prominent composers from the Baroque, Classical, Romantic eras, in addition to analyzing popular music from the 20th and 21st centuries, we found that the complexity of musical compositions has generally increased over time. However, there are noticeable differences in the complexity of musical works from distinct stylistic periods, with those from the Romantic era generally exhibiting greater complexity than those from the Classical era. Furthermore, there are noticeable disparities in the melodic and harmonic complexities of songs from the pre- and post-World War II periods, with the latter exhibiting more intricate designs. These findings suggest that there may be a correlation between the societal context in which music is created and the characteristics of that music. A fundamental outcome of a reinforcement process is that, in the long run, a Markovian reinforcement process will become persistent in one or more states with probability 1, provided that a criterion known as Forni's condition is met. This condition essentially demands that the sum of the Q-matrix's positive and negative off-diagonal elements be positive. Under these circumstances, the probability of becoming persistent in multiple states approaches zero, except in the case where the Q-matrix is irreducible, in which case the probability is nonzero. A direct statistical test is developed to determine whether a given Markovian reinforcement process is persistent in one or more states. Furthermore, a simulation is conducted using randomly generated Q-matrices to examine how often the following phenomenon occurs: a Markovian reinforcement process becomes persistent in more than one state. It is demonstrated that a Markovian reinforcement process is unlikely to be persistent in both the initial and final states unless the process is irreducible or the transition probabilities are equal to 1 or 0. The study also explores the relationship between the spectral properties of the Q-matrix, its off-diagonal elements, and the distribution of its eigenvalues. A Markovian reinforcement process is shown to be persistent in one state with probability 1 if the absolute value of the Q-matrix's smallest eigenvalue is greater than 1. Similarly, a Markovian reinforcement process is persistent in more than one state if the absolute value of the Q-matrix's second smallest eigenvalue is greater than 1. A Markovian reinforcement process is persistent in more than two states if the absolute value of the Q-matrix's third smallest eigenvalue is greater than 1, and so on. A comprehensive mathematical analysis is provided to explain these findings. The direct statistical test and the proposed asymptotic results can be effectively applied to evaluate the long-term persistence of a Markovian reinforcement process, thereby expanding upon existing theoretical outcomes. Ludics is a mathematical framework for concurrent interactions that are governed by a unique notion of harmony. This concept replaces traditional equivalence, emphasizing compatibility in the context of computational systems. By integrating Ludics with a fragment of intuitionistic logic, we can examine the properties of harmony within this modified framework. Although harmony no longer adheres to a equivalence relation, it retains essential characteristics. For instance, harmony is still preserved under composition and affects the behavior of operations, such as those involving cut and fusion. By analyzing Ludics, we gain insights into the fundamental properties of harmony, which ultimately enables efficient proof analysis based on the framework's structural characteristics. Our research demonstrates that proofs can be evaluated at a shallow level, resulting in significant computational benefits. Furthermore, both shallow and deep reasoning methods are shown to be compatible with each other. Since Ludics can mimic the behavior of higher-order and linear logic within a computational setting, our findings are equally applicable to these domains. Moreover, we successfully modeled a fragment of the Coq core calculus, which includes a finite subset of the principles from the SML language, within Ludics. This provides a computational context for the majority of the principles examined in the paper. By analyzing harmony, we gain valuable insights into the programming language domain. These insights are relevant to programming languages that incorporate separate compilation, modular verification, and shallow embedding of logic. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the interactive behavior of programming languages, leveraging the fundamental properties of Ludics. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through visual aids, we segment the agent's experience into distinct regions, enabling us to connect learned preferences with their corresponding states and evaluate the consequences, ultimately driving robust, time-efficient exploration and reward learning. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated in complex 3D environments, where traditional reward learning methods often require substantial rewards. Our technique successfully facilitates learning within visually and conceptually connected environments with comparable richness of information. This framework contributes to optimal reward learning to the same extent as previous methods that utilize extensive, individually marked data. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/bryanwiz/VRL_HRL/blob/main/visual_aid.py. This method offers a practical solution to the long-standing issue of maximizing an unsupervised environment's reward potential. To validate our approach, we employed evaluations on both simulated data and real-world scenarios within the Roomba environment, comparing it against state-of-the-art learning methods that rely on raw states or local maps. The results show that our model achieves comparable performance to learning methods that utilize raw states or local maps when evaluating the environment's richness, while significantly outperforming them when that richness is limited. The time spent by human labelers on our approach is directly proportional to the environment's connected components, resulting in up to a 9-fold reduction in labeling time compared to learning methods that utilize raw states or local maps. The connection between visual components and environmental concepts was quantified using the concept similarity matrix, which measures the likelihood of two states being connected based on their reward profiles. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/bryanwiz/VRl_HRL/blob/main/visual_aids.py. This approach in reward learning is grounded on two key methodological innovations. Firstly, we efficiently learn environmental preferences using an unsupervised agent, which prefers states that are rich in rewards and conceptually connected. Secondly, we effectively condense the environmental space into visually connected components using the concept similarity matrix, enabling robust mappings between visual aids and rewarding consequences. We show that a topological space can be assigned a refined structure, known as a Smyth space, in a way that preserves certain key properties. Specifically, we establish that Smyth spaces with a established correspondence structure are inherently core-compact. Moreover, this core-compact property is core to the established correspondence structure itself, providing a fundamental criterion for its consistency. Additionally, we examine the core-compact property in the context of two distinct interpretations of Smyth spaces, known as weak and strong Smyth spaces, and find that it applies uniformly to both interpretations. This deepens our understanding of the core-compact property and its relationship to the two interpretations, and presents a uniform framework for examining the core-compact property. Furthermore, we identify a family of core-compact spaces that serve as a stable foundation for the Smyth space structure, and establish a key relationship between the core-compact property and the presence of these spaces. Specifically, we show that core-compact spaces can be embedded in a strong Smyth space if and only if the space has a certain structural property, known as sup-inf closure stability. This presents a fundamental criterion for the core-compact property, and clarifies its relationship to the presence of core-compact spaces. Finally, we examine the relationship between core-compact spaces and a particular type of core-compact topology, known as the Smyth topology. Specifically, we show that the Smyth topology induced by a strong Smyth space is core-compact if and only if the space has a certain structural property, known as weak compatibility. This presents a fundamental criterion for the core-compact topology, and clarifies its relationship to the presence of core-compact spaces. Additionally, we establish a key relationship between the core-compact property and the presence of two distinct types of maps, known as continuous and weakly uniform continuous maps. Specifically, we show that these maps can be extended to a strong Smyth space if and only if the map is continuous, and presents a fundamental criterion for this extension. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between core-compact spaces and a particular type of core-compact structure, known as the Scott information structure. Specifically, we show that the Scott topology induced by a strong Smyth space with Scott information structure is core-compact, and presents a fundamental criterion for this property. A significant issue in causal inference arises when applying weighted estimation techniques, particularly inverse probability weighting (IPW), due to the uncertainty and variability of weighted estimators caused by model fitting inaccuracies in the prediction of propensity scores. Although standardized IPW has been shown to yield lower variance compared to IPW within the context of parametric models, its effectiveness in the case of nonparametric models, where predictions are often more inaccurate, is untested. In nonparametric models, the performance of weighted estimators is severely hindered by model specification errors in propensity score predictions, leading to large biases and additional variances beyond the usual asymptotic rates. To address this challenge, we introduce a standardized augmented IPW (SAIPW) estimator that incorporates an estimated alternative propensity score to mitigate the negative effects of inaccurate standardization. By leveraging neural network predictions for both treatment and alternative treatment conditions, SAIPW estimators can effectively identify causal effects while controlling for potential model risks. Notably, our results indicate that SAIPW estimators achieve the standard asymptotic rates of convergence, and the methods' performance is demonstrated through simulations and an application to a real-world healthcare study. Furthermore, the findings provide insights into the potential biases and variances of weighted estimators due to model specification errors in propensity score predictions. To reduce potential biases, we also propose a cross-validation procedure that utilizes neighboring samples to estimate the augmented propensity score, and provide theoretical justifications for the methods' consistency and convergence. The advantages of these estimators have been demonstrated through additional simulations and an application to a real-world healthcare study. The numerical studies reveal that leveraging neighboring samples for the estimation of augmented propensity scores can reduce bias while increasing efficiency compared to other weighted estimators. The methods' code can be accessed via the open-source repository at https://github.com/yunyangw/SAIPW. YM has previously presented an early version of the results at the 2021 CaImagE workshop. A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted with different temperature gradients while maintaining a constant Coriolis parameter, and the obtained results demonstrated a direct relationship between the strength of temperature gradients and the resulting baroclinic wave characteristics. Comparing the observed wave behaviors to corresponding numerical model outcomes, notable agreements were found in terms of cyclogenesis rates and wave patterns. However, discrepancies between the experimental and computational results were also identified, and their causes were explored. The obtained data suggest that the formation and development of baroclinic waves in the laboratory model closely mirror those observed in atmospheric systems, and the similarities between the laboratory and numerical results provide confidence in using the setup as an effective tool for testing various parameterizations and understanding the inherent dynamics of complex systems. Moreover, the possibilities of employing this setup for evaluating the impacts of different modeling choices and assessing the efficacy of novel baroclinic wave cure strategies were pondered. In conclusion, the effectiveness of the laboratory model as a tool for studying the underlying processes involved in the development of baroclinic waves was reaffirmed, and its potential as a resource for investigating various research hypotheses remains to be fully utilized. In Offline Reinforcement Learning, a pre-trained Q-function is refined using batch RL without continued interaction with the environment. However, if the data used for this process is contaminated with corrupted samples, the resulting policy will be suboptimal. Building on the concept of corruption-resilient data collection in RL, this research focuses on developing robust offline RL policies that can function under various levels of environmental corruption. We have created a framework to evaluate the degree of corruption in RL datasets and have applied it to develop robust Q-learning and model-free Thompson Sampling methods. We have tested these algorithms using synthetic data and compared them with existing robust RL methods, demonstrating that they can perform well in scenarios with moderate levels of corruption. Additionally, these robust methods exhibit key advantages: (1) they can function without prior knowledge of the environment dynamics; (2) they can be used across various types of RL problems; and (3) they can be applied both online and offline. The source code for these methods has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/prahl-yu/CRRRL. Moreover, the environment used in this research, including its variants with increasing levels of corruption, can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/prahl-yu/CorruptedEnv. This model allows for a detailed analytical examination of the engines' behavior, facilitated by the comparison of two statistical systems, effectively linking the subatomic world to the macro world. To test the universality of our model, we've conducted numerical simulations using realistic parameters related to molecular engines and found that its dynamics closely mirrors that of well-known self-assembly systems. Additionally, we've found that our model has a substantial influence on the engines' long-term behavior, notably in their capacity to convert thermal noise into directed motion at two distinct tunneling regimes. At regular tunneling rates, the engines exhibit substantial, yet irregular movements, whereas at rapid tunneling rates, they demonstrate more predictable, though less extreme movements. To validate our model's practical applications, we've successfully matched its results with those obtained from an alternative, intricate model based on Markov processes. To summarize, our proposed model provides a practical, analytically verifiable mechanism for the operation of Brownian molecular engines, offering new insights into their behavior and potential uses. Additionally, we've outlined possible pathways for the implementation of this model in experimental research. It's plausible that these efforts will lead to the development of molecular engines capable of converting thermal noise into mechanical work at high efficiency levels, potentially even exceeding that of biological systems. At regular tunneling rates, the emergence of dynamic equilibrium is characterized by oscillating movements around a central point, whereas at rapid tunneling rates, it's marked by a smooth, predictable trajectory. Furthermore, we've derived mathematical expressions for the correlation functions of flux and orientation, triggering fluctuations in the engines' motion, as well as for the distribution of orientation, further demonstrating the dynamical nature of the engines' movement. The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large datasets, yet its reliability is compromised when exposed to noise.  By utilizing kernel methods in conjunction with dynamic mode decomposition, we introduce LANDO - a kernel learning approach for deriving an optimal kernel operator that can effectively process noisy data under limited training.  Through theoretical analysis, we establish the optimal kernel operator's capacity to regenerate the system's governing equations across multiple dimensions.  By demonstrating that this optimal kernel operator is unique, we are also able to show that it remains stable in the presence of small perturbations.  Through both simulated and real-world examples, we illustrate LANDO's ability to create accurate models from small datasets, thereby facilitating the discovery of low-dimensional structures within high-dimensional data.  Furthermore, our technique enables the development of reduced-order models for tracking systems with partial information available.  By generalizing dynamic mode decomposition to accommodate nonlinear systems, we find that LANDO remains an effective method for deriving low-dimensional representations across various contexts. distinguishable patterns within different categories of openings, which we

This research examines the process of neutron star formation in the cores of ancient galaxy structures through the analysis of antileptonic interaction phenomena in dim white dwarfs. By combining theoretical models from stellar evolution and numerical simulations of particle beam collisions, we have derived the basic parameters required for millisecond pulsar formation, including the initial central density, radius, and mass of these stars. Our findings demonstrate that dense stellar cores with a central density between 4.7 to 11.1 (in 10$^{9}$ g/cm$^3$) and a radius between 0.88 to 5.40 (in 10$^{8}$ cm) can give rise to millisecond pulsars with a rotational period between 20 to 5000 ms. Additionally, our research links the duration of these stars' spin-down rates to their mass, estimating a range between 0.15 to 25 ms/yr for a pale white dwarf mass of 0.10 to 0.40 M$_{\odot}$. By analyzing the core properties at the moment of neutron star birth, our research makes possible the estimation of various pale dwarf core parameters, including its radius, core mass, and gravitational constant. Moreover, our research modifies the expected duration of neutron star birth, estimating a time frame of tens of millions of years. Finally, our research assesses the neutron star spin-down power, estimating a range between 10$^{31}$ to 10$^{41}$ erg/s for various pale dwarf masses. Our research makes possible a link between neutron star spin-down power and the energy released via radiation from ancient galaxy structures, influencing the local X-ray background intensity. These estimates may also be applied to other star types undergoing stellar evolution, such as other dim white dwarfs and neutron stars in ancient galaxy structures. Further research is needed to refine these estimates, such as obtaining more precise data on pale dwarf properties and conducting numerical simulations of neutron star formation to confirm these results. Moreover, our research facilitates an analysis of the local gamma-ray background intensity, predicting a ratio between this intensity and the local X-ray background at a specific wavelength of 2 keV. Despite the feasibility of this model in certain situations, its application is rendered invalid by the necessarily negative value of the adiabatic index, $\Gamma$, in accordance with the Einstein equations. Consequently, this model is unable to replicate the observed phenomena of supernovae and compact objects. Furthermore, we examine the model's implications in the context of general relativity and find that a cosmological constant is generated, leading to a negatively infinite mass for the resulting system. Additionally, we explore the model's behavior in the limit of low-density fluids and identify a potential discrepancy with commonly accepted understanding. To confirm our analysis, we outline specific pathways for which the model's characteristics could be experimentally verified. Our analysis highlights the necessity of a more complex equation of state in order to understand the observed distributions of compact stars and supernovae through the lens of general relativity. Our findings align with the views of notable researchers within the field, as referenced in the paper. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the mass and angular momentum of extreme black holes following arbitrary perturbations. This method is versatile and can be applied to various spacetimes and perturbation types. We have demonstrated that for an extremal black hole in a background spacetime with $f(R)$ gravity, the mass and angular momentum corrections are linked to the Ricci scalar derivative of the $f(R)$ function. Furthermore, our approach can be used to derive corrections in the presence of scalar fields, such as a Klein-Gordon field, where we have found that the extremality condition is affected by the scalar field energy-momentum tensor. We have also shown that for an extremal black hole in a horizonally asymptotically flat spacetime, the mass and angular momentum corrections are localized and resident solely on the horizon, with key properties depending on the form of the perturbation. Additionally, our results are consistent for both inner and outer horizons in cases where the perturbation is small. We have performed a case study for a collision of two black holes, illustrating the application of our method and the significance of considerations like the domain of the perturbation and the which-way question. Finally, our work has been complemented by a new simplification for determining surface terms in surface terms-based formalisms, which we hope will be useful in other contexts. This method could potentially enable the efficient calculation of surface terms, thereby simplifying the Iyer-Wald formalism and making it more computationally accessible. We ultimately expect our corrections approach to contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of black holes and the AdS/CFT correspondence. We have also made available our code for the surface term calculations at https://github.com/jmuncs/Surface-Term-Catalogue. This repository contains a comprehensive collection of surface term lookup tools, which can be used to speed up the Iyer-Wald formalism in a wide range of spacetimes and black hole configurations. We hope that our code will be useful in other research projects. We specifically anticipate that our approach will be valuable for analyzing the thermodynamic properties of black holes and for exploring the holographic duals of these systems, with a particular focus on the entropy and other robust physical characteristics that emerge during a black hole merger. We expect that our results will provide new insights and perspectives on these fundamental aspects of black hole physics. We have further supplemented our work with a detailed discussion of the surface term catalog, which we developed to facilitate efficient calculations

A major objective in robotics is to facilitate effective motor learning for task execution. The basic concept of motor learning is the process by which performance improves with practice, and researchers aim to make this learning more efficient. Current studies, however, often examine the outcomes of motor learning in a static manner, without exploring the underlying processes. To promote end-effect investigation to drive motor learning, we propose a method that generates an instantaneous comparison of the current effect to the ideal outcome. This comparison motivates the robot to correct its movement and leads to improved performance. We tested our method in a simple experiment using a spider robot, where the robot learned to navigate through an uneven terrain by navigating towards a virtual target. The results show that the robot achieved faster learning rates and superior performance compared to random-based learning. The study indicates that end-effect investigation can facilitate effective motor learning by promoting direct investigation of the outcome of the robot's movement. The code for the study is available at https://github.com/whui2019/End-Effect-Investigation. The dataset is available at https://github.com/whui2019/End-Effect-Investigation/tree/main/data. The video is available at https://youtu.be/zk8R3M9yR3M. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse goal types but struggle with tasks that involve multiple objectives.
We introduce MemoNav, a novel framework that addresses this challenge by allowing agents to recall and selectively choose relevant memories associated with each objective.
MemoNav effectively handles multiple objectives and diverse goal types, outperforming existing methods on a range of tasks. 
For more information, refer to our paper titled "Selecting Relevant Memories for Visual Navigation" at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.14464. 
We also provide our code and dataset at https://github.com/affunai/MemoNav and multiply-processed YouTube links for benchmark evaluation. 
Our results demonstrate MemoNav's ability to consistently excel in various scenarios, with state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. 
A particularly intriguing finding is that MemoNav significantly outperformsments that have been trained using advanced video data, despite being trained using image data. 
We hypothesize that MemoNav's ability to selectively remember goal-related information contributes to its superior performance. 
We also conduct ablation studies to validate the contributions of individual components and examine alternative memory retrieval methods. 
Overall, MemoNav presents an innovative solution for visual navigation tasks that leverages memory selection to achieve better outcomes. 
To facilitate reproducibility, we include a multiply-processed YouTube dataset for benchmark evaluation, along with our code at https://github.com/affunai/MemoNav. 
Visit our website at https://affunai.github.io/MemoNav for a user-friendly interface that allows you to interact with MemoNav and observe its performance on specific tasks. 
We invite researchers to replicate our work and examine the potential for MemoNav to be applied in diverse real-world scenarios. 
Future research can build upon MemoNav by investigating various memory retrieval techniques and enhancing the framework's overall performance. 
In particular, MemoNav may benefit from the incorporation of multiple memory banks to better retain information and improve navigation outcomes. 
We also plan to expand the framework to enable navigation in three-dimensional environments, which could further boost MemoNav's potential for real-world application. 
It is noteworthy that MemoNav's selective memory retrieval mechanism allows it to outperform models trained using video data, indicating its potential to be adapted for three-dimensional visual navigation tasks. 
We envision MemoNav to be a versatile framework that can be utilized in various real-world scenarios, such as guiding robots to navigate between visually identified objectives in diverse environments.

We conduct a study on the relationship between different methods for describing the growth of local algebras in quantum field theory and conformal field theory.  By matching the definitions of these methods, we create a unified framework that allows us to examine their common properties and behaviors.  A notable finding is that methods that track the growth of local algebras at different scales are inherently linked, and we demonstrate this connection through a set of universal laws governing their relationships.  Furthermore, our research shows that one method's rate of growth is tied to the scale at which another method begins to incorporate contributions from the boundary.  In a specific case, we prove that the growth of local algebras in the Potts quantum field theory follows a particular pattern, and this result offers a potential explanation for a long-standing open problem. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare them with corresponding data. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2021 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to validate factual information and locate supporting evidence for comparative analysis of tabular data. The dataset comprises 945 annotated tables selected from PubMed and Wikipedia, as well as two sub-task categories to assess automated systems: (1) fact validation, which involves determining whether a specific table cell matches the corresponding reference, and (2) evidence finding, which involves pinpointing the exact reference that supports a particular table cell value. We evaluated systems through two tiers of processing: a blind phase and a revised processing stage, incorporating feedback from annotators to adjust system submissions. A total of 29 teams participated in the competition, with 23 submitting systems for task completion. Notably, both top-ranked teams in sub-task 1 (automated fact validation) achieved exceptional results, with scores of 0.87 for revision 1 and 0.94 for revision 2, indicating significant improvement from 0.59 in the initial submission. Meanwhile, the leading team for sub-task 2 (automated evidence finding) showed impressive progression from 0.41 in the initial submission to 0.85 in the revised submission. We will provide an in-depth examination of the results, discuss the systems employed, and explore avenues for future research within this domain. Finally, the dataset, along with the task specifications and source code, is freely accessible for reproduction of our results and potential future applications, hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/emorynlp/SEM-TAB-FACTS. Additionally, the dataset has also been shared on Figshare: https://doi.org/10.6084/ensign.2021.000001.

We address the inherent ambiguity of complex numbers within the mathematical framework of quantum mechanics by proposing that they represent proportional distributions of oscillating physical entities. In this context, complex coefficients are interpreted as magnitudes controlling the fluctuations of corresponding physical properties. Specifically, we examine the harmonic oscillator and apply this interpretation to both constant and time-varying situations. By doing so, we demonstrate that complex coefficients can be expressed in terms of real frequency components and associated oscillating patterns, thereby providing a possible justification for the use of complex Hilbert spaces in quantum mechanics. Furthermore, this understanding may serve as a foundation for developing a real-valued representation of wave functions in non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Although our analysis focuses on simple systems, the proposed idea of fluctuating fields can contribute to a more intuitive and less formal approach to quantum mechanics. It also offers a potential means of introducing and visualizing quantum fluctuations, which is particularly relevant to the ongoing development of relativistic quantum field theories. Lastly, we speculate that this interpretation may also apply to the real vector spaces of the relativistic quantum theory, thereby providing a tangible connection between quantum mechanics and the proposed fluctuating field interpretation. To support our approach, we cite the example of electromagnetic waves, which can be accurately described using real-valued oscillating patterns and corresponding complex coefficients that represent varying amplitudes of these waves. In conclusion, we suggest that the proposed distribution of oscillating physical entities offers a reasonable justification for utilizing complex numbers in quantum mechanics, thereby paving the way for a real-valued formulation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics and potentially serving as a foundation for the real-valued representation of the relativistic quantum field theory. It also provides a predictable means of introducing and handling quantum fluctuations, which may aid in understanding the behavior of particles in low-energy scenarios. In addition, we hope that this interpretation will inspire those reading this to better visualize and connect with the underlying physical principles governing quantum mechanics. It is particularly notable for its potential application to the real-valued representation of the relativistic quantum field theory, which may serve as a guiding principle for researchers, and may also provide a meaningful and intuitive understanding of the physical world at the lowest levels of existence. We therefore hope that our approach will encourage readers to join us in exploring the underlying physical principles governing quantum mechanics, and to share our vision of developing a tangible and intuitive connection to the quantum world, which we believe can be achieved through the proposed interpretation. These notes document my process of reviewing equations for distant groundwater movement 
and water table changes. They note that the current set of equations assumes steady-state 
conditions, neglects vertical flow and relies on an incorrect approximation that equates 
horizontal conductivity with depth. Additionally, the widely used "thin water table" 
approximation is not applicable for shallow or highly conductive aquifers. Furthermore, 
the widely adopted "sharp interface" approximation assumes vertical flow is negligible, yet 
overlooks that this assumption may not always hold. Finally, these notes point out 
that many numerical models mistakenly assume steady-state conditions and use an incorrect 
approximation, even when such assumptions are not valid. As such, these notes aim to 
encourage a more thorough examination of equation assumptions in other areas of hydrology 
and groundwater flow modeling.

By limiting the comparison range, PrunedDTW disables backsliding, resulting in a more linear time complexity of O(m+n) and enables real-time proximity searches. Nevertheless, the PrunedDTW method only functions accurately when the first pattern reaches its end, meaning its results may not align with the DTW distance in some cases. To resolve this limitation, we introduce a modified version of PrunedDTW, referred to as EDPrunedDTW, which ensures early discarding compared to the original PrunedDTW. In this study, we integrate EDPrunedDTW into the PrunedDTW-based similarity search framework, aiming to accelerate query processing and reduce memory consumption. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed PrunedDTW-based method outperforms existing DTW-based methods in terms of runtime performance and memory usage while producing comparable accuracy levels. Additionally, the early discarding property of PrunedDTW enables the development of more efficient index structures, allowing databases to be indexed in a timely manner. Importantly, the proposed approach retains both PrunedDTW's computational complexity and early discarding properties simultaneously, marking a significant improvement over previous DTW-based methods. To showcase our approach, we introduced an open-source PrunedDTW-indexed database using EuStockMarket time-series data, which can be accessed via a GitHub repository. Our approach has potential applications in various domains, such as finance and audio, where the need to evaluate the similarity of time-series patterns is common. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide extensive feedback
after completion or prompt conceptual feedback throughout the learning process.
In this research, we examine how instructor-student interactions are affected
when inquiry-based testing, which encourages questioning, is integrated into
class assignments. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 120 college
students, who were divided into two groups: one received immediate feedback
and the other was prompted to think critically. As a result, students in the
conceptual feedback group demonstrated higher test scores, greater retention of
testing concepts, and more engaging class participation compared to their
peers in the thorough feedback group. Additionally, instructors reported that
the conceptual feedback group was easier to manage and provided more in-depth
feedback. An investigation of student survey responses revealed that the
retention benefits observed with the conceptual feedback group may be attributed
to changed attitudes toward testing. This research shows that inquiry-based
testing can be an effective way to combine testing education and promote
conceptual feedback. Such an approach can lead to improved educational
outcomes, increased student engagement, and reduced instructor workload. This
model can potentially be applied to other areas of software education. Words:

In practical applications, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have demonstrated excellent performance in node classification based on graph data. However, these models face challenges when dealing with large graphs, leading to accuracy deterioration. To improve GCN's capability beyond shallow models, researchers have proposed multiple approaches, but a comprehensive understanding of their limitations remains elusive. This study conducts a thorough evaluation of current approaches and highlights the need for more accurate model representation. To achieve this, we identify GCN's oversmoothing issue, which arises from repeatedly applying graph convolutional layers, ultimately resulting in model simplification. Through experimental comparison of GCN-based methods on six benchmark datasets, we validate the models' categorization and provide insights into their strengths and weaknesses. Moreover, we establish a comprehensive model classification system and conduct a detailed analysis of each category. To enhance GCN-based models' performance, we propose strategies for addressing the oversmoothing issue, including leveraging self-supervised learning, utilizing stack of GCN layers with various widths, selecting appropriate activation functions, and selecting suitable graph pooling methods. These functions maintain symmetry with respect to $k_\parallel$ and $k_\perp$ and are connected through a relationship similar to that of Dirac's equation, enabling them to capture the essence of strong interactions. One of these functions, however, exhibits freedom from non-perturbative influences, thereby providing a more direct mapping of $k_\perp$ dependencies. Notably, these functions are capable of expressing both quasi-particle and antiparticle behaviors. Additionally, they can be used to describe $k_\perp$ distributions of gluons, effectively extending our approach to all particles involved in strong interactions. As an illustration of its utility, this formalism is applied to re-evaluate collision energy dependencies in the mass spectra of various hadrons. Our method, however, does not preclude the emergence of non-perturbative components in the distribution functions that may potentially give rise to phenomena beyond the scope of perturbative physics. We establish an association between certain regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties and a type of finite, graded poset, which can be partitioned based on a key transformation. This partition is linked to the construction of specific Gr\"obner bases for an associated algebra, resulting from a particular generation mechanism related to the poset's elements. Moreover, this algebra's Gr\"obner basis generation leads to a novel demonstration of a significant theorem regarding Frobenius partitions, as proven by the second author and T. Williamson. Additionally, we have found that the underlying posets exhibit significant symmetries, which can be quantitatively reflected in the structure of their Gr\"obner bases, as well as the central charge in the context of Laumon's sectionality criterion for Hessenberg varieties. This technique allows for the computation of central charges for a wide range of Hessenberg functions. In a broader scope, our method may contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the algebra through the filtration of its elements according to their combinatorial significance. This, in turn, could lead to insights on the corresponding K-theory class's behavior under the action of certain algebraic transformations, as specified in a recent conjecture by the first author and R. Phan. We have found that our method yields the exact results predicted by this conjecture for a particular class of Hessenberg varieties associated with the algebra. We expect our geometric vertex decomposition to find applications in fields such as combinatorics, algebraic geometry, and physics, as well as in the study of Uq(g)-modules, where q is a positive real value greater than 1. Lastly, our analysis provides the basis for an extensive study on the early generators of Uq(g), and we have discovered that our poset structure can be generalized to the context of Solomon's algebra for finite W, which is a nilpotent algebra, under the action of the W group. We have found that the central charge in the context of Laumon's sectionality criterion for Hessenberg varieties can also be computed using our method, as well as in the context of Solomon's algebra for finite W, where the results predicted by a recent conjecture by the first author and R. Phan are exactly reached. We have further found that our poset structure can be applied to the context of Hessenberg varieties for type An, where we have computed the central charge and the results predicted by a recent conjecture by the first author and R. Our study investigates the creative potential of neural networks as tools for artistic creation, particularly through the use of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). By employing a painting brush as an input device, we demonstrate that VAEs can be exploited to generate diverse images. Notably, our research reveals that painters who are inexperienced with neural networks still manage to create novel images even when inspired by the model's capabilities. Interestingly, the artists' outcomes exhibit a noticeable correlation across different painting sessions, indicating that the VAE's capabilities continue to influence their work even after initial exposure. Importantly, our findings emphasize the significance of interactive mechanisms in facilitating collaborative human-neural network creative partnerships. We address the anomalies observed in $K$ decays and $B$ meson systems, adopting a vector-like composite model where a vector quark $Q$ combines with the Higgs boson to produce the standard model quark masses. The model inherently includes a tree-level diagram explaining the $K^+$$\to$$\pi^+$ anomaly, and we find it consistent with unitarity constraints involving the matrix element $Qud$. Additionally, we have determined that this model can account for a $1$ part per million deviation in $B^0$$\to$$K^0$$\pi^0$ zero momentum limit, and it naturally generates a small irreducible CP asymmetry. However, a detailed fit across multiple fronts reveals that the model fails to adequately explain the full scope of the $K$ decay anomalies when subjected to a thorough sensitivity analysis. Although we identified parameter regions able to explain individual anomalies, these areas are found to be disconnected. Nevertheless, a related complication in the $B$ meson system, specifically affecting the $B^0$$\to$$K^0$$\pi^0$ transition, may pose a problem unless the mass of the lightest vector-like quark $Q$ can be accounted for at a scale of approximately $501$ GeV. The model also leaves unaddressed the $K^0$$\to$$\pi^0$ anomaly and invites further investigation into potential connections with lepton-flavor universality violations in $B$ meson decays as well as issues with gauge boson compositeness. Our analysis underscores the need for a more nuanced understanding of this type of vector-like composite model in order to effectively resolve observed anomalies in meson systems. Academic research paper citations contain valuable information like knowledge-seeking questions, answers, and contexts that remain underutilized due to the lack of a suitable interface for querying and retrieving relevant papers. To address this, we've compiled a dataset of 3,779 questions and answers from 1,048 researchers and users of the KnowledgeStep platform, helping us achieve our goal of creating a system for finding relevant papers based on users' informational needs. Our approach involves developing an ensemble-based system that suggests questions, answers, and research papers to users, facilitating knowledge work through targeted search and an informed language understanding of scientific knowledge. 

Additionally, we've conducted an in-depth analysis of our dataset and found that natural language processing models perform better when combining multiple sources of text from research papers, along with questions from similar domains, as input. Model ensembles also exhibit improved performance when processing text from diverse scientific fields, and when incorporating context from entire research papers rather than just abstracts. These findings have guided us in designing the anfresco platform for finding and linking relevant research papers based on users' knowledge needs. To ensure the quality of our dataset, we've implemented an evaluation process that assesses the accuracy of provided questions, answers, and their relevance to research papers through a crowd-sourced testing procedure. 

Through an initial evaluation of our dataset and designed system, we've achieved a 70% success rate in linking questions with relevant research papers and providing accurate answers. Moreover, 80% of users reported finding the platform useful, and more than 90% preferred targeted searches over general search engines. These results indicate that the anfresco platform can effectively facilitate knowledge work by providing targeted searches for relevant research papers based on users' knowledge needs. To further refine our dataset and approach, we're seeking feedback from the academic community through a crowd-sourced testing procedure, aiming to achieve a 0.90 success rate in linking questions with relevant research papers and providing accurate answers by including additional metadata from research papers and incorporating contextual information from entire papers. 

In achieving this goal, we're collaborating with knowledge system developers to establish a possible future trajectory for targeting searches and improving the understanding of scientific knowledge through an informed language analysis. To facilitate this, we're making our compiled dataset and designed approach available to the academic community for further development and refinement. 
Our approach involves leveraging the accumulated knowledge from research papers in various domains for answering questions and providing targeted searches for other questions, enabling a range of possible applications beyond academic knowledge work and providing an informed language understanding of scientific knowledge.

Acronyms and abbreviations are commonly used in various domains like government reports, medical research, software programming, and technical writing on the web. MadDog is an interactive web-based tool designed for teaching computer science students the task of acronym disambiguation. Currently, no comprehensive platform exists that combines acronym definition lookup and context-specific disambiguation. MadDog addresses this gap by integrating three key components: a database of domain-specific acronym definitions, a web interface for user input and processing, and a programming environment for users to write and run code on. The tool guides students through the entire workflow of acronym identification, definition extraction, and disambiguation using their compiled code. MadDog also offers an automatic evaluation option to compare the performance of students' codes on predefined test cases. The tool is freely accessible at https://cag.cs.stonybrook.edu/maddog/. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of MadDog in enhancing the performance of computer science students learning Java or Python. The tool can be utilized for teaching various programming skills using API libraries for acronym definition lookup and custom programming tasks. MadDog supports its users by providing a knowledge base of 502 acute chest radiography abbreviations and 281 computed tomography abbreviations. Moreover, its database is expandable to accommodate a wide range of domains including medical research and government reports. MadDog is versatile, allowing instructors to modify or replace its predefined input data for teaching different acronym datasets in various contexts. To improve the tool's usability, instructors can upload their own datasets of acronym definitions using MadDog's interactive web interface or via a downloadable Java or Python zip file via email. The tool evaluates student performance using an automatic evaluator or by comparing the output of each student's code on a predefined test suite. The tool's efficacy was evaluated in a study that involved 54 computer science students who demonstrated improved performance after using MadDog. The tool outperformed human performance with an average of 92% accuracy and provided a mean absolute error of 3.14 when identifying and confirming acronym definitions using users' compiled code. The tool's documentation is available at https://cag.cs.stonybrook.edu/maddog_docs/. Its Java and Python source code can be accessed at https://cag.cs.stonybrook.edu/maddog_source.html. Our innovative approach to DNA storage introduces a new, flexible structure that enhances the existing "generalized suffix tree" framework, offering several key improvements. Firstly, it introduces a clear hierarchy of data organizations to optimize read and write access. Secondly, it introduces a unified method for managing updates across all levels of the hierarchy. This comprehensive system streamlines the process of modifying existing data, eliminating the need to switch between different methods and algorithms as data is retrieved from faster, but more expensive, and updated in slower, but more cost-effective, storage facilities. This uniform strategy allows for seamless data migration between the fast and slow storages, thus far a major source of complexity. This structure targets the specific challenges posed by write operations, providing an efficient solution that can be applied to a wide range of DNA storage use cases. Our results show that this organization remains highly efficient even after numerous updates, validating our approach's effectiveness in the context of DNA storage. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this new structure offers superior read performance, especially when combined with additional optimizations not previously available to DNA storage systems. Our work enables the development of a robust, efficient, and highly scalable data management system for DNA storage, facilitating the practical application of this technology to high data rate video caching. This application is included as a concrete example in our research. Read and write performance for our current DNA storage system were evaluated, leading to the discovery of the need for a data placement policy that strikes a balance between these competing priorities. This characterization of storage needs guides the design of a novel storage organization that enhances the existing generalized suffix tree framework, offering a clear hierarchy of data organizations and efficient read and write access. This optimized system was found to offer a read/write ratio of 1000:1, surpassing the current state-of-the-art ratio of 10:1. This research further refines the storage organization by introducing a method for managing updates, ensuring that data is only written to storage at the lowest possible level. Our results show that this approach offers a 25% reduction in the number of writes compared to a previous optimization. Additionally, we have developed a data management system that combines our storage organization with an efficient policy for managing data updates. This combination was found to offer a 30% reduction in the number of requests needed to update existing data in DNA storage. This work enables the practical application of DNA storage to video caching, offering improvements in both read and write performance. Furthermore, our research has characterized the needs of high data rate video, guiding the design of a novel DNA storage organization

This progress in momentum topology is driven by exotic nodal lines, which are linear dispersions in momentum space that have topological characteristics. This review focuses on nodal lines resulting from the intersection of two topological bands, examining the underlying physics and the various realizations of these features in systems that are not necessarily quantum. It also discusses recent experiments employing photonic systems, along with developments in other platforms, including bosonic systems and materials exhibiting superconductivity. One particular area of focus is the realization of non-linear nodal lines through the combination of two topological bands with different powers of the wavevector. This topic is also supplemented by an online public database containing a wide range of nodal line topological structures. This public database can provide researchers with access to diverse momentum topological structures, including various types of nodal lines, as well as novel gyroscopic phenomena and Weyl points that have not been covered in this review. It is expected that the public database will facilitate research in the field of momentum topography. This will involve studying various artificial materials and their applications in photonic and other fields, as well as exploring the connection between electronic momentum topography and nodal lines resulting from the zero-energy states at vortices, as observed in superconductors and topological materials. In oscillatory media, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to traveling waves, which are crucial in various cellular networks. These waves, which are controlled by ion channels, are essential in circadian, olfactory, and cardiac systems, with a particular importance in cardiac rhythm regulation, where waves from specialized pacemaker regions ensure a coordinated heartbeat. Researchers are interested in understanding how fast waves originating from pacemaker areas can spread to adjacent regions. To achieve this, we developed analytical methods to estimate pacemaker-generated wave speeds in two-dimensional and three-dimensional tissues, using simple and accurate calculations that can be applied to real-world applications. Recent research on transport networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling demand and system performance probabilistically, rather than fixedly. This work addresses the challenge of making statistical inference about origin-destination road usage patterns, which are represented as a stochastic matrix, using observational data from transport systems. We investigate two main approaches: one, based on large-data assumptions, uses linear algebra and matrix factorization to estimate demand patterns; the other, rooted in Bayesian inference, incorporates prior knowledge and uncertainty, leading to the development of posterior distributions for the demand matrix. These methods are applied to real-world data from the North Jylland region of Denmark, where day-to-day demand patterns are estimated through the analysis of traffic congestion patterns. The results show that Bayesian inference tends to produce more precise estimates, particularly when prior knowledge is available. Additionally, the Bayesian approach exhibits greater resilience to sampling noise and irregularities in the data, making it more suitable for small and medium-sized datasets. The work presents a novel application of transport models in practical inference problems. It contributes to the existing literature by integrating transport and statistical models, merging the paradigms of relativism and realism in transport modeling and Bayesian inference. The research offers transport practitioners and researchers a practical framework for estimating origin-destination road patterns and managing uncertainty, which can inform strategic policy-making and decision-making processes. The study also creates opportunities for further integration of transport and statistical modeling, paving the way for future developments in probabilistic demand modeling and inference. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal learning capabilities. The dataset facilitates the development of unified representations for sheet music, song lyrics, and audio. Combining existing datasets, MusicTM-Dataset comprises three core sections: AudioTM, SheetMusicTM, and LyricTM. The AudioTM segment features pairs of corresponding audio, transcriptions, and lyrics from the Jamestowne dataset. The SheetMusicTM section, powered by MIDI files from the MuseScore library, includes accompanying lyrics. LyricTM, derived from lyrics without audible content, comprises three datasets: LargeSong, Lyricpedia, and OpenLit. Our methodology employs a two-stage approach to pre-train three independent language models, one each for audio spectrograms, MIDI tokens, and language-based representations of lyrics and sheet music. The proposed method enables robust zero-shot learning and cross-modal retrieval tasks. To showcase the MusicTM-Dataset's potential, we experimented with various cross-modal learning techniques, demonstrating improved performance in retrieval tasks. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/philcrump/music-tm-dataset and https://www.csc.kth.se/~philcr/musictm-dataset/. If you utilize the MusicTM-Dataset, please cite our paper at https://doi.org/10.1109/ICME52576.2021.6406551. Recent research in stellarators has highlighted the need for a design optimization framework with minimal dependence on the magnetic configuration's specific characteristics.
This study introduces an enhanced coil design approach, building upon previous work, which enables the creation of stellarators with a wide range of magnetic ellipticity and quasi-axisymmetry.
A demonstration design was developed utilizing a generalized NCT loss minimization method, which demonstrated its effectiveness in finding optimal solutions across various configuration types.

Due to the large size of these models, direct solutions are impractical, making multilevel preconditioning methods viable options. Nonetheless, a common problem with this approach is the difficulty in accurately estimating the inverse of the heart model's stiffness matrix. Although second-order approximation in multilevel preconditioning systems may initially contribute to accuracy, it introduces sparsity that hinders performance when dealing with multiple levels. In contrast, third-order approximation tends to result in a more efficient matrix representation; however, implementing it increases computational costs. This work evaluates the performance of two such multilevel preconditioning systems with third-order approximation, balancing efficiency and accuracy, and demonstrates the possibility of achieving a third-order, two-level implementation that surpasses a second-order, multi-level approach in solver convergence, all while maintaining manageable computational costs for 2D and 3D models of realistic heart muscles. Mobile IAB can provide advertisers with precise targeting capabilities and measure advertising effectiveness, leading to higher returns on investment. Compared to traditional television advertising, however, mobile IAB faces unique difficulties in achieving accuracy and validity due to differences in measurement methods and metrics. This paper examines the pitfalls of traditional IAB measurement and highlights the complexities of verifying advertising effectiveness during transitions between online and offline periods. To address these issues, the authors propose an integrated approach for tracking IAB across both mobile and TV platforms, emphasizing the importance of convergence to provide a comprehensive understanding of advertising impact. Achieving this requires overcoming key obstacles, and the authors highlight potential solutions to these challenges, paving the way for further development in this area. Ultimately, the authors call for industry-wide collaboration to bridge the gaps between advertising measurement, analytics, and advertising-driven business models. The authors hope that their approach will stimulate discussions and promote advancements in mobile IAB measurement and advertising effectiveness verification. The interpretation of quantum wave functions remains contentious, and several methods have been proposed for determining physical property distributions. This study examines one such method, the Born rule, by exploring its justification and comparison with an alternative approach, both of which yield a Laplace transform of the wave function and lead to similar results for property distributions. However, the conventional Born method exhibits a critical advantage in simplicity and accuracy, particularly in cases involving broad distributions. This advantage is illustrated through a comparison of two methods for calculating electron diamagnetism, where the conventional Born method demonstrates greater precision with reduced computational complexity. Additionally, our analysis indicates that a direct comparison of property densities is inappropriate due to discrepancies in their behaviors, particularly as parameters approach critical values. This study also clarifies the relationship between the Born method and classical probability theory, demonstrating that the latter's requirements are not fully met by wave functions in unbounded domains. Our investigation further extends the conventional Born method to complex phases, where it yields a real, even probability density from an odd wave function, and we provide supporting evidence from momentum sampling. Furthermore, our analysis explores the direct determination of magnetic susceptibility distributions using the wave function's derivative, which can be achieved through numerical differentiation of the wave function in real space. This method, known as real-space differentiation, is demonstrated with an example and shown to be comparable to the conventional Born method. Finally, our investigation examines the direct determination of electron magnetization as a function of radiation frequency in radiology, which can be calculated through the wave function's derivative in reciprocal space, and we showcase its application with an example. Our analysis concludes with a consideration of the conventional Born method's domain generalization and potential violations, and we propose modifications to address potential discrepancies and to facilitate direct property determinations. We also explore the potential for wave function transformations in imaginary phases to improve bound wave function behaviors in negative energy domains. Our investigation provides arguments for maintaining the conventional Born method for property distribution calculations, and we recommend against alternative methods due to their comparative inadequacy, complexity, and potential failures. Our analysis seeks to clarify the conventional Born method's purposes and domains, and we endeavor to distill its fundamental principles into simple proofs, which may also provide new insights into quantum theory. Our investigation attempts to revive and reinterpret the conventional Born method as a fundamental principle of quantum theory and seeks to reconcile it with modern quantum field theory. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, which can incorporate knowledge from past experiences to perform well on subsequent tasks. To address this issue, researchers require platforms for comprehensive and systematic evaluation of their techniques. Unfortunately, developing such evaluation environments is often overlooked, with researchers often relying on simplified benchmarks that fail to mimic the complexities of real-world problems. In this work, we introduce L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation framework that simulates an ongoing process of exploration and learning across a continuously expanding portfolio of diverse learning tasks. This benchmark is grounded in a realistic scenario of discovering and mastering learning objectives in unfamiliar environments. In addition to its core challenges, L2Explorer also presents instances of partial coverage, where agents may encounter tasks that are easier to master than those they could accomplish. Our research involves rigorous evaluation of established lifelong learning methods, which reveals areas for improvement and inspires future research in this domain. The source code for L2Explorer and our experimental setup is openly available, enabling reproduction of our results and inspiring future research. Our research aims to contribute to the advancement of evaluation methods that are more realistic and meaningful, ultimately leading to more significant and impactful breakthroughs in the field of lifelong reinforcement learning. In addition, we investigate several promising strategies for motivating robust generalization through the concept of 'preparing' for anticipated future tasks. These experimental studies serve as a starting point for stimulating further research in this area. Overall, our research emphasizes the need to address theoretical limitations, devise more realistic evaluation protocols, and explore novel approaches for enhancing the lifelong learning methods that will drive progress in this domain. The source code for L2Explorer and our experimental results is openly accessible on https://github.com/facebookresearch/L2Explorer. In addition, a video demonstrating our environment is posted on YouTube at https://youtu.be/3H0Q34L4TDM.
