We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
Its key components allow for transaction amount validation, link generation for previously sent funds, and exclusion of visible values from transaction data.
In particular, Delegated RingCT improves upon the original RingCT by incorporating a publicly verifiable mechanism for identifying fake transactions and enhancing general RingCT functionality with support for stealth addresses.
Furthermore, Delegated RingCT includes optimized functionality for maintaining transaction data integrity and efficient processing of stealth address-related transactions.
Our implementation of Delegated RingCT is currently being integrated into the Nano wallet and blockchain applications. 
For convenience, the specification of Delegated RingCT is presented in detail, and the source code is publicly accessible via a GitHub repository at https://github.com/keicki/nano-ringct. 
In addition, a comprehensive documentation of Delegated RingCT is available via IPFS at https://ipfs.

In various applications of linear algebra, solving multiple related systems of equations under different coefficients can be an essential task.  Researchers have previously developed algorithms based on the common assumption that the systems' underlying grid remains unchanged, but these algorithms may not be optimal when the grid changes, which occurs when the problem is said to be unsymmetric.  To tackle this issue, we introduce the concept of space toughness as a measure of efficiency in handling different grids for a given system of linear equations.  It is shown that common algorithms have a space toughness of more than one, indicating they do not offer the most efficient solution.  We then introduce new algorithms with space toughness of one, effectively providing more direct solutions to the problem.  We also extend the developed techniques to handle matrix decomposition.  In addition, we tested the presented methods against existing approaches using benchmark suites and observed significant improvements in memory usage and efficiency.  The novel algorithms are implemented in an open-source package named SpaceTracker.  It is further demonstrated that space toughness can be an invaluable tool in understanding algorithmic variability through the analysis of real-world applications.  The work presents space toughness as a valuable framework for designing and evaluating algorithms to solve linear equations efficiently.  It is based on a fundamental observation of linear algebra variability. These results are compared with theoretical predictions, and the capacity to detect deviations from the expected values in future experiments at the LHC is investigated. This includes a proposed 100 fb$^{-1}$ dataset, which would increase the sensitivity to new physics at 95% confidence by up to 30%, and a proposed 3 ab$^{-1}$ dataset, which would improve this by up to 100%. A rapidly evolving field coupled with limited availability of experimental data in real-world applications results in statistical uncertainties that can significantly impact predictions and decision-making processes. Improving model accuracy through Bayesian analysis incorporates uncertainty, yet relies heavily on prior distribution parameters that are often difficult to establish. This work proposes a novel approach, called collaborative data-driven modeling, where multiple Bayesian models share resources, and their parameters are optimized using shared data, thereby eliminating the need to set up uncertain prior distributions. This framework is versatile, supporting various types of models and efficient, suitable for large datasets. Our approach is successfully applied to two applications, including predictive modeling for integer domains and state estimation in dynamic systems. The former involves ascending ascending paths in bilevel optimization, while the latter uses reactive power control strategies in power systems. The results demonstrate that our methodology outperforms traditional Bayesian methods in precision and computational efficiency. This research aims to inspire a new class of models and algorithms, and the accompanying software, including model implementations and example data, is available at cdm.io. The way bits within coded data connect through degree-degree correlations significantly influences how well LDPC codes resist errors in channels where data loss occurs. Research has established methods for measuring degree-degree correlations in regular and irregular LDPC codes, but these techniques haven't been adapted for designs that change with every message, known as density-evolution (DE) codes. In this research, a method is developed for measuring degree-degree correlations in Slepian-Wolf coded data and the way it affects the performance of binary deletion channels. It's found that degree-degree correlations in SW codes lead to an early loss of information and a failure to reach the channel's capacity, besides limiting the code's ability to achieve the maximum possible error-correcting radius. Two methods are proposed to control degree-degree correlations: one involves rearranging the code's parity-check matrix and, if that's not possible due to pre-existing connections, a method of breaking existing connections. It's shown that these methods can expand the range of radial distances a code can have and allow a family of LDPC codes to reach the maximum possible error-correcting radius. The techniques presented can be applied to enhance existing LDPC code designs. Additionally, the tools developed can be used to investigate the properties and potential applications of density-evolution codes. It's confirmed that these codes can offer superior performance in channels where data loss occurs and achieve higher radial distances than codes with constant connections. Nevertheless, controlling degree-degree correlations may result in decreased performance in channels that cause errors instead of data loss. Further research may be needed to successfully use these codes on channels that cause errors instead of data loss. The techniques and approaches presented can be applied to develop improved LDPC codes for channels where data loss occurs and achieve better results than codes with constant connections. The boundary between density-evolution codes and traditional LDPC codes can offer new possibilities for designing better codes. Similarly, degree-degree correlations can be measured in convolutional codes to investigate their properties and potential applications. In theory, degree-degree correlations can impact convolutional codes' ability to achieve the maximum possible error-correcting radius. The techniques and approaches presented can potentially improve the performance of conventional LDPC codes used in practical systems. Galaxy cluster subclusters are encapsulated in cooling clouds that eventually vanish as their gas dissipates, a process influenced by factors like convection, magnetic fields, and radiation. We simulated 10 billion years of accretion and loss for 12 subclusters within a $\sim 0.5$ arcminute radius, considering 72 combinations of cooling rates, magnetic field strengths, and thermal conductivity. The formation and destruction of these cooling clouds follow identical patterns, despite significant variations in initial conditions. Strong magnetic fields and high cooling rates break clouds more quickly, while high thermal conductivity actually delays destruction, likely due to increased system heat. After 1 billion years, all systems show a core gas density above 10 times the initial value, whereas the surrounding atmosphere becomes less dense. This density discrepancy creates a situation in which further cooling creates more dense core areas, eventually leading to subcluster mergers that could yield massive, star-forming gas supplies. The rate at which this material is converted to stars depends on various factors, including a possible initial burst of star formation triggered by the initial cloud breakdown. Overall, our findings indicate that the equilibrium between cloud formation and destruction determines the amount of accreted gas available for star formation. Moreover, the role of magnetic fields, cooling processes, and thermal conduction must be carefully considered in order to accurately determine the resulting stellar masses. A crucial factor in our simulation is the effectiveness of magnetic field at breaking down cooling clouds, making it essential to determine the actual magnetic field strength within these subclusters. Additionally, our data indicate the importance of large-scale cluster potentials in equilibrating the rates of cloud breakdown and accretion, which could also be influenced by other galaxy cluster subclusters. This study represents a fundamental step in understanding the dynamics of galaxy cluster subclusters, their development and evolution, and the role of various physical processes within them. Moreover, our findings provide new insights into the accretion rates of galaxy clusters, which could affect their further development and the ultimate stellar masses of their gas supplies. In turn, this research can be applied to simulate the development of other galaxy cluster subclusters, as well as their potential to form new cluster fragments. A key consideration for such future studies is the potential for bias resulting from the fact that our simulation sample was derived from a particular type of galaxy cluster, namely loose spirals. The objective-synthesis method for voice synthesis disregards linguistic knowledge, relying solely on acoustic information to create new sounds. We explore using untreated audio as input to this method, bypassing the usual transcription step, to make the system more robust and adaptable. A significant challenge arises from the need for rapid and accurate acoustic unit segmentation to provide the synthesis algorithm with essential frequency domain templates. To address this, we developed a novel approach to identifying these units within a short timeframe without requiring access to written language or previous synthesized speech. This segmentation technique is rooted in human listeners' auditory feedback and is evaluated based on the success of derived from perception (DFP) synthesis systems to replicate held audio recordings. New technologies such as voice assistants and intelligent robots would greatly benefit from being able to create new voices without needing transcripts, a capability we call zero-resource voice synthesis. We examine a related strategy involving the synthesis of acoustic units identified through the analysis of speech, a process we call zero-resource synthesis. This strategy requires the automatic detection of phonetic segments in speech, and we propose leveraging listeners' auditory feedback to achieve this end. To evaluate our approach to extracting acoustic units for synthesis, we compare the performance of derived from perception (DFP) synthesis systems to those using transcriptions from automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Notably, our method achieves a vocal similarity score of 83% and a similarity score of 76% as recommended by the Voice Quality Assessment challenge, surpassing the ASR-based method and serving as a starting point for future enhancements. Moreover, we demonstrate that a system trained on a single voice can successfully replicate a second speaker's voice, achieving a vocal similarity score of 79%, and that a system trained on short sentences can extend its output to cover entire paragraphs. A system trained to transcribe its own speech to create new voices, a capability we call self-derived synthesis, also emerges as a viable option, yielding vocal similarity scores of 67% and 62% for short and long inputs, respectively. Building on these findings, we propose several strategies for refining the extraction of acoustic units for synthesis, including incorporating prior knowledge of language, limiting units to those with consistent meanings, and leveraging auditory feedback from multiple speakers, which we term derived from perception by aggregation (DPA). This approach requires integrating the transcripts of multiple speakers to improve the detection and definition of acoustic units for synthesis, and we show that a DPA-based synthesis system trained on a single speaker achieves a vocal similarity score of 81%. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' movement is a complex task that involves solving a high-dimensional optimization problem. By breaking down this problem into smaller, interconnected optimization tasks, we can leverage structured coupling relationships between these tasks to facilitate motion planning. Each task is an individual convex optimization problem, and we introduce coupled relaxation schemes that utilize McCormick envelope relaxations to model their interactions. To apply these schemes effectively, we develop a novel method to approximate relevant quadratic expressions with bounded variables. The proposed multi-task approach is a convex optimization problem that addresses limitations in previous motion planning strategies. By testing our method on diverse robot configurations and optimization scenarios, we showcase its capability to accomplish complex tasks and outperform competing methods in various applications. These movements result in the coffee liquid shifting between ordered and turbulent states as the carrying hand moves in circular motions. The primary factors influencing the liquid's motion are the amplitude and frequency of the carrier's movements. In the context of pendulum dynamics, the liquid's transition between these states can be less than 10% when the movement frequency is within the parametric resonance range. To better understand this phenomenon, we developed a mathematical model based on the Lagrange equation to analyze the behavior of the coupled oscillator and diffuser systems. Our results reveal how the amplitude and frequency of the carrier's movements affect the liquid's motion and where within the hand's circular motion the liquid might reside. Our theoretical findings are further supported by experimental observations shown in the video included in the article. In our research paper, focusing on the limitations of standard decentralized algorithms, we develop a new method to handle the challenges of decentralized training in machine learning across connected networks. This challenge involves minimizing the overall cost function for multiple clients connected in a graph structure, where each client has its unique data distribution. To overcome this difficulty, we employ distributional robustness concepts to create a robust optimization problem, and then based on the worst-case data distribution, we devise a decentralized training algorithm using the smallest possible majorization method. This new algorithm, DR-DSGD, and its associated convergence results, demonstrate a $O(\sqrt{K}}/N)$ convergence rate, where $K$ represents the number of clients and $N$ is the largest degree in the graph. Furthermore, we have tested our algorithm by applying it to standard machine learning models, and the results show that DR-DSGD achieves faster convergence compared to current state-of-the-art methods. This significant improvement confirms that DR-DSGD is more efficient, and thus, a more effective decentralized training method. Our code is publicly available for other researchers to use. We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, we derive equations that enable us to calculate the volume of the initial energy state and the number of gluons within it utilizing final-state particle data. This allows us to investigate the characteristics of the initial energy state in relativistic nuclear collisions. We leverage this information to extract the characteristics of the energy state in the most primitive stages of cosmic matter, thereby extending our understanding to times less than $10^{-12}$ seconds. Additionally, we develop methods to relate attractor parameters to observable quantities, such as particle spectra and 2-component fluctuations in mean squared transverse momentum. These developments offer new perspectives for extracting initial conditions from experimental data and enhance our understanding of the transition from energy states to freely flowing matter. Furthermore, we identify a thermodynamic process causing particles to be produced at a rate higher than predicted by simple scaling theories, and we outline avenues for an in-depth theoretical explanation. This research explores how solar radiation pressure affects the movement of artificial objects in orbit around the Earth. By employing a formal mathematical method and analyzing the object's orbit equations, we identify and study a specific type of resonance that can impact the object's trajectory. Our findings reveal that, theoretically, the resonance occurs frequently but, through numerical simulations, we find that it tends to happen less often in reality. Moreover, we've developed an approximate formula to estimate the time intervals between resonances that can be applied for a broad range of orbits. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that solar radiation pressure's impact on the Earth's artificial objects is mainly sporadic and, as such, the resonance phenomenon is largely transient. Nonetheless, it's crucial to account for it, especially when studying the long-term movements of artificial objects over extended periods. Interestingly, our investigations into the resonance phenomenon also reveal its potential connection to a well-documented astronomical phenomenon, known as the "Great Arrow." Lastly, focusing on the resonance's effects, we've discovered that it essentially doesn't alter the artificial object's orbital shape but does change its orientation. Interestingly, our findings also suggest that the resonance affects the object's nodal precession period. To verify our theoretical math-based results, we performed over 15 billion numerical simulations, covering a vast range of orbits. In particular, we examined orbits with eccentricities up to 0.95, focusing on objects whose orbits intersect with the Earth. Our analyses also take into account various factors, such as the Earth's slightly ellipsoidal shape and its gravitational pull. It's worth noting that, as artificial objects age, their orbits change due to the solar radiation pressure's impact. As a result, we've categorized the resonance phenomenon into two distinct periods. First, there's the initial phase, driven by the solar radiation pressure's rapid changes, and the latter phase, characterized to date, that is driven by the Earth's gravitational pull. Consequently, the resonance phenomenon is primarily associated with the solar radiation pressure's impact during the initial phase, while in the latter phase, the resonance phenomenon is essentially non-existent. The Cauchy distribution, characterized by a single parameter b, represents a proper ranking of location-scale family members. Calculating the mean of this distribution is impossible, and thus traditional confidence intervals are unusable. However, by leveraging the sample median and half-length as an estimator, we develop a confidence interval for the parameter b of the Cauchy distribution. Additionally, we define and provide the formula for the square of the Cauchy distribution's interval estimator, showcasing its consistency and applying this to the parameter b under both simple random sampling and rank-based sampling methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the interval estimator's performance through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness, particularly in rank-based sampling, and highlighting the importance of accurately determining sample sizes to achieve desired confidence levels and width specifications. The provided R code facilitates the implementation of these methods and simulation results. As an extension, we apply the proposed methods to the location-scale family, obtaining reliable estimates of both location (m) and scale (s) parameters, and thus the standard deviation (σ) as well. The theoretical basis for these methods stems from well-established principles in nonparametric statistics, including the consistency of median-based estimators, as well as the distribution of ranking statistics. The study presents its main findings, supporting previous works on Cauchy distributions, and providing novel contributions to the literature on this topic. The parameter b's confidence interval exhibits variability, but ultimately converges to a specific value, while the square of the Cauchy distribution's interval estimator shows variability at first but eventually becomes stable, and demonstrates consistency both theoretically and practically. The proposed methods display goodness-of-fit and show that the standard deviation (σ) can be effectively estimated. The confidence interval and square of the Cauchy distribution interval estimators display asymptotic normality, and can be applied to real-world data, as demonstrated by analyzing the distribution of 2019-2021 basketball players' free throw percentages. The analysis reveals that b is greater than 2, and shows a shift towards greater values of b in 2021 compared to 2019. The proposed methods thus offer reliable estimators of the Cauchy distribution's parameter (b), and can be used to investigate changes in distributions of quantitative data over time. A new statistical approach is developed for basket trials to determine the required sample size by strategically sharing information between subsets of patients. This methodology uses Bayesian principles to calculate the most suitable sample sizes for each patient group and the overall study, taking into account the expected statistical power and a desired threshold for clinical significance. A method is also devised to assess the optimal level of information sharing by maintaining desired levels of type I and type II errors. Two case studies are presented to illustrate the methodology's application in real-world scenarios: the first involves a basket trial evaluating multiple patient subgroups in a phase II clinical study, and the second considers trials with varying levels of sample size optimization. The findings show that basket trials can achieve greater efficiency and precision by borrowing information between patient groups, and that a well-designed sample size assessment based on Bayesian principles can lead to more accurate results. Furthermore, basket trials offer opportunities for concurrent analysis across different patient subgroups. The methodology's results provide a framework for implementing a Bayesian-based sample size assessment in clinical trials and research studies. The approaches outlined in this paper are available as R functions in the repository https://github.com/grasp-ubh/BasketTrials. This work presents a novel strategy, called sequential loop tightening, for enhancing performance in linear parameter varying systems. By addressing polytopes individually, it facilitates the application of sequential loop tightening to complex systems with significant uncertainties. As implemented on a motion simulator, experimental results demonstrate that this method yields superior performance compared to traditional techniques. Specifically, results show that sequential loop tightening outperforms existing approaches by reducing positioning errors and enhancing tracking resilience, particularly in challenging conditions. Notably, a notable improvement of nearly 90% in position accuracy is achieved with minimal increase in actuation efforts, offering a direct link between performance and energy consumption. We introduce a general framework, PRNet, for aligning partial point clouds, where we can select and align any subset of points from each cloud. This framework is versatile and can be applied to various tasks, such as object pose estimation, partial object recognition, and synthetic to real image translation. PRNet learns aligning features and a geometric transformation in a self-supervised manner, using correspondences learned from one or more iteratively refined layers. To robustly generate correspondences for each layer, we propagate and refine correspondences from above using a query-based nearest neighbor search. We evaluate PRNet on widely used benchmarks for object recognition and object pose estimation, where we report performance that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, specifically, an estimated 89.6% accuracy for partial object recognition and 0.07 NDE for object pose estimation, using the same number of samples as comparison methods. Future high-energy collider designs are crucial in determining the threshold value for the Higgs instability. Considering the feasibility and cost of different colliders, we evaluate three potential options: the high-energy upgrade of the LHC, the International Linear Collider, and the Future Circular Collider based on a 100 TeV proton-proton design. To estimate the instability threshold, we take into account factors such as energy reach, detector capabilities, luminosity, and potential sensitivity to beyond-standard-model physics. Combining these factors, we conclude that the high-luminosity phase of the LHC, the International Linear Collider, and the Future Circular Collider based on a 100 TeV proton-proton design are equally capable of detecting a 1 TeV Higgs boson and are thus comparable in determining the instability threshold. However, if the 100 TeV proton-proton design becomes the first collider to achieve a high-energy, 50-100 TeV, it would offer the best opportunity to determine the instability threshold value. In a 100 TeV proton-proton scenario, we explore the potential for the Higgs instability to be detected using the standard model at its minimum with the help of advanced analyses and a more sensitive measurement of the Higgs self-coupling. Additionally, we observe that electroweak symmetries and sensitivity to a scalar or fermion beyond the standard model at intermediate energy scales could also provide crucial information about the instability threshold. In a 100 TeV proton-proton scenario, we assess the potential for the Higgs instability to be detected using beyond-standard-model sectors such as a scalar or fermion at its minimum with the help of a more sensitive measurement of the Higgs vertex and a more extensive phase space in particle decays. Furthermore, we emphasize the value of equipping the International Linear Collider with a detector capable of detecting low-energy particles or using other approaches such as electron-pose or recoil systems to enhance its sensitivity to beyond-standard-model physics and the instability threshold at low energy. In a 100 TeV proton-proton scenario, we investigate the potential for the Higgs instability to be detected using a more extensive phase space in particle decays and multiple secondary decays with the help of a more extensive measurement of the Higgs vertex. To optimize the sensitivity of future high-energy colliders, we recommend combining the International Linear Collider and the Future Circular Collider based on a 100 TeV proton-proton design, with the former investigating the standard model at its minimum and the latter exploring standard model decays at its minimum.

In medical image segmentation, underdetermined data poses significant challenges due to incomplete labels, leading to difficulties in training segmentation models. Unlike traditional segmentation tasks that have fully labeled data, in underdetermined data we only have information on one labeled modality, while other important modalities remain unlabeled, making manual annotation impractical. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel approach called CycDivGAN that leverages cyclic consistency and division GAN techniques. This approach first segments the fully labeled modality using a segmentation model, then uses a GAN to divide the segments into regions. Selecting the unlabeled modality with the highest frequency in these regions leads to accurate segmentation results. Our experiments on two complex medical datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we showcase the capabilities of our method in multi-modality underdetermined data by achieving successful segmentation results on two modalities without any additional labels. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Keywords: Medical Image Segmentation, Underdetermined Data, Unlabeled Modalities, Cyclic Division GAN, Fully Convolutional Neural Networks. is a challenging task known as future action prediction (FAP).  To overcome
this challenge, we develop a novel neural network architecture combining
recurrent neural networks (RNN) with radial basis function kernels to map agent
states to future action probabilities.  Empirical results on three diverse
benchmark datasets reveal that our model outperforms existing methods, and our
source code is available at https://github.com ShakedNet/FeatureMappingRNN. 
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model specifically leverages the
structural information inherent in sequences to forecast future actions.

kernelization, using the widely employed MuJoCo dataset as a case study. 
Key findings reveal that our model: 1) recognizes the presence of latent
structural patterns within trajectories that correspond to the duration of
sub-episodes; 2) forecasts future actions by recognizing the start of sub-
episodes; and 3) fails to forecast future actions after the conclusion of
episodes, even when presented with explicit episode terminations.

To better understand flare effects on stars similar to the Sun, researchers simulated a major flare that occurred on AD Leo in 1985 using laboratory-measured atmospheric data and 1-dimensional stellar models. The team employed a numerical code to simulate flare propagation through the star's atmosphere and computed various spectral and spatial observations. By comparing simulated and actual optical/UV observations, researchers estimated flare temperatures and densities, testing theories of stellar flare behavior and providing insights into flare physical processes. Furthermore, researchers used these simulations to model the impacts of flares on chemical elements within the star, predicting changes in line strengths based on flare temperature and photospheric coverage. The team calculated average line strength variations of -30% to -40% for certain elements, but noted significant deviations for specific lines, suggesting changes in line strength could be influenced by non-thermal processes. Finally, researchers estimated energy dissipation times and compared these to convection times in the upper photosphere, and proposed that energy from this event may still be released in the form of oscillations. The team suggested that these oscillations could lead to additional UV emission, potentially explaining observed differences between simulated and actual UV data. The study concludes that energy from this flare has not been completely dissipated, and may continue to influence the star's behavior in the days following the event. The team noted that observations of AD Leo by the Kepler telescope have captured fluctuations consistent with their theory. Using data from the All Sky Survey, researchers estimated that flares with energies less than 10^30 erg/s-hr are widespread among M-dwarf stars, and proposed that such flares could have significant impacts on exoplanet atmospheres and search for biosignatures. Based on their simulation, researchers recommended that future stellar flare studies include near-UV continuum observations to accurately model flare behavior. The team Dr. Robert L. Kurucz and Dr. Robert G. Strom provided key contributions to this research, and noted that without their work, accurately modeling flare behavior would not have been possible. The team expressed appreciation for the collaborations that made this research possible, and noted that further study is needed to fully understand flare behavior. The team made available a code for simulating stellar flares, allowing other researchers to model flare behavior using atmospheric data and 1-dimensional stellar models. The code was developed using Python and is based on the LOUVAIN code, which was provided by Dr. Robert G. Strom. The team made available a range of supporting data, including tables of spectral line strength, and 1-dimensional stellar models for various stars

A $p$-core $p'$-sequence is an integer sequence that increases at a rate of $p$ or higher with each step $p'$, where $p$ and $p'$ are prime numbers under or equal to $7$. The origin of such sequences, when $p = 2$, has its roots in binary coding, while its variant, called $\mathcal{N}$-sequences, has its foundation in non-binary coding using the digits $1, \ldots, n$. The $\mathcal{N}$-sequences are associated with a random walk on the additive residue graph $\Gamma_n$ that results in a random $\mathcal{N}$-sequence when starting at an arbitrary vertex and continuing indefinitely with steps of irrevocable random walks of length $p$. The core property of these sequences, when the number of steps $p'$ is fixed, is that they are uniformly distributed over the set of all $p'$-core $p'$-sequences. This work expands upon this distribution by examining the limit of the distribution of arbitrary $p$-core $p'$-sequences for any prime $p$ and number of steps $p'$ when the number of steps $p'$ approaches infinity. The limit of the distribution is found to be a uniform distribution over the set of all integer sequences that increase at a rate of at least $p$ with each step $p'$. This result can also be applied to random walks on the additive residue graph $\Gamma_n$ that results in a random integer sequence when starting at an arbitrary vertex and continuing indefinitely with steps of irrevocable random walks of length $p$ by considering the limit of the distribution of arbitrary $\mathcal{N}$-sequences for any prime $p$ when the number of steps $p'$ approaches infinity. Neural network-based encoders that translate LiDAR or RGBD data into semantic point cloud models have seen significant progress, but achieving high-quality predictions away from training LiDAR data poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, a novel framework called TPC is proposed, employing a unique combination of LiDAR and image features to generate reliable point cloud models in LiDAR-deficient scenarios. TPC leverages a unique translation-invariant smoothing technique to refine LiDAR-based point cloud models, effectively removing noise and producing accurate results on public datasets. By combining LiDAR and image features, TPC achieves a metric accuracy of 85.46%, surpassing previous methods by nearly 10% in this domain. Additionally, TPC's performance on LiDAR data remains comparable to state-of-the-art models, confirming its ability to improve the overall quality of semantic point cloud models. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/learnarr/TPC. Supplemental materials can be accessed at https://arrlearn.github.io/TPC/. This leads to a simplified definition, analogous to the original but without requiring the choice of connection. It preserves key properties, including preservation of the bracket operation. Furthermore, it aligns with the principle of localizing Lie algebras, a concept related to equivariant localization. This connection establishes that flat equivalence is a form of equivariant localization when the Lie group is one-dimensional. However, it does not generally extend to higher-dimensional groups. In response to growing demand for vehicle safety features, automotive manufacturers have incorporated fail-operational systems that enable driving even in the event of component failure. However, fail-operational capabilities introduce complexities in terms of safety guarantee validity, given the inherent unpredictability of such failures. To address this, we undertake a formal modeling and analysis of a fail-operational driving system, consisting of steering-assisted parking system, with the aim of ensuring that in the event of a failure, the system remains within predetermined parking boundaries. Using abstract state machines and Temporal Specification, we identified and resolved potential issues of run-time failures, migration issues, and alignment problems, ultimately verifying that parking will be successfully completed within specified time and spatial constraints, even in the event of component failure. The proposed approach can serve as a validation protocol for similar fail-operational systems, providing users with transparent system guarantees and reassuring system behavior. It has the potential to improve predictive modeling, identifying critical system components and understanding how small changes affect systems when equilibrium is lost. This study provides an in-depth examination of Leibniz's concepts for derivatives and integrals in modern mathematical contexts. We articulate three contemporary interpretations of Leibniz's calculus, drawing on the fundamental ideas of Landau, Bernoulli, and Euler. Each framework is evaluated for its coherence, expressive power, and conservativity. Specifically, we show that Leibniz's calculus, viewed through the lens of sequences or nets, aligns with the methods of the 18th and 19th centuries, as seen in the work of Cauchy, although this alignment was not fully realized until the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Notably, we find that Leibniz's use of derivatives implies the validity of the fundamental theorem of calculus. Moreover, we highlight that Euler's approach to calculus, expressed in terms of increments and limits, is equivalent to a modern $L^1$-framework, as recently proposed by Roblar and Rousar. Our study offers a systematic understanding of the development of Leibnizian calculus and its connection to the integral theories of Barrow, Newton, and Jakob Bernoulli, demonstrating that Bernoulian calculus constitutes a coherent and fully developed system of classical Leibnizian calculus. We explore the potential for a similar account of the development of calculus from the perspective of proof within the framework of a modern proof-assistant, as recently shown for the calculus of variations, and emphasize the importance of acknowledging the significant contributions of independent thinkers like Leibniz, as well as the fluid exchange of ideas among the frequency and visibility of mathematical correspondences during the early modern period. Finally, we highlight that Euler's approach to calculus, as well as that of Lagrange and Weierstrass, is consistent with a modern $L^2$-framework, as recently demonstrated by Roblar and Rousar. Using computer simulations, we study how large-scale intergalactic gas clouds affect measurements made with a proposed HI intensity mapping experiment on a large scale of about 2000 km/s. Our findings reveal that certain patterns in the data are consistent across different models of the universe and are unaffected by the interferometer's structure, whereas other patterns are influenced by the specifics of the universe's structure and the interferometer's design. By comparing different models, we determine the level to which measurements are biased due to foreground effects like the interferometer's response and the universe's cosmological properties. Our analysis shows that while it's possible to eliminate the influence of the interferometer's structure, it's challenging to remove the effects of the universe's cosmological properties. However, by cross-correlating the data with other datasets, it's possible to separate out the effects of the interferometer and gain insights into the universe's structure on a large scale. Our simulations assume a perfect measurement and realisation, and we plan to repeat this study with more realistic data by incorporating the effects of beam smearing and measurement noise. Additionally, we find that utilizing an experiment design that covers a large frequency range of around 100 and has a small, equally spaced arrangement of 15 elements allows us to make the most of our data and gain insights into the universe on a large scale without loss of information. This is in contrast to an experiment design that has more elements but covers a smaller frequency range. Our study also reveals that although it's possible to make up for lost information by using an experiment design with more elements, it does not improve the accuracy of our findings on a large scale. Finally, we find that for a desired level of precision, the necessary survey area or time scales for our HI intensity mapping experiment increases as the square of the frequency range it covers and is independent of the interferometer's structure arrangement. Additionally, we find that a larger frequency range will yield more precise measurements of the universe's structure, while its cosmological properties remain unchanged. Our predictions from these simulations can be used to inform future design choices and planning for upcoming HI intensity mapping experiments. They also provide a theoretical framework for modelling the performance and capabilities of such experiments based on their design and the characteristics of the interferometer. By applying a scaled approach, our predictions can also be used to inform the design of such experiments at other wavelengths, such as CMB experiments using a similar technique known as cross-correlation cosmology. Finally, our study also highlights the importance of considering the specific characteristics of the interferometer

Although hybrid models integrating multiple methods have been extensively explored, incorporating and valuing diverse sources of information in hybrid systems remains underrepresented. To address this, we present a hybrid framework that integrates a context-aware model and a behavior-based model, and demonstrate its effectiveness through an implementation combining LaTeX document recommender and a general recommendation system using user behavior and document context information. The context-aware model and the hybrid system are evaluated against existing state-of-the-art methods, and the results show significant improvements in accuracy and a higher overall satisfaction level for users. Furthermore, our findings confirm that the hybrid system achieves better performance through feature interaction and dimensionality reduction. The implementation details, source code, and experiment results are made available for reproduction of the study. We develop a new concept of spectral openness, denoted by $B(\delta)$, for non-commutative matrices, in addition to establishing its relationship with the $B$-transform. This relationship is utilized to investigate the non-commutative cyclic von Neumann algebras associated with random matrices, specifically matrices whose elements follow an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) model with arbitrary non-truncated distributions. We demonstrate that the spectral measure of a given unitary matrix, applied in sequence to the matrices of the Cuntz-Toeplitz algebra, satisfies the openness condition, provided its singular value spectrum lies within a specified $\sqrt{s}$-neighborhood. This leads to the determination that the spectral measure of a unitary matrix, expressed as a product of i.i.d. standard Gaussian matrices, meets the openness condition, thus providing a theoretical framework for explaining the zero-law in the study of the eigenvalues of Hermitian matrices. We also investigate the wandering subset created by the irrational rotation action on the circle, as well as the intersection of Spec($T_n$), where $T_n$ is a Toeplitz operator, with the set of square-integers. We find that this intersection does not satisfy the openness condition, as it exhibits a specific mode of behavior. Lastly, this investigation retrieves a particular result of Anderson-Bernstein, as well as a related finding of Yuh-Dau Lin for polynomial matrices, while additionally extending their consequence to the setting of non-commutative matrices. We revisited and expanded the primary method of specifying and evaluating timing constraints in real-time systems, known as Ramadge-Wing's timed regular expressions. The original approach defined the semantics of these constraints by combining timing limits with the underlying regular expressions. It also identified the maximum and minimum possible time intervals between two specified events and established a closure property for this timing framework. However, Ramadge-Wing's method did not provide an efficient algorithmic means of verifying whether a system meets the specified timing requirements. Furthermore, as the size of the state space in the regular expressions grew, the associated closure property became infeasible. In our revisit, we introduce a new algorithmic framework for the timely satisfaction of specific conditions. This approach, known as HTOP, offers a more efficient means of verifying system compliance with timing constraints compared to Ramadge-Wing's method. Additionally, HTOP's results demonstrate that the chosen evaluation strategy for timing limits does not impact the overall correctness, while also showcasing the advantages of HTOP over alternative evaluation strategies. Moreover, HTOP's algorithmic framework is capable of handling more complex situations than the existing automated tools for checking real-time systems. In particular, HTOP is well-suited for modeling systems with varying execution durations and concurrent processes, while also facilitating the specification of timing limits for individual transitions and groups of synchronized transitions. Finally, HTOP's results are presented in a way that allows for the easy integration of the proposed algorithm into existing regular expression evaluators, thus enabling a straightforward comparison between HTOP and the existing evaluation methods. HTOP's performance was evaluated through practical experiments, where we demonstrated its efficiency and scalability by testing it against the standard automatic verification tools for checking real-time systems. In these experiments, HTOP emerged as a more efficient alternative to the standard automatic verification tools, while also showcasing its capacity to handle more complex scenarios. Additionally, we used HTOP to verify the compliance of two industrial systems with specified timing requirements. In particular, we applied HTOP to the (industrial) software model of the MDHD driver and the (industrial) hardware model of the Freescale CPU, thereby successfully verifying that both systems meet the specified timing limits in all cases. Furthermore, we used HTOP to identify the maximum and minimum possible time intervals between two specified events in the (industrial) hardware model of the Freescale CPU. We introduce an optimization problem, called the generalized k-center problem, where customers located at points in a metric space must be assigned to centers with minimal total cost, subject to anisotropic cost functions and capacity constraints. A key research question in this area is establishing a relationship between the cost of finding doubling centers and the cost of finding centers located near customers, which is defined in terms of the freeway dimension. Our study focuses on two cost functions: the doubling cost and the quasi doubling cost. For doubling metrics, we developed an approximation algorithm capable of finding centers within a factor of 12 of the optimal solution, and we demonstrated that this approximation is best possible by showing an intrinsic lower bound of at least 8 in certain situations. We also established a relationship between the doubling dimension and the freeway dimension, showing that a certain ratio is bounded above by 2, and we identified an infinite class of spaces for which this bound is best possible. Our research also considers the specialized case of minimizing quasi doubling costs. Although we were unable to find an approximation algorithm for this problem, we proposed new lower bounds on the parameter q in terms of the freeway dimension, and we demonstrated that this parameter must be at least 4 when considering certain classes of spaces with fixed and constant cost ratios. We also established a relationship between the quasi doubling dimension and the freeway dimension, showing that a certain ratio must be greater than or equal to 2, and we identified an infinite class of situations for which this inequality holds best. Additionally, we presented new freeway dimension lower bounds on well-known spaces, such as the dyadic lattice and the infinite binary tree. In exotic nuclei, electron scattering at low energies is primarily driven by the nuclear response, whereas at higher energies, it is largely influenced by the free-nucleon and relativistic corrections. We investigate the relativistic corrections to the elastic and inelastic cross-sections of $^{16}$O, $^{18}$O, $^{14}$N, and $^{17}$O through their decomposition into energy packages. It is found that the higher energy packages are largely unaffected by relativistic corrections. Furthermore, it is discovered that relativistic corrections tend to increase the lower energy packages, especially for inelastic channels, thus accurately modeling them is crucial for experimental analysis. Given that direct $e^{-}e^{+}$ production is generally dominated by the $2\gamma$ process, our analysis likely applies to electromagnetic probes in general. We suggest that our findings could be verified through relativistic ab initio calculations, particularly by examining the development of relativistic many-body theories for nuclear physics, and that this study's results could be further tested with high-energy collision experiments at facilities like the RIKEN Radioisotope Beam Factory. Additionally, our investigation indicates that relativistic corrections to the elastic and inelastic cross-sections of $^{16}$O, $^{18}$O, $^{14}$N, and $^{17}$O should be calculated up to an energy range of around 500-600 MeV. We also outline the future potential for relativistic corrections to be applied to other nuclear reactions, such as fragmentation and proton scattering. Lastly, it is noted that direct $e^{-}e^{+}$ production could be influenced by parity-symmetry-protected package emission, thereby enabling a distinct signature of parity non-conservation in nuclear interactions at high energies. We propose that this idea could be tested through relativistic $e^{-}e^{+}$ production measurements at future collider experiments, such as the Future Circular Collider. In this scenario, it is possible that the phenomenon of parity non-conservation could be observed, thereby confirming our understanding of the fundamental electroweak interaction, thereby establishing a landmark achievement in the history of particle physics. We suggest that the development of the FCC could a pivotal moment for this endeavor, allowing scientists to make a groundbreaking contribution to the advancement of particle physics. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements. This model was validated through detailed comparisons with extensive experimental data, yielding average deviations of approximately $0.25\%$ for the gas phase compressibility, $0.50\%$ for the surface tension, and $0.30\%$ for the ionization energy. This validation confers a high degree of precision on the obtained analytical equations, thereby establishing a strong foundation for theoretical calculations of thermodynamic properties, equations of state, and phase diagrams. As such, this model can serve as a robust starting point for theoretical screenings in materials design, equilibrium conditions in astrophysical environments, and chemical reactions, among other applications. Moreover, this work may inspire the development of corresponding analytical models for non-ideal electrons and the strong interaction between electrons and nuclei within the framework of density functional theory. This model may further be adapted for coatings and thin films, wherein the confinement effect can give rise to divergent behavior at elevated pressures, thereby highlighting the significance of accurate phase behavior analysis in this domain. Finally, this work can be expanded to investigate non-equilibrium phenomena, thereby facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the alkali metals' state diagram, which may be of great benefit for modeling various astrophysical environments, including white dwarfs, brown dwarfs, and low-mass stars. In the context of a specific gauge-model of vector mesons interacting with a complex medium possessing chiral characteristics and assisted by fermion-antifermion pairs, we examine the spectrum of vector mesons as they move through the medium. By incorporating 't Hooft loops to represent the influence of fermion-antifermion pairs and using the saddle-point method to analyze the effective action of the gauge-field, we are able to derive a set of differential equations defining the spectrum of vector mesons. Our findings reveal that the spectrum exhibits a mass dependence that is linear, rather than the usual Regge trajectory, and that the spacing between consecutive masses increases as momentum grows. Additionally, we have calculated the width of vector mesons at both rest and in motion, and our results indicate that the width increases in direct proportion to the square of the momentum, rather than the fourth power as might be expected. Our research also shows that the ratio of the width to the mass is constant and unaffected by the mass itself. Finally, we have found that the imaginary component of the self-energy of vector mesons is nonzero at zero momentum, indicating a breakdown of the Wess-Zumino relation, and that this discrepancy increases as momentum grows. Our work contradicts the conclusions of Wambach et al. regarding the viability of the Wess-Zumino relation in a similar context. Instead, we have demonstrated that the relation can be satisfied only if the medium is either entirely chiral or entirely antichiral. Furthermore, we have calculated the extent to chiral and antichiral components contribute to the normal and anomalous kinetic terms in the effective action of gauge-field. Our results indicate that the anomalous term is entirely due to the chiral aspect of the medium, whereas the normal term is entirely due to the antichiral aspect. Moreover, we have found that the effective action of gauge-field is symmetric under a change of chiral parameters, and that this symmetry can be used to derive relations linking various components of the self-energy of vector mesons. We investigate the problem of accurate distance estimation at a large scale in complex networks, despite the presence of malicious actors (byzantine failures), where the number of malicious entities is limited to less than one-third of the total nodes. This problem is linked to the issue of robust average estimation in networks. We have found that average estimation is possible under specific conditions and that this insight enables reliable distance estimation on an area-by-area basis. However, ensuring network-wide distance accuracy proves to be computationally infeasible. To resolve this issue, we have developed a simple and efficient protocol that achieves accurate distance estimation for the entire network. This protocol's accuracy approaches that of an ideal, fault-free system, with the exception of a marginally increased error rate of roughly $O(\log^2 n)$ for very large networks. The complexity of this protocol spans two components: a centralized unit and network nodes, with the former requiring $O(\sqrt{T} \log^2 T)$ operations and the latter $O(\log^2 T)$ on their respective ends. The efficacy of this protocol is demonstrated through theoretical analysis, validated by experimental results, proving its superiority over alternative methods. Our study thus provides a solution to a previously unstudied problem of robust distance estimation in large, complex networks. The techniques developed here can also be applied to support efficient and accurate distance-based data processing applications. Furthermore, this work expands our understanding of the principles governing robust estimation in networks. The code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub. \end{itemize}

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of conformal metric variables. By bypassing the issues of variable damping rates, our method enables a unified strategy for determining all metric variables via an iterative process similar to the L2 method. Our code, a modification of the RR based on the Carter-Lomberg algorithm, is particularly effective for patterns with high spatial symmetry. For instance, when considering spherical symmetry, we find that two iterations are sufficient to meet a predetermined tolerance level. Similarly, for axisymmetric scenarios, three iterations are required. Our approach also exhibits minimal residual minima that correlate with the frequency of the source pattern, indicating that additional iterations may be required to eliminate residual fluctuations. Although this method performs well for scenarios with moderate levels of complexity, it struggles with extremely intricate patterns, such as those found in binary black hole merger simulations, due to the vast number of degrees of freedom involved. However, in such cases, combining our method with an approximate solution for the Hamiltonian constraint can lead to a substantial reduction in residual minima. Potential future research directions could involve leveraging machine learning skills to enhance our approach and extending our code to incorporate matter fields beyond pure gravity simulations in numerical relativity. By doing so, we may unlock fresh insights into how initial data for these complex scenarios impacts the subsequent gravitational wave signals. Moreover, there are numerous unresolved issues related to the behavior of residual minima as the grid resolution changes, which necessitates further research to fully understand our method's limitations. By addressing these questions and optimizing our approach, we may ultimately develop a more efficient and robust tool for generating initial data configurations in numerical relativity, which could expand our understanding of how gravitational waves behave in various astrophysical and cosmological environments. Our code is publicly available at https://git.io/RR-CTTK. In addition, we have released a series of educational tutorials that demonstrate how our method can be used to solve initial data configurations for specific scenarios with complex matter patterns, which can be accessed at https://git.io/RR-CTTK-tutorials. We hope that these educational resources will enable researchers to easily replicate our results and introduce various aspects of numerical relativity related to conformal transverse-traceless decompositions. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. This distortion can be problematic for various applications, including multi-band imaging and polarimetry. To better understand and mitigate this effect, researchers have developed on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion using a unique device called a broadband analyzer of the atmosphere. This device has been successfully tested at several observatories around the world, including the Submillimeter Array in Hawaii and the Atacama Large Millimeter/meter Observatory in Chile. These measurements have revealed that atmospheric dispersion models often fail to accurately predict this effect, with an average discrepancy of around 10%. Notably, the worst-case discrepancy was observed at a 42-degree atmospheric angle of refraction and varied depending on the atmospheric water content. These results indicate that while some telescopes are minimally affected by this issue, others may need to account for significant dispersion biases in their instruments. Therefore, researchers and instrument designers should carefully consider and possibly implement atmospheric dispersion corrections to ensure optimal performance. Finally, the implementation of an on-sky, active atmospheric dispersion corrector at the Submillimeter Array is shown to be an effective solution to this problem. This device has been successfully used to reduce a polarimeter's wavelength bias by around 90%, demonstrating the importance of accounting for this effect to achieve the highest possible precision. Additionally, the code used to calculate dispersion expectations has been released as a user-friendly interface that allows researchers to input their specific telescope and instrument characteristics and output the expected dispersion biases. This interface can help researchers to quickly assess the likelihood and impact of this effect and make informed decisions about whether to implement a solution. This paper explores the mathematical concept of basis pursuit, a method used to solve underdetermined linear equations by minimizing the magnitude of coefficients against a predefined threshold. Our research examines whether a single solution exists and if that solution is unique. To address this, we developed a metric space based on the threshold value and established an algorithm's ability to produce a unique outcome within this space. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrated that any solution to the basis pursuit problem can be expressed as a weighted sum of optimal solutions obtained with progressively increasing threshold values. This property allows us to attribute coherence-damaging structures to specific levels of threshold values, and ultimately, to isolate and characterize the basis pursuit solution set in terms of solutions from levels with sufficiently high threshold values. Conversely, our investigation also shows that solutions from levels with sufficiently low threshold values can be attributed to an overcomplete dictionary's spanning property. As a result, we derived conditions for various dictionary types - including random, structured, and random structured - that guarantee not only the existence of a solution, but also the solution's uniqueness and uniqueness up to a set of negligible coefficients. To demonstrate the practical utility of our findings, we showed that our analysis yields a polynomial-time algorithm for computing the basis pursuit solution in the case of an orthogonal dictionary. This method involves repeatedly solving a series of classical least-squares problems using classical optimization techniques. Conversely, our investigation also shows that a similar algorithm exists for solving basis pursuit with a general orthogonal dictionary. While our work here builds upon prior research in sparse solution uniqueness, our unique contribution lies in our continuous-formization of the basis pursuit problem, which we believe will be a valuable tool for future research in sparse solution uniqueness. Additionally, our results imply the continuity of sparse solution sets, an implication we rigorously proved, and further, our investigation shows that this sparsity-induced continuity implies the continuity of solution sets for related problems such as the Lp pursuit problem for p in the range [0,2]. To demonstrate the practical utility of our results, we showed that our findings can be used to give a simple proof of approximate stability for the basis pursuit problem. A combination of decentralized computation and centralized parameter updating, federated learning circumvents data protection concerns by processing data on the client side. This framework is particularly useful because it allows multiple organizations to train a machine learning model jointly without sharing their private data, which is valuable for organizations operating under confidentiality requirements. This work delves into the intersection of fairness and differential privacy in federated learning, exploring the challenges and potential solutions for balancing these three critical elements when applying FL to ML model development. To begin with, the framework for combining differential privacy and fairness is discussed from a machine learning perspective, highlighting privacy's role in maintaining statistical fairness. Subsequently, the focus shifts to empirical studies, which demonstrate that simply applying the differential privacy mechanism to the local stochastic gradient method leads to decreased accuracy and longer convergence rates. To address this shortcoming, the model averaging technique is presented as a possible remedy, although it fails to achieve optimal convergence rates. Building upon this approach, two novel algorithms are introduced that combine model averaging with local gradient sharing to achieve improved accuracy and convergence rates while maintaining differential privacy and fairness. This paper introduces an innovative approach called regional critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing multiple critics to coordinate structural updates in large neural networks. Building upon previous experiences with distributed training, it adapts the concept to neural networks composed of interconnected layers and modules. Experimental validation is performed on a variety of image classification tasks, demonstrating that regional critic training can effectively facilitate structural updates and lead to improved model efficiency through parameter reduction. Notably, it achieves a substantial reduction of up to 80% in non-essential parameters for models of comparable accuracy in simple scenarios, and between 40% to 60% in complex cases. Additionally, it shows potential for application in task-parallel learning, where multiple tasks are simultaneously coordinated across connected models. Code and model parameters for this research are publicly available for reproduction of results. Keywords: deep neural networks, model-parallel learning, regional critic training, structural updates, distributed training. Conclusion: Regional critic training offers a viable method for model-parallel learning of deep neural networks, boasting several desirable characteristics such as reduced communication overhead, structural representation, and task flexibility. It successfully achieves significant reductions in non-essential parameters for simple models and shows potential for various applications with extensive datasets, making it a suitable method for distributed deep neural networks. It also outperforms model-parallel learning methods based on gradient alignment and graph neural networks in reducing parameters by 10% and 26%, respectively. Finally, regional critic training demonstrates potential for use in task-parallel learning and a variety of other applications, solidifying its position as a versatile model-parallel learning method. However, detecting complex network attacks in real-time can be a significant challenge, particularly for limited-resource devices. To address this issue, our research introduces NBcoded, a lightweight classifier system designed to identify network attacks using simplified traffic patterns and naive Bayes classification. To optimize performance on resource-constrained devices, NBcoded is implemented using Python with a focus on minimal memory requirements and efficient processing. Additionally, NBcoded showcases its ability to operate effectively across various hardware platforms, even with very limited resources, such as the Raspberry Pi and the Intel NTP computer. Developing hybrid digital-analog quantum computing may offer a potential solution, combining analog quantum systems with digital error correction. We investigate the feasibility of using this approach to emulate fermionic systems, focusing on a one-dimensional fermionic system and the fermionic bosonization method to derive an analog quantum circuit. Despite analog errors, our results show that the reduced fermion number and bosonization ratio remain accurate to the fourth decimal place, indicating the potential for successfully emulating fermionic systems on analog quantum devices. However, the bounce back phenomenon remains a concern, suggesting that the fermion number could reset to its initial state after some time. To mitigate this issue, we propose delaying the measurement until the fermion number fluctuates rapidly and minimize the associated time gap. Furthermore, scaling up the system may introduce complications such as entanglement between qubits and increased analog errors. While these issues are yet to be fully addressed, our research brings quantum simulations closer to practical application. It's conceivable that future advancements in analog quantum devices could be utilized for extensively simulating the behavior of materials with fermionic spin. The hybrid approach could then provide the necessary support to account for systematic digital errors during such experiments. A critical issue in machine learning is striking a balance between optimizing performance and ensuring robust learning capabilities across different datasets. 
A fundamental challenge arises from methods like data augmentation, which make predictive models overconfident but improve generalization.
Our research focuses on addressing this problem by introducing the concept of wealth features.
Every category in a model's training dataset is assigned a wealth value, which serves as the basis for an inequality.
By incorporating wealth features into the model, it is possible to achieve generalized solutions that work equally well across all categories, as long as the inequality's condition is met.
Our approach is demonstrated through theoretical examples and experiments involving the training of neural networks, where the addition of wealth features enables generalization to datasets with different sizes and dimensions, as long as the inequality's condition remains satisfied.
Furthermore, wealth features facilitate the adaptation of models to new datasets with distinct labels, as long as the inequality's condition remains unchanged or improves.
Ultimately, the methodology of wealth features presents a novel, adaptable solution to the optimization-generalization dilemma in machine learning. 
It enables the detection of situations in which optimization performance comes at the cost of generalizability and provides actionable recommendations for addressing such dilemmas. 
Moreover, the framework of wealth features offers a comprehensive understanding of generalizability and performance, as well as the theoretical and practical mechanisms underlying it. 
The code used in the research is publicly accessible via the link https://github.com/grtgrt123/Neural-Walth-Generalization. 
It can be employed for the post-hoc addition of wealth features to any model and offers a range of features that mimic the behavior of wealth features. 
Additionally, the research presents a range of potential applications of wealth features in various domains, as illustrated through the theoretical examples presented. 
Lastly, the methodology of wealth features presents a range of open research queries that require further investigation. 
In particular, the possibility of training wealth features directly from data, as well as the development of algorithms for identifying and targeting situations in which optimization performance comes at the cost of generalizability, are areas that warrant further study. 
It is hypothesized that the underlying principles of wealth features can be applied to address these issues. 
In particular, the possibility of training wealth features directly from data may involve leveraging the underlying structures and relationships present in the data, as may be the case in semi-supervised or unsupervised learning scenarios. 
The development of algorithms for identifying and targeting situations in which optimization performance comes at the cost of generalizability may involve employing heuristic methods

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to reduced power consumption, increased radiation resistance, and superior time resolution. These characteristics make them ideal for tracking rare events in experiments. Building on the successful monolithic sensor development, the CLICTD collaboration is creating a prototype with a large collection electrode, and this demonstration is particularly relevant to future leptonic particle physics investigations. To optimize performance, CMOS sensors can be fabricated with varying active layer thicknesses and on various substrate materials. In this investigation, CLICTD's monolithic sensor technology was evaluated using different beam test configurations, and the results from 200um thick sensors fabricated on high-resistivity Czochralski Cz Silicon, 450um thick sensors made on semi-insulating planar Cz Silicon, and 500um thick sensors made on semi-insulating ingot Zns Silicon were recorded. Time resolution values of around 30ps were achieved, and the findings indicate that time resolution is heavily dependent on particle energy and direction, with the best performance observed at high energies and forward angles. Additionally, the data suggest that using a high-resistivity substrate rather than a semi-insulating type results in improved charge collection efficiency and time resolution performance. This study explicitly shows the benefits of choosing a 200um thick active layer and a high-resistivity substrate for the CLICTD project. Lastly, recommendations for future research and development in CLICTD technology are presented. Future CLICTD R&D efforts will concentrate on reducing the size and capacity of the readout system to accommodate the detector's novel topology. To achieve this, the team will investigate a reduced capacitance CMOS design, custom-designed amplifiers with decreased bias currents, new charge-to-digital conversion techniques, and tailored filter architectures. These modifications will likely yield a detector capable of comprehensive particle tracking at frequencies below 1 MHz. To validate CLICTD's performance in an real-world experiment, the team is planning a test using a real detector setup and the conditions found in the experiment's beam pipe will be replicated. This will involve placing the detector directly in the LHC beam, and the team will record data while navigating through regions of varying luminosity across the particle spectrum. This will allow them to assess CLICTD's capabilities under actual conditions and compare its performance to other detection methods. Moreover, the team is collaborating with the PIEPER project to develop and test CLICTD in an actual particle detection environment. This involves utilizing CLICTD in the test beam facility for pieper and assessing its capabilities

Our study presents the first real-world test of a groundbreaking technique known as Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera (FASTIASC), which utilizes the coherence of light to directly measure the remaining speckles after adaptive optics correction,  in the Santa Cruz AO laboratory.  This laboratory offers controlled atmospheric conditions for testing,  allowing us to investigate the application of FASTIISC on a 200 pixel CCD,  with results showing the effectiveness of wavefront reconstruction from these pixels.  Our findings also compare the performance of FASTIASC to other alternative techniques,  such as MIAO and PLOCS,  which rely on polynomial approximation to describe the wavefront.  In terms of reconstruction error,  we observed a 1.8 times improvement when using FASTIASC over MIAO and a 2.3 times improvement when comparing FASTIASC to PLOCS.  Additionally,  we found that FASTIASC can achieve better performance even when only a smaller subset of pixels are used for wavefront reconstruction.  In terms of computational efficiency,  we noticed that FASTIASC requires significantly fewer iterations to achieve a stable result compared to PLOCS.  In particular,  we found that FASTIASC can produce a stable result in approximately 20-30 iterations,  in contrast to 100-150 iterations for PLOCS.  This remarkable difference in performance highlights the efficiency of FASTIASC and suggests various possible enhancements to further improve its performance and potentially lead to new areas of research. Meta-analyses that compare two groups often rely on paired data but typically ignore this relationship when conducting unpaired analyses, which can lead to biased results.  In the context of meta-regression, ignoring this pairing can result in inflated residual variance and biased estimates.  Building upon existing robust cluster-based variance estimators, this research extends its application to the analysis of paired data in meta-analyses.  By combining the benefits of robust and cluster-based methods, this study provides new approaches for conducting meta-analyses on paired data in the context of regression models.  The research further illustrates its application through a simulation example and a comparison with existing methods.  The proposed methods are implemented in the R package metaclust.
