To address this, we employed a unified approach based on the Bogoliubov transformation to analyze both cases. Specifically, we examined how particle creation impacts the fluid's conservation laws and found that in both scenarios, the energy emitted originates from the fluctuations that "resonate" at decreasing rates, causing them to lose energy, which is transferred to the fluid, thereby generating non-zero particle numbers. This resonant energy loss process is accelerated when the fluctuation rates diverge. Moreover, we showed that the probabilities of particle creation are indeed related to the negative fluctuations in energy density, as observed in both cases. We also compared the classical aspects of the two processes and found that the acoustic case corresponds to a non-local stress-tensor, whereas the gravitational case is associated with local stress-tensor properties. Finally, we discussed the implications of our findings on the paradigm of quantum particles being created from "vacuum fluctuations." Rather, we propose that the source of particle creation lies within the non-trivial average field configurations that give rise to the fluctuations. As such, we argue that the term "thermal Unruh/Hawking radiation" might be more appropriate to describe this phenomenon. We also consider the potential extensions of our analysis to the fermionic scenario. Given the similarities between our investigations and the black hole and sound wave contexts, we anticipate that our conclusions will yield insightful physical meanings that can be extracted by studying these two scenarios. We also provide potential directions for this endeavor. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to ensure reliable operation.  Despite advances in hardware, such as the integration of non-volatile memory, developing robust systems remains a complex task.  Memory errors can still occur and require immediate correction to prevent data corruption.  Since hardware correction is often impractical due to performance constraints, developers must implement their own fault correction mechanisms.  These algorithms can be slow, leading to a potential hot-spot for performance degradation.  In this research, we introduce an innovative technique to accelerate fault correction in high-performance computing systems.  Capitalizing on opportunities for parallel processing, our method can be efficiently distributed across multiple CPU cores.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through crash consistency tests using the HPC application, ROMIO, on a testbed with CPU cores.  Our results showcase that this algorithm can provide fault correction performance comparable to that of recent hardware, often exceeding it in reliability.  Furthermore, this method can be adaptable to various hardware architectures with minimal modification and can be incorporated into existing software frameworks with limited revision.  Moreover, this research reveals that hardware correction can be inefficient due to unnecessary system crashes, including one observed in our testbed, highlighting the need for optimized fault correction algorithms.  We propose a novel metric to evaluate fault correction performance, considering both algorithmic and hardware options.  This study sets the stage for a future research direction, investigating whether hardware designers can leverage this performance information to develop more effective fault correction mechanisms.  We make our testbed, including the software framework ROMIO, available for public use, allowing other researchers to replicate our results and build upon our work. The advent of large information networks has necessitated the development of complex systems that can efficiently compute hierarchical relationships among their constituent elements. This application has far-reaching implications for domains such as knowledge management, search engine optimization, and topic modeling in natural language processing. While substantial research has focused on designing algorithms for hierarchical clustering, relatively little attention has been devoted to creating scalable systems that can effectively handle large-scale networks. This study introduces two high-performance architectures for computing hierarchies in information networks, leveraging the power of graph databases for flexible query execution and stream processing engines for real-time hierarchy construction. By integrating these components, we demonstrate the feasibility of our methods in real-world applications and achieve up to 2.5 times faster performance over existing methodologies. This work presents novel solutions for building hierarchical systems that can easily accommodate the demands of evolving networks, thus ensuring seamless integration of updates into the graph structure. Two use cases, involving Wikipedia categories and search results, are also demonstrated to illustrate the broad applicability of our approaches in practical scenarios. Recent research has focused on understanding stellar dynamics within the context of the three-body problem. This area of study has both theoretical and practical significance, as it can help explain why binary systems often escape their parent clouds without losing mass. Previous work revealed a relationship between the rates of binary and scattering formation, which led to the development of the flux-driven statistical model. This model demonstrates excellent agreement with existing data across a wide range of masses, spaning from black holes to the sun. This model's performance is evaluated by analyzing previously collected binary-evolution data, as well as through the creation of artificial scenarios, where the model's predictions are compared to those of various codes designed to simulate the three-body problem. These codes include semi-analytical models, such as Broadway, which was not previously tested against experimental data, and fully hybrid methods like N-body Monte Carlo simulations using the Sherlock code. When tested against binary-evolution data, the flux-driven statistical model exhibits errors more contained, being roughly six times smaller than those of hybrid methods. Similarly, when examining artificial scenarios, hybrid methods consistently struggle to match the precision achieved by the flux-driven statistical model. This level of precision holds across various initial conditions, including those that favor either binary or scattering formation. As a result, the flux-driven statistical model emerges as a highly accurate solution for the three-body problem, outperforming hybrid methods while also exhibiting physical and mathematically intuitive characteristics. This model's success may also translate to other areas of stellar dynamics, such as the treatment of binary systems that escape their parent clouds without losing mass. Therefore, the flux-driven statistical model represents a significant advancement in the field, providing a highly accurate solution for the three-body problem. This model's accuracy may also have practical implications, such as increasing our understanding of binary-evolution processes and the distribution of binary systems. Moreover, the flux-driven statistical model may help reduce the necessary time steps and computational resources required for simulations, thus potenially simplifying codes like Broadway and Sherlock, as well as other hybrid and N-body Monte Carlo methods. Additionally, the flux-driven statistical model could be used as a starting point or approximate solution, which can then be improved upon by hybrid methods. This model's code is publicly available at https://github.com/jaimehnunez/ThreeBodyProblem. The LHCb experiment measures charmonium production in lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy. Analyses of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons, using data collected in 2015 with a 1.7 nb$^{-1}$ luminosity, are presented. Comparisons with theoretical models, including calculations of prompt and nonprompt charmonium suppression, are made to assess the effects of nuclear interactions and energy loss in the quark-gluon plasma. When addressing complex software systems, developers face challenges related to selecting suitable test cases to execute, given limited resources and objectives varying with risk assessment, which necessitate a thorough evaluation of testing options. Despite the existence of methods for optimal test case selection, these methods are inflexible and incapable of adapting to changes in risk assessment, thus hindering practical applications. Furthermore, since each test case typically represents a sequential operation, selecting them individually impedes the concurrent processing of tests. To overcome these limitations, a new algorithm has been developed to facilitate parallel execution of test cases by selecting an optimal subset with the highest risk assessment and applying a singular value decomposition method. To streamline the algorithm's scalability, a parallel version has been created using distributed arrays and verified through benchmarks. This new algorithm serves as an efficient solution for selecting test cases, enabling parallel execution and thus prioritizing the reduction of overall costs. To demonstrate its efficacy, benchmarks have been conducted using the OpenCL, CUDA, and TBB libraries to compare the algorithm's performance as a standalone solution for selecting test cases. However, we aim to integrate this algorithm into the ICS-CFD software system as a means of improving the management of its test cases. To achieve this, we will employ the TBB and OpenCL libraries to ensure compatibility with various development environments. This new test case selection algorithm will enable us to overcome the limitations of sequential execution, thus maximizing the utilization of CPU cores, improving the algorithm's asymptotic complexity, and streamlining the code for interacting with the SVD library. Ultimately, this will enable parallel execution of test cases with a time complexity of O(N), where N represents the number of test cases. This expanded definition is demonstrated through the analysis of two examples: a two-dimensional electron gas subjected to a varying magnetic field and an edge channel connected to a point defect, both of which exhibit a nonzero Witten effect. In the first example, we find that the electric current generated in the gas can exhibit a nonlocal, nonlinear response to the varying magnetic field. We have established a standard interpretation for the lambda calculus with
randomness, meeting basic requirements for soundness, and we demonstrate that
two programs are equivalent if their corresponding denial and admission relations
indicate equality, including the equivalence of normal order and call-by-value
evaluation algorithms. Additionally, we have identified a critical property of
admissible strategies, namely that the alternation of strategies must occur on
the same thread, and we have outlined the implications for higher-order parallel
programming. Finally, we have shown that the standard interpretation meets
expectations for the expressive power of the lambda calculus with randomness. 

This research was inspired by a seminar on denotational semantics, and we have
combined various concepts from other sematics disciplines to create a unified
interpretation for the lambda calculus with randomness. We have leveraged the
framework of universal semantics by Klebanov to construct our standard
interpretation, and we have applied a formal proof assistant, Coq, to ensure the
correctness of our model. Moreover, we have employed the Curry-Howard
correspondence to establish that two programs are equivalent based on the
equality of their denotations, and we have applied a notion of strategy to
investigate the properties of the standard interpretation. Finally, we have
applied a technique for testing the expressive power of programming languages to
determine the limits of the lambda calculus with randomness. 

This paper provides a comprehensive view of the outcomes from our research seminar
on sematics, and we hope that the various concepts and techniques employed in
this paper will be of interest to readers beyond the specific problems initially
posed by the research seminar.

Our focus is on accelerating proximal-gradient methods for optimizing nonlinear optimization problems set against a varying manifold background. To expedite these algorithms, we develop an approach reminiscent of the Newton acceleration, applicable to any variational problem. Importantly, this method requires only minimal additional computational investment. We further establish that this procedure is automatically aware of the underlying manifold structure, even when it is impossible to parameterize. To facilitate theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that proximal-gradient methods consistently generate a continuous path leading to the optimal solution. Building on this understanding, we show that the accelerated procedure remains stable and converges robustly. Moreover, we illustrate the efficacy of this approach through numerical experiments involving optimization problems derived from real-world science and engineering applications. Specifically, we examine positive semidefinite matrix factorization and optimal transport on Riemannian manifolds. Furthermore, we describe potential future applications involving nonnegative matrix factorization and Poincaré inequality based methods. The proposed acceleration technique is implemented as a PySERPy package, available for public use at https://github.com/floppa/pyman. It also integrates seamlessly with Manopt, a comprehensive toolbox for nonlinear optimization on manifolds, available at http://www.stanford.edu/~boyd/PROXIMAL/. Hierarchically organized notes, summarizing theory and code, are accessible at https://tinyurl.com/newton-on-manifolds. The authors also invite feedback, with questions addressed in an accompanying addendum. Key words: nonlinear optimization, variational problems, acceleration techniques, proximal-gradient methods, manifold structures, positive semidefinite matrix factorization, optimal transport. road damage. Our system is founded on a sophisticated, deep learning model
that's been trained on a vast, combined dataset of road images from various
countries. This combined dataset, referred to as RIDE, comprises 31,183 images
of different types of road damage, gathered from partnerships with experts in
New Zealand and Australia. To increase efficiency and reduce complexity, we've
applied transfer learning to our model, enabling training with a reduced
dataset. Our results demonstrate that with as few as 500 image annotations, we
can achieve accuracy rates of 85% or higher for classifying different types
of road damage. Furthermore, we've successfully tested and refined our model
using data from various countries, including the United States, India, and
South Africa, showcasing its versatility and potential to benefit a wide range
of road authorities. Our research aims to inspire the development of advanced
automated systems for evaluating road damage on a larger scale. The RIDE
dataset is available at ride-dataset.com, and our model source code can be
accessed at github.com/ride-dataset/ride-dataset.git. Several integrated

If compelled mental health treatment is effective, it could positively impact those who need it most – individuals within the criminal justice system. Using a national outcomes database, I examined the impact of required angageement in mental health services on the overall health of convicted offenders. The analysis revealed that, contrary to expectations, required treatment had a negative impact on the mental and emotional well-being of convicted offenders. Furthermore, it had a sizeable and long-lasting adverse effect, even after factors such as initial health issues are taken into account. The results also show that, prior to enrolling in the programme, those who would be required to engage in mental health services experienced a steady decline in overall health. By targeting those who need it most, such programmes may have unintended negative consequences, ultimately doing more harm than good. 

The analysis was conducted with data from the National Outcomes Treatment Instrument, which measures the mental and emotional health of individuals within the criminal justice system. A treatment effect analysis was used to determine the impact of required engagement in mental health services on overall health, with results showing a negative effect. To put this into context, even though the results show that required treatment has a sizeable and long-lasting adverse effect, it does not necessarily mean that it has no benefits. The interpretation of the results must also consider that, in order to participate in the programme, evidence of a mental disorder must be provided through a standardized diagnostic process. Therefore, it can be assumed that required treatment has a positive impact on those who need it, but a negative impact on those who do not require it. 

It is also worth noting that, in order to participate in the programme, convicted offenders must serve their sentence in a correctional facility. The interpretation of the results must also consider that, during this time, they experience isolation from friends and family, as well as heightened levels of stress. Therefore, it can be assumed that required treatment has a negative impact on overall health, even though it may have a positive impact on those who need it most – individuals within the criminal justice system who require mental health services. 

In conclusion, the results show that, in order to determine the most effective ways to improve mental health services, compelled treatment must not be given to all convicted offenders uniformly. Instead, it must be tailored to those who need it most – individuals within the criminal justice system who require mental health services. The government must also take steps to improve mental health services, such as increasing funding for programmes that target the mental health of convicted offenders and providing support during the sentencing process.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronization issues arise due to communication constraints, causing training inefficiencies. Direct asynchronous aggregation leads to errors and performance degradation. Current solutions either discard device updates or impose unnecessary synchronization, hindering overall efficiency. We introduce a new framework addressing these problems by proposing a buffered asynchronous aggregation method that maintains update integrity and precludes the need for synchronization at the server. We substitute stochastic gradient estimators, typically used in asynchronous learning, to handle complex problems more effectively, yielding faster convergence. We develop a novel update algorithm that combines asynchronous aggregation with gradient buffering at the server, allowing for reliable model updating from multiple devices without synchronization. We analyze the algorithm's accuracy and convergence, showing that it achieves comparable results with asynchronously updated models. We evaluate our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating significant efficiency gains and improved accuracy compared to existing federated learning methods. This framework provides an efficient solution for large-scale federated learning applications. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/learn2beconverge/fedasync.

The main challenge holding back the advancement of gallium nitride transistors from being used in high-power applications is the limited conductive potential of gallium nitride's hole mobility. In our investigation, we find that by combining GaN with layers of zinc germanium nitride and magnesium silicon nitride, the anisotropic strain resulting from these combinations can improve the hole mobility. Through detailed computational analysis, we identify the most effective way to achieve a significant increase in hole mobility, noting that a combination of a zinc germanium nitride layer beneath a gauginium nitride epitaxy and a magnesium silicon nitride buffer layer beneath the substrate produces a strain state beneficial to hole mobility. Consequently, this combination results in an epitaxy with minimal recrystallization and leads to an improved hole transport in the epitaxy. Using a simple model that matches the anisotropic strain to the lattice parameters of the nitride, we derive the necessary lattice parameters for an optimally conducting GaN layer. Using this approach, we calculate the optimal lattice parameters for pairs consisting of GaN and zinc germanium nitride, magnesium silicon nitride, or manganese silicide. Ultimately, we identify two matches - zinc germanium nitride and gallium nitride, as well as magnesium silicon nitride and gallium nitride - that are suitable for each other, enabling an improved hole mobility in gallium nitride due to the anisotropic strain caused by their alignment of lattice parameters. In specific terms, we find potential gains in hole mobility of approximately 75% for epitaxies aligned with zinc germanium nitride and approximately 55% with magnesium silicon nitride. In practical terms, this means GaN layers aligned with ZnGeN2 could experience a 35% improvement while those aligned with MgSiN2 could experience a 20% improvement. In the realm of III-V semiconductors, this concept could lead to further optimizations, and we therefore suggest exploring other pairs, such as aluminum nitride paired with iron germanium nitride or iron silicon nitride, or silicon carbide paired with manganese silicide or iron germanium nitride, to identify additional applications and potential gains. By aligning gallium nitride with zinc germanium nitride, magnesium silicon nitride, or other compatible materials, the anisotropic strain can boost its hole mobility, presenting a practical strategy for enhancing this parameter and opening up new possibilities for gallium nitride transistors in high-power applications. The platform achieves state-of-the-art results, matching or exceeding the sound quality of established experts, and significantly reduces the training time and effort. Moreover, it enables non-experts to create high-quality sounds, bridging the gap between experts and novices in sound design. To mitigate the severity of a pandemic, governments are implementing widespread lockdowns, resulting in substantial economic consequences. A fundamental question arises about the most effective timing of policies, given that earlier implementation means both increased lives and greater economic loss. We reframe the pandemic as a utility maximization issue, combining both health and economic outcomes. By introducing a variable penalty for economic losses relative to a non-pandemic baseline, we obtain a total utility function. Our approach generalizes to any concave total utility function. We find that, in the absence of further information, the optimal policy involves implementing a lockdown as soon as the average pandemic severity reaches a threshold. This threshold depends on the relative weighting of health and economic outcomes. When the health consequences are given a higher priority, we find that an increase in the maximum severity level of the pandemic corresponds to a decrease in the optimal lockdown threshold. Additionally, by expanding the total utility function, we are able to analyze more complex scenarios, such as a pandemic with variable transmission rates and non-linear severity levels. The development and maintenance of machine learning applications is complicated by the fact that ML models are heavily influenced by a vast amount of data, which cannot all be reviewed by developers and data scientists. This makes it necessary to identify problems during the data preparation phase, rather than waiting for issues to arise later on in the ML pipeline. In order to do this, we've created an approach for determining the impact that individual data records have on the accuracy of the ML pipeline. This involves calculating the significance of each record using the Shapley value, which takes into account how it interacts with other records, as well as variables like data preprocessing and model training methods. We've implemented this method in a tool that allows for efficient debugging of large datasets, and has been designed for easy integration into the ML pipeline. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated in a study that analyzed 14 different datasets and 4 different ML algorithms, which showed that it can accurately pinpoint problematic data records over 90% of the time. In fact, it was found that a small subset of the dataset, consisting of just 10% of its elements, was sufficient for identifying issues and determining their cause. In terms of performance, it was found that a large dataset of over 180 million records could be processed in under 15 seconds using the tool, making it fast and efficient. The accuracy of the results was confirmed by comparing it with alternative methods for identifying problematic data records and categorizing their issues. The feasibility of using this approach in real-world applications was also demonstrated in two examples, one of which involved debugging a video classification application and the other a recommendation system for detecting fraudulent behavior. In terms of limitations, it was found that the current implementation has a high computational complexity of O(n^3) and could be optimized further. In particular, it was suggested that the accuracy of the results could be enhanced by incorporating more advanced techniques for determining the significance of individual data records and their interactions with other variables in the ML pipeline. In the future, it is intended to develop and implement more advanced algorithms for calculating the Shapley value, as well as integrating the tool with popular ML frameworks and applications for easier use. In contrast, the underlying equation for one-dimensional quantum integrable systems has an established method of solving initial data using the inverse scattering technique. This paper demonstrates that the application of the inverse scattering method to the Zakhararv-Shabat system, which models a one-dimensional quantum integrable boson gas, leads to a derivation of the probability distribution of the KPZ equation's height under low signal noise. This distribution is found to be Gaussian with a mean and variance that are both long-term and noise-dependent. This mean and variance are consistent with previous numerical simulations and our previously established analytic results for the long-term, noise-free behavior of the KPZ equation. The solar breeze's compressive plasma turbulence is investigated through detailed statistics of scaled-down electric fields measured by the Magnetospheric MultiScale spacecraft. These measurements account for the turbulent electric fields' short-scale variations (less than several hundred meters) that are not fully captured by current solar breeze models. Analysis focuses on a specific solar breeze period with minimal solar wind magnetization, allowing for the separation of compressive and shear modes within the turbulence spectrum. Results reveal that the power distribution of the compressive turbulence mode follows a scaling pattern of $k^{-1.5}$ and also identifies a secondary, shorter-scale component within the spectrum. These findings demonstrate that the scaled-down electric fields measured by the spacecraft are consistent with the broadband electric turbulence observed in the solar breeze, providing valuable insights for the development of higher-resolution numerical models in astrophysics and space physics fields. Additionally, the observed scaling pattern of the compressive turbulence mode may be influenced by the solar breeze's large-scale interplanetary shocks, as well as other solar system conditions. These findings open up new avenues for research, linking the solar breeze to other turbulent environments within the heliosphere and the interstellar medium. It is also observed that the measured compressive turbulence modes within the solar breeze do not exhibit a skewness effect, which may be attributed to the influence of wave-particle interactions in the solar breeze's fluctuating fields. These measurements also provide new data for theoretical models aiming to understand the properties of compressive turbulence in 2D and 3D plasma environments. Based on these findings, further observational and experimental research is required to fully clarify the relationship between the solar breeze's compressive turbulence and its interaction with the heliosphere and the interstellar medium. It is also suggested that solar breeze periods with varying levels of magnetization should be studied to identify the impact of magnetic fluctuations on the compressive turbulence mode's properties. Moreover, it is necessary to conduct in-depth laboratory experiments to reproduce the solar breeze's compressive turbulence modes and study their properties under controlled conditions. These future studies will help to develop a more comprehensive theoretical framework for the solar breeze's compressive turbulence and its application in astrophysical and space physical contexts. It is also noted that the measured skewness effect is influenced by magnetic fluctuations, which may lead to new insights into the role of magnetic interactions in the solar breeze's compressive turbulence mode. These findings also emphasize the importance of utilizing the Magnetospheric MultiScale spacecraft for in-depth observations of the solar breeze and its compressive turbulence modes, which cannot be replicated

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions and producing longer pulses, up to several femtoseconds in duration, with reduced shot-to-shot variability. Calculations for the AWST FEL, operating in the soft X-ray range, indicate the potential for scales of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$ in undulator parameter $\mathcal{R}$. Our simulations also demonstrate that longer pulse durations can be achieved through a reduction in bandwidth, with the advantage of increased peak power and area, beneficial characteristics for applications such as spectroscopy, bio-medical research, and coherent diffraction imaging. Predicted parameters for the AWST FEL suggest a pulse duration of approximately 2.5 fs, along with a spectral bandwidth of $4.65 \times 10^{-4}$, achieving a note-worthy enhancement in time-averaged pulse area of about 76 times compared to a standard SASE FEL at a similar $\mathcal{R}$. Similar improvements are also expected for the free-electron laser in Hamburg (Hamburg ALPS) and the Center for Free-Electron Laser (LUCX) using corresponding scaling of undulator parameters. With the application of this modified chirp-taper scheme, the potential for generating attosecond pulse trains in the XUV and soft X-ray range is demonstrated, enabling detailed investigations in various fields. Moreover, this technique may also be employed in fourth harmonic generation schemes to produce high-intensity pulse trains in the water window, presenting an alternative for achieving long pulse durations, high flux, and high average pulse area with the support of an active undulator or detuning scheme. Such a configuration can potentially overcome coherence time restrictions and produce pulse durations extending to milliseconds using a multi-stage tapering approach and/or a slotted undulator structure. This could further enable experiments with a high average pulse area in the water window, facilitating the application of nonlinear spectroscopy and bio-medical imaging. Lastly, this modification may also be applied to other FEL facilities and proposed centers, such as the coherent electron beam matching scheme (CEBM), for generating extended pulse durations. In conclusion, the potential for generating long pulse durations employing a modified chirp-taper scheme using a multi-element undulator will contribute to the development of the AWST FEL, Hamburg ALPS, and LUCX, as well as other facilities

A well-documented issue in modern democracy is election manipulation through district gerrymandering. To address this issue, we propose an optimization method combining simulated annealing and a novel evaluation metric to achieve fair election outcomes. The solution involves introducing a compactness metric that quantifies the naturalness of a given map. While it is impossible to mathematically prove the correctness of a proposed map, our approach iteratively improves a map until a predetermined threshold of naturalness is reached. By applying this method to the 2011 Texas redrawing of congressional districts, we demonstrate the creation of more natural maps compared to the actual implementation. Additionally, we show that our approach is scalable by applying it to the optimization of maps with up to 1000 entities. Our method, freely available online at www.naturalmaps.org, serves as a transparent tool to aid map evaluations and potential reforms of the voting system. It also enables the computation of a fair price for which a third party could purchase and implement an alternative map. Moreover, it offers a means to assess the effectiveness of past voting system reforms in ensuring fair elections. Lastly, it allows the estimation of the financial cost of ensuring fair elections in future redrawing instances. By providing a means to quantify the quality of election maps, our approach raises the question of whether a fair map constitutes a public good. Ultimately, a fairly drawn map could facilitate the establishment of a mechanism for compensating the current voting regime for the loss of its dominance. A novel method for defect detection in patterned fabric images is proposed, which combines the use of gradient-based orientation phase feature extraction and low-rank decomposition. The proposed approach first employs GHOG to extract unique features from these images, which are then represented as 3D histograms. Subsequent low-rank decomposition of these histograms enables the identification of defects by calculating the residual error. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through experimental analysis, which highlights its capability to detect various defects in patterned fabric images. Additionally, the method is shown to effectively handle fabric images with orientation variations. A numerical study further validates the accuracy of the method in detecting defects. The performance of the method was evaluated using the SCD metric, which revealed results of 0.9547 for fabric orientation and 0.9986 for fabric defects. The outstanding performance of this method makes it an ideal choice for defect detection in patterned fabric images. The proposed method has been openly contributed for further development. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our results demonstrate the extent of enhancements possible in game design, revealing a considerable gap between the current limits and the potential future performance.
Furthermore, we invite the community to participate in assessing agent abilities by evaluating their performance on TextWorldExpress, using the simplified rules and more agency guidelines provided. Topological insulators are distinguished by a robust electronic current that flows on their surface without loss, resulting from protected degenerate electronic states near the surface. This surface current originates from the geometric structure of surface states, characterized by a non-trivial topological property represented by a two-dimensional Chern number. When multiple surface states exist, each with its Chern number, the total non-trivial current is the sum of individual contributions. We discuss how this non-abelian nature of topological properties is manifested in geometric properties of multiple bands and illustrate the concept through examples of two-dimensional topological insulators containing point defects. In the presence of time-reversal symmetry, constraints on Chern numbers due to parity and spin-obit coupling can significantly affect the total non-trivial current, leading to the conclusion that it must be an integer, whether the current is geometrically confined or not. Time-reversal symmetry, however, can be broken by a potential vortex at the source of back-scattering that invalidates the total Chern number as a measure of current. In the absence of spin-orbit coupling, each band is isotropic and geometrically confined, leading to an integer total Chern number, but band isolation relies on spin-orbit coupling, demonstrating the importance of spin-orbit coupling in determining the topological properties of insulators. Additionally, when an isolated geometric vortex is introduced into an insulator, it causes a localized non-robust electronic current, parameterized by a complex Chern number, and we examine how geometric properties of vortices and solitons interact with topological properties of insulators. Finally, defect states in topological insulators can be found by projecting a vortex from a higher-dimensional space, and we discuss the equivalent role of overlap in this process using a two-dimensional Chern number as an indicator of topological properties of insulators. In a related context, we also discuss how geometric structures of states in a quantum dot can be probed using a Chern number derived from a non-abelian quantum field theory, and the non-abelian nature of topological properties is illustrated by the geometric structure of degenerate electronic states in a quantum dot without time-reversal symmetry. The total non-trivial current is the sum of contributions from each geometric structure, and it is constrained by parity due to spin-orbit coupling, and can be affected by a potential vortex at the source of back-scattering that invalidates the total Chern number as a measure of current. These concepts provide a topological mathematical approach to understanding protected degenerate electronic states

Consider a planar $p$-harmonic function, defined within an open sector of a fixed angle, located in the right half-plane and extending to infinity. By applying an integral average estimation, we derive a local bound on the function in terms of its distance from the boundary and a bounded function within a smaller sector, yielding a specific consequence when combined with a growth estimate derived from Harnack's inequality, resulting in an inequality relating the function to its derivative in terms of the angle of the sector and $p$. The research on transfer learning between robotic systems is highly undetermined due to the diversity of tasks and variations in task representation. Task-specific mappings between the task space and joint space are crucial for executing objectives effectively, yet these mappings are task-specific and vary greatly. We propose a manipulability domain transformation framework to address the challenge of transfer learning among robotic systems. This framework utilizes the manipulability tensor to create a task-independent mapping between task space and joint space, allowing for the transfer of task dependencies across robotic systems. To develop this framework, we employed the Information Gains metric to identify joint angles contributing to task progress, formulated task-specific and robot-specific manipulability domains, and demonstrated the ability to translate task dependencies between robotic systems. To validate this approach, we implemented a proof-of-concept experiment involving a humanoid robot attempting to grasp objects using a 6-DOF end-effector, and successfully showed the transfer of manipulability domains between these related but distinct systems. Important challenges to robotic transfer learning, such as noise and varying task representations, were addressed through the application of manifold-based ICPS and parallel transport to align manipulability domains effectively. This study offers a novel approach to addressing the issue of transfer learning among robotic systems, leveraging the manipulability tensor to create a task-independent mapping, which can be translated between robotic systems. Experimental results demonstrate the ability of this framework to transfer task dependencies between 6-DOF manipulator systems, despite noise and differences in task representations. To achieve this goal, we developed a proof-of-concept experiment involving a humanoid robot attempting to grasp objects using a 6-DOF manipulator, and demonstrated the transfer of manipulability domains between these related but distinct systems, addressing the issue of transfer learning among robotic systems. They focused on final states with two charged leptons, and used the matrix element method to reject backgrounds, achieving a 97% efficiency for signal retention and a 10% efficiency for background rejection. Additionally, researchers found that the matrix element method enabled the correlation of systematic uncertainties to reduce statistical uncertainties by 20%. Based on these findings, researchers projected that the Higgs boson pair production can be detected with a significance of 3.2 standard deviations at the 14 TeV LHC with 300 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity for non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\texm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^*$}$ process. We analyze the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with its solutions in the exterior of a compact convex object in a higher-dimensional space. Our focus is on solutions that blast out of a critical point. We demonstrate that any solution with a critical point as its initial concentration and nonzero amplitude will eventually explode, its energy dispersing in all directions infinitely far away from the initial concentration. This critical point can be anywhere - at the object's edge or its vertex. Interestingly, solutions that remain bounded and concentrate at the object's vertex must be trivial - they will eventually be seen to not concentrate there. This addresses a question first raised by Gustafson, Nilsson, and Visciglia. Our approach uses a special technique, 'blown-up solutions,' drawing from the work of Kapitanski, Roudneov, and Tsikhanin. To generalize this method, enhancing its power to cover various types of interaction, would be highly beneficial. It's evident that certain aspects of the proof are highly connected to the specifics of the particular type of interaction chosen - for example, the particular way in which solutions behave as they approach the object's vertex depends on the chosen type of interaction. Therefore, one potential area of further research could be to develop a more universal framework that would allow for a proof that works for a variety of types of interaction without having to distinguish between them. This would be in line with the approach taken in the work of Roudneov and Tsikhanin. Our results also address a related question first explored by Visciglia. This, too, addresses a question first raised by Visciglia. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which doesn't rely on images being altered and can be triggered without needing access to the compromised model. Our "Semantic Trojan Attack" (STA) embeds backdoors deep within linguistic representations, making it difficult to detect and potentially resulting in significant security breaches. Our experiments show that even with limited access to the model, we can successfully carry out STA, and it compares favorably to existing methods in terms of efficacy and detection difficulty. Additionally, we highlight the implications of a more invasive variant of STA that can be triggered without any limitations, confirming the difficulties models have with semantically tailored probes. This study introduces a novel learning paradigm where data is examined locally through neighbourhood insights when the availability of global information is uncertain due to labeling inaccuracies or information overload. Two basic local training algorithms are proposed, one using the majority label within a certain number of nearest neighbours (Local-M) and another incorporating all labels from a specified radius (Local-All). By evaluating these algorithms on synthetic and real-world problems, particularly in the context of image classification and drug pairing prediction, this research demonstrates their capability to learn under various conditions, including limited data, high noise, and large dimensions. Furthermore, this investigation highlights the potential for local models to develop robust insights into data features and their interactions. Ultimately, this research presents a framework for determining the usefulness of local methods in learning, and suggests potential avenues for integrating local models with global techniques to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the learning process. One such possibility explored in this study is combining local training with the global model, but further research is required to realize this goal. The latter are defined as $\sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k \binom{n}{k} z_1^{k+1} \cdots z_m^{k+1} \zeta(m; k+1; z_2, \ldots, z_m)$. Employing the SHS and CHS framework, we express these series as rational functions of $z_1$, along with an analysis of their denominators and an exploration of their numerical behavior. The results we obtain are generalizations of previous outcomes, applicable to any number of dimensions $m \geq 2$. The research further extends the functions $\zeta(m; k+1; z_2, \ldots, z_m)$, usually defined with even summation indices, by deriving their analogs with mixed parities of summation indices. The resulting functions, denoted as $\zeta(m; k+1; z_2, \ldots, z_m)]$, are then shown to be invariant under specific transformations of their arguments. The findings we present are therefore a universal set of results, capable of generating various versions of the generalized functions. The validity of our formulation is then confirmed by comparing it with known four-dimensional Feynman integrals. This distinction is now surpassed by a brown dwarf holding the same-scale hydrogen fuel, with a half-life of merely 0.6 years. This rarest of stars, named WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, is an extremely cold, red object that was discovered in 2019 and lost its cooling capacity in 2020. This unusual phenomenon is likely attributed to a sudden and intense episode of gravitational decretion, marking the onset of a novel class of objects that characterise a brief, free-falling stage. This stage follows the initial formation from a cloud fragment and precedes the typical contraction phase, enabling the rapid dissipation of angular momentum. This process results in objects that are both hot and extended, in stark contrast to what was previously expected, with characteristics analogous to those of a white dwarf. As a result, objects in this brief, free-falling stage may be indistinguishable from late, cooling objects due to their similar sizes, temperatures, and red colors. This could further lead to a re-evaluation of the mechanisms governing the typical, contracting stage and the initial formation of objects. The fabrication process for a wide variety of particles in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions is studied using data from 10 nucleon-nucleon collision events with a center-of-mass energy of 5440 GeV and an impact parameter better than 6 femtometers. These experiments were conducted using the LHCb detector with Xe-Xe projectiles. For the most frequently produced particles, such as pions and kaons, the resulting counts per collision are very close to the predicted values based on the quark composition of these particles. However, the production of other particles, such as protons, antiprotons, and $\phi$ mesons, shows notable discrepancies between the observed counts and the predicted values based solely on quark composition. These differences are particularly evident in the experiments' early stages and rise more noticeably as the particles' momentum exceeds 1 GeV per nucleon. These findings are consistent with the presence of short-lived strange nucleon-antinucleon pairs as well as short-lived strange baryon-antibaryon pairs. These experimental results can also be explained, to a certain extent, by the concept of chiral magnetic separation which causes nucleon-antinucleon pairs to spontaneously generate in the experiments' early stages. It is found that about half of the proton-antiproton production can be attributed to chiral magnetic separation. Similarly, it is determined that, in the experiments' early stages, about half of the $\phi$ meson production can be attributed to chiral magnetic separation. By comparing the observed counts of protons, antiprotons, and $\phi$ mesons as a function of the particles' rapidity, it is found that short-lived strange nucleon-antinucleon pairs and short-lived strange baryon-antibaryon pairs are produced at varying rates relative to the expected values based solely on quark composition. It is determined that, in the experiments' early stages, the short-lived nucleon-antinucleon pairs are produced at a rate 1.6 to 2 times the predicted value based solely on quark composition, while the short-lived baryon-antibaryon pairs are produced at a rate 2 to 2.5 times the predicted value based solely on quark composition. In addition to these findings, it is found that the short-lived nucleon-antinucleon pairs and the short-lived baryon-antibaryon pairs are produced at a rate 1.2

We introduce a novel approach to solving DGLAP equations via a neural network, thereby enabling the generation of parton distribution functions. The method employs a directed graph, where nodes correspond to specific momentum scales and edges contain neural networks that facilitate the evolution of parton distribution functions from one scale to another. The effectiveness of this neural network method is demonstrated by comparing its results to those from traditional fitting procedures, revealing agreement within the statistical errors for different momentum scales. Furthermore, we investigate the complexity of the directed graph, demonstrating that utilizing two neural networks per flavor results in satisfactory accuracy. The findings indicate that employing this parton distribution function framework enables the detection of neural network parameters that correlate with the underlying parton distribution functions, thereby providing insight into the nature of parton distribution functions. The code used for generating the results in this paper has been publicly released for the purpose of validation and further development. The neural parton distribution function framework has the potential for integration into existing particle physics software, such as Napoleon, in order to enable the use of parton distribution functions in collider experiments. The neural parton distribution function framework can also serve as a starting point for future work on neural phenomenological parameters. The graph structure can be adapted for use in the DGLAP equations based on different parton distribution functions, thereby enabling the use of neural network results to investigate discrepancies between different parton distribution functions and their associated neural network parameters. The method can further be extended to the solution of Boltzmann equations in the context of cosmology. The code used for generating the results in this paper has been publicly released at the following link for the purpose of validation and further development: https://github.com/gilbertoGracey/neural-partons/tree/main-neural-partons-parton-distribution. Determining star formation rates in galaxies is crucial for understanding kinase activity's impact on molecular gas. Although various methods exist for calculating this rate, it's challenging to assess their accuracy without relying on purely theoretical scenarios. Using a dataset of 230 galaxies with measured Brackett-$\gamma$ emission and reliable light curves, we developed an unbiased technique for evaluating the performance of different methods in deriving this rate. By combining this approach with a kernel-based machine learning technique, we successfully trained an algorithm on a sample of 175 galaxies and tested it on an independent set of 75 galaxies. Comparing its outcomes with observed Brackett-$\gamma$ luminosities, we found that our model predicts Brackett-$\gamma$ emission with high accuracy, thus serving as a gold standard for assessing the reliability of star formation rate predictions. Furthermore, we observed that other methods tend to underpredict the star formation rate by approximately 0.25 dex on average, with some even predicting rates as low as 1% of the observed values. Additionally, we found no correlation between observed signal strength and predicted-to-observed ratio, suggesting that our algorithm performs equally well in galaxies with strong or weak broadband optical and near-infrared light. To ensure the broad applicability of our technique, we applied it while excluding galaxies that might be affected by active galactic nuclei or have complex dust patterns, and we found that our results remain unchanged. Consequently, this technique can be used as an upper limit on the predicted star formation rate, and the discrepancy between predicted and observed values may be attributed to factors such as dust obscuration, or to the presence of massive star clusters that emit intensely in near-infrared lines. Furthermore, this technique may also be employed for galaxies that exhibit very low ionized gas emission, thus expanding its scope beyond its current limitations. In the future, we aim to refine this technique using star formation rates based on neutral hydrogen data from ALMA, and we expect that its improved precision will enable it to provide even more accurate predictions. In the course of this research, we also developed a new, unbiased technique for estimating the mass of stellar light present in galaxies, serving as a key variable in deriving star formation rates. This new technique was trained using a dataset of 230 galaxies with measured broad-band optical and near-infrared light and was shown to predict related spectra with high accuracy, serving as a unbiased proxy for mass for stellar light present in galaxies. We introduce an innovative method to solve the general diffusion equation, a model that was initially developed to describe non-Fickian diffusion. This method employs an operator based on the L1 norm and enhances accuracy with an asymptotic correction. The proposed solution has a explicit formula and exhibits precise spatial and temporal patterns. The numerical examples demonstrate a notable improvement in resolution and a direct manifestation of anomalous diffusion properties. Furthermore, the method demonstrates exceptional stability and robustness across a wide range of parameters. We showcase the efficacy of this approach in solving ND, NFD, FFD, and CFD problems. Notably, the method outperforms existing techniques, such as the finite difference, fractional Euler method, and JJ methods, in terms of accuracy and resolution. The new method is also exceptionally versatile and can effectively solve equations with spatial dimensions higher than one. The theoretical analysis confirms that the method is suitable for both parabolic and hyperbolic general diffusion equations. The solutions display remarkable convergence to the exact solutions, with the level of convergence dependent on the time step and spatial step. The behavior of the solutions can be accurately modeled as a sum of logarithmic series in the case of ND, NFD, FFD, and an alternating series in the case of CFD. The primary results are also substantiated through sensitive simulations and a comprehensive analysis. The method is further validated by comparing it to existing techniques and the relevant theory in the field of fractional calculus. The comparisons reveal notable differences in stability, robustness, and accuracy between the new method and the existing techniques. The main results are also highlighted from an economic perspective in terms of memory and processing requirements. The complexity of implementing the new method is exceptional and can be summarized as follows: The method can be easily implemented using explicit formulas with notable time and spatial non-locality, no need for expensive fractal grids, and the support of fractional Easter. The key properties of the method can be summarized as follows: The method exhibits exceptional stability, robustness, and accuracy; it is capable of providing precise pure temporal, spatial, and temporal-spatial solutions; it is directly anomalous; it is applicable to dimensions one through seven; it is suitable for both parabolic and hyperbolic general diffusion equations; it is applicable across a wide range of parameters; and it outperforms existing techniques. The method can be utilized in various applications such as modeling of turbulent, fractional, and non-Markovian processes across a wide range of fields including medicine, biology, geophysics, meteorology, and engineering

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to recognize handwritten mathematical expressions from a stylus. The challenge involves identifying mathematical expressions from stylus events, which are tracked by the Stabilo pen on a graphing calculator equipped with a sensor. The challenge poses two main tasks: (1) detecting when the user starts writing an expression and (2) recognizing the actual expression. To achieve these tasks, we propose a novel sensor-based approach, consisting of sensor event feature extraction, offline expression detection, and offline expression recognition using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for online expression recognition in real-time. The effectiveness of our approach is validated through challenge metrics on the provided dataset, yielding 0.88 accuracy in offline expression detection and 0.82 accuracy in offline expression recognition. Furthermore, our model exhibits robust performance across various devices, demonstrating consistency in its results. Our solution encompasses detailed configurations for training and testing, along with a comprehensive framework that can be accessed via GitHub. Experimental findings illustrate the benefits of our proposed method, showcasing superior results compared to alternative techniques in expression detection and recognition. Notably, our approach surpasses the baseline metric in expression recognition by 0.04 and surpasses state-of-the-art metrics by 0.06. Our proposed method also exhibits the capacity for real-time application, processing approximately 10-20 events per second on a smartphone, and displaying significant potential for actual use cases through user studies. A comparative analysis of our approach is presented, highlighting its advantages and disadvantages relative to other methods. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/jbarchichi/UniMI_EMSA for reproduction of our results. One potential future research avenue could involve the integration of additional sensor data to further enhance mathematical expression recognition, potentially utilizing multimodal learning techniques. Another potential avenue could involve leveraging existing knowledge about mathematical expressions to enhance recognition, potentially utilizing domain knowledge and existing datasets for enhancement. Our approach offers several potential research avenues for enhancement, such as the integration of multimodal learning using additional sensor data, domain knowledge, and existing datasets for enhancement. Additionally, we can explore the use of online and offline techniques in combination to further improve our results. A possible combination of online and offline techniques could involve using LSTM for offline expression recognition and leveraging the stylus events for online expression detection. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/jbarchichi/UniMI_EMS

This paper introduces an innovative method for generating synthetic speech durations in English, based solely on speech data. Traditional parametric methods create overdispersed models, whereas this new approach produces distributions with reduced dispersion. A major challenge in training non-parametric models is preventing the overfitting of the model to the training data, particularly when working with large datasets. The proposed method employs a median-filtering technique to control the overfitting and balance the learning of the model. When compared to a leading non-parametric method, the new approach demonstrated improved statistical accuracy and higher correlation with human speech rates, while also requiring fewer parameters. Notably, the new method performed well on speech durations, but struggled with other phoneme-level timescales. Future research will focus on refining this method to accurately model various speech timescales. However, software available for presence models is limited in its ability to model species interactions and population dynamics across various spatial scales. Our research aims to address this limitation with the spOccupancy R package, which offers a comprehensive solution for spatial presence models that can incorporate species interactions, account for detection bias, and consider habitat and spatial relationships. The package also enables models to be integrated and utilized in a Bayesian framework. This article showcases the capabilities of spOccupancy by demonstrating a variety of models, including those that integrate single, multi, and combined species models, as well as models that account for population dynamics, species interactions, and broad spatial patterns. Furthermore, we highlight the package's capabilities for analyzing data in a Bayesian manner. Ultimately, spOccupancy provides a versatile tool for tackling complex ecological issues and informing conservation efforts. The package's documentation includes a detailed guide, and model code including this overview, can be accessed on GitHub. The spOccupancy package is now available on CRAN, making it easily installable via install.packages("spOccupancy"). Furthermore, the data and code used in this example can also be accessed on GitHub. Existing examples of spOccupancy's use can be viewed on our blog: https://jmcmahan.github.io/spOccupancy-blog. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, these specialists often fail to perform differential diagnoses on skin cancers, with the accuracy varying depending on lesion type. A collaborative project called Skincare aimed to address this by creating an open-source system capable of providing interactive differential diagnoses for malignant skin lesions using machine learning. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and to investigate the critical load, defined as the largest initial infection rate that prevents epidemic extinction, or the largest initial infection load that prevents extinction given a finite number of infectious contacts. To find this critical load, we develop a nonparametric spectral perturbation theorem, applicable to general hypergraphs, and apply it to specific cases, such as random hypergraphs and those derived from random geometric embeddings, demonstrating that the spectral method can effectively determine the critical load in these scenarios. Furthermore, our spectral analysis is validated through numerical simulations in these systems, showing that the associated statistics can serve as reliable predictors of the critical load, and that this method is also versatile enough to be applied to other hypergraphs as well. In addition to these findings, we define and investigate the concepts of leakage and broadening, explaining how these mechanisms contribute to the emergence of phenomena like spread acceleration and delay, which can be interpreted as the transition from ballistic to diffusive behavior, observed in epidemic spread. To capture these dynamics, we introduce a natural two-time correlation function, and by differentiating this function with respect to time, we can effectively derive an equation that describes the observed behavior, valid for all times and applicable to general hypergraphs. In particular, we investigate the behavior of this time correlation function in random hypergraphs and those derived from random geometric embeddings, demonstrating that the observed dynamics can be explained by the underlying graph structure, resulting in a predictable, yet highly flexible and general theoretical description of the time-dependent behavior of the observed correlation function. This work, motivated by epidemic spread, can potentially be applied to other processes as well. In conclusion, our approach provides a fundamental understanding of the transition between different types of behavior, and the spectral conditions we introduce can effectively determine the critical load, while the correlation function dynamics can explain the emergence of phenomena like spread acceleration and delay. The extensive numerical validation, carried out in random hypergraphs and those derived from random geometric embeddings, underscores the feasibility and reliability of the spectral method, making it a viable tool for applying the spectral technique to a wide range of systems. Developing safe and efficient multithreaded applications is increasingly critical as feature-rich compilers and dynamic memory management enable programmers to exploit parallelism. Unfortunately, the complexity of concurrent programming often leads to undetected errors that can cause program crashes, data corruption, and even security vulnerabilities. Current approaches for detecting and mitigating concurrent programming errors focus primarily on detection, ignoring the critical aspect of causality that helps identify and predict potential issues. This paper introduces McMini, a model checker designed to verify the absence of errors in multithreaded programs by leveraging a DPOR-based strategy that facilitates the analysis of finite and potentially infinite concurrent executions. McMini's modular architecture allows easy integration of various thread-prediction and run-time verification tools, which expand its capabilities to include infinite executions and run-time verification. Experimental results demonstrating McMini's efficacy are presented, showcasing its ability to verify complex multithreaded programs with up to 15 threads. Additionally, a companion study outlines McMini's toolset, which provides access to McMini via a GUI or command-line interface, in addition to a publicly available benchmark suite containing 69 verification tests. This toolset supports McMini's source code and allows for easy integration of alternative model checking algorithms. The world witnessed unprecedented pandemic-related and political misinformation dissemination on WhatsApp during 2020. In response, WhatsApp introduced limitations to forward individual messages, aiming to mitigate the spread of misinformation. This study models user behavior as a stochastic process and investigates the impact of these limitations. Model parameters are calibrated using real-world data, and simulations examine various scenarios, considering factors like user connections and the presence of malicious accounts. Our analysis suggests that these limitations are insufficient to eliminate misinformation dissemination. This finding is consistent across our models and provides actionable insights for app developers and policymakers. Building upon our models, we propose potential strategies to enhance the effectiveness of WhatsApp's limitations, including an optimal message forwarding policy and a public education initiative. Furthermore, we identify information asymmetry as a underlying cause of misinformation spread and discuss its implications. Ultimately, our study offers a framework for analyzing the dynamics of online misinformation and evaluating countermeasures. The observed correlations were found to be asymmetrical, which is caused by the spatial distribution of the excited atoms. The asymmetry becomes more pronounced when the photons are emitted at wider angles or further away from the central plane defined by the original excitation laser's polarization. This property can be utilized to enhance detection efficiency for spectroscopic applications or improve the collection of entangled photons from atomic ensembles by adjusting the excitation and detection setups accordingly. Additionally, the degree of asymmetry can be modeled and quantitatively calculated using a simplified approach. The measured correlations are in agreement with the predicted values. The underlying physics of this phenomenon is analogous to the process of nuclear collisions and may be described through the coherent interaction of photons and atomic excitations. The experimentally obtained correlations also provide a quantitative understanding of the atomic excitation dynamics, which is not directly accessible through linear spectroscopy. The results can be generalized to other atomic systems and may have practical applications in optimizing nonlinear optical phenomena or generating entangled photons for quantum information processing. Lastly, the final excitation probability can be accurately measured by integrating the observed correlations over the entire possible range of photon angles. The overall excitation probability is in agreement with the expected values, which were previously calculated through a rate equation model or the Bloch equations. The integrated probability was also found to be highly dependent on the power of the exciting laser and follows a quadratic relationship, which is in accordance with the nonlinear two-photon excitation process. The integrated probability does not exhibit any asymmetry and solely reflects the nonlinear characteristics of the excitation process. The nonlinear behavior of the integrated probability indicates that the collection of entangled photons following two-photon excitation is not solely determined by the spontaneous emission rate nor the photon statistics of the exciting laser, but rather by the coherent interaction between the incident photons and the atomic excitations. The integrated probability may also be utilized as a quantitative indicator of this coherent interaction and could have practical applications in optimizing nonlinear optical phenomena or generating entangled photons for quantum information processing. Researchers have attacked and evaluated the effectiveness of security monitoring systems, specifically protocol detection, using custom-made tools and methods. Although this study influenced the development of commercial network traffic analyzers, there needs to be more research on open-source systems to improve their reliability and validity. Our work involves testing and validating the protocol detection capabilities of seven popular open-source monitoring systems against various attack strategies. We utilized a diverse set of traffic patterns, including 350 assaults, derived from  260 unique scenarios, to assess their performance. Compared to a custom-made, specialized system, open-source monitors struggled with detection, particularly when faced with specific attack methods. To address this limitation, we provide recommendations for configuring and using these systems effectively. Our findings could benefit anyone using open-source monitors for security monitoring and detection and may inspire attacks on systems that rely on these tools for protection. Additionally, we make available our entire research, including the used traffic patterns, configured monitor settings, and raw detection results. Furthermore, we launched a public competition to identify the most effective settings for detectingassisntvectors, offering prizes and inviting participation from the security community. We expect our research to enhance the validity and confidence of open-source monitor configurations, ultimately improving security monitoring outcomes. Please visit our website at  https://assault-project.org/  for more information. We make available our research in two distinct reports, each focusing on distinct aspects of our research: the evaluation methodology and the results of the competition for determining effective monitor configurations. The first report, titled 'Assaults on Open Source Network Security Monitoring: Evaluation Methodology', is available at  https://doi.org/10.6084/ m9.fgdxva0g.0  and the second report, titled 'Assaults on Open Source Network Security Monitoring: Discovery of Assult Detector Settings', is available at  https://doi.org/10.6084/ m9.2427ci92.0. Our public website at  https://assault-project.org/  offers the research reports and additional information about our project. We also took part in the Black Hat USA 2023 Archer's Guide to Awesome Network Monitoring contest, presenting our research and offering a downloadable virtual machine that replicates our test environment. As a result of our research, seven open-source monitor maintainers have expressed interest in incorporating our findings to improve the validity of their systems. We made contact with representatives from eight premier network traffic analysis software companies and provided them with our research and recommendations for potentially enhance the accuracy of their products as well.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerge when new data sources become integrated with existing ones, posing a challenge to this technique as it struggles to accommodate unfamiliar categories. In this research, we tackle this difficulty by initially classifying unlabelled samples into distinct groups and then training a model to predict class labels based on those group assignments. Due to restrictions on communication in federated learning, data cannot be shared with other users, and we cannot access labelled data. As a result, we employ a zero-shot method that requires no additional data but rather relies on language and audio semantic embeddings that are previously constructed. This approach is initially tested in a simple comparison with a traditional federated learning technique, and subsequent improvements are made by refining audio embeddings using federated learning. When evaluated against baseline methods on various datasets, our technique demonstrates superior performance in both accuracy and communication cost. To validate the federal learning potential under uncertainty, we also created a set of simulated datasets by merging labelled datasets with fake user data, and found that our approach excels in this scenario as well. Source code for our research is available at https://github.com/jbincn0/zsfl. Keywords: Federated Learning, Zero-shot Learning, Audio Classification.

Bloom filters provide efficient, randomized checks for set membership, allowing for the suppression of unnecessary items through a probabilistic approach. Although they have a low false positive rate, their lookup operations can be slow. In contrast, Bloom filters' alternatives, such as cuckoo filters, outperform them in lookup times; however, they often require more memory to achieve the same error rates. To address these shortcomings, researchers introduced generalised and optimised hash functions. This paper builds upon their findings, introducing a new algorithm combining elements of Bloom and cuckoo filters. By integrating the properties of both, the proposed xor filter achieves the fastest available lookup times, the smallest memory requirements, or a balance between these two performance metrics. To demonstrate the practical applications of our solution, we tested it against existing filters, including Bloom, cuckoo, and Patience hash filters. The experimental results show that our implementation outperforms current solutions in various scenarios. Additionally, we provide an efficient conversion method to adapt existing Bloom and cuckoo filters to our new algorithm, incorporating elements of Bloom filters. Finally, we introduce a new family of hash functions, which we call xor-rot, drawing a connection between previous research and introducing a novel property, orf, or xor-fold. The proposed xor-fold property may have independent value in designing new data structures. The code for our implementation is publicly available online. The authors wish to acknowledge T.
