This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it operates efficiently without obstructing performance. Evaluation on various datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively prevents Byzantine attacks and offers competitive accuracy compared to the unmodified FL baseline, all achieved with the maintenance of client anonymity. Our code is openly accessible via the provided link for replication purposes. Keywords: Federated Learning, Byzantine learning, Deep learning, Distance computing, Data clustering, Anonymity. Milletti et al. (2022) published a related work "Voogd: Efficient and Anonymous Federated Learning", which is referenced in this research. Voogd's protocol was found efficient however vulnerable to Byzantine attacks, which led to the development of FLVoogd addressing these limitations. FLVoogd is evaluated on several datasets, providing recovery results for MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and Reuters datasets. It remains to be seen whether Voogd can be enhanced to resist Byzantine attacks. It is also open to investigation if FLVoogd can function without servers, potentially making it a more decentralized platform. Moreover, there could be a possibility of Voogd being improved to operate with multiple servers for an enhanced performance. Inspired by the brain's efficient learning and storage capabilities, spiking neural networks have the potential to revolutionize sequence-based AI applications. However, developing a robust learning framework for spiking neural networks remains an complex challenge. This work proposes a novel framework, SPIN, which empowers spiking neural networks to effectively learn and retrieve arbitrary temporal patterns, even in the presence of corruptions. This framework relies on the principles of synaptic plasticity, such as Hebbian principles and stabilization techniques, to ensure biologically plausible learning. To test the SPIN framework, we evaluated it on multiple temporal pattern learning tasks and compared it to other popular deep learning methods, even though they are not designed for spiking neural networks. According to our results, SPIN outperforms other methods by a significant margin, especially when dealing with sequence lengths of 10 or more steps. Furthermore, our model exhibits exceptional robustness to various types of corruptions, such as noise and perturbations. This benchmark demonstrates that spiking neural networks can efficiently model temporal patterns using a minimal number of parameters, thereby achieving unparalleled performance compared to other deep learning methods. This benchmark provides a robust foundation for developing more sophisticated spiking neural networks that can effectively learn and retrieve complex temporal patterns. To validate the biological feasibility of our model, we examined the consistency of our results by analyzing the distribution of weights and the dependency of hidden neuron activity, ensuring that our model remains true to its biological inspirations. This validation reinforces the belief that spiking neural networks can serve as an efficient and biological plug for sequence-based AI applications. To showcase the practical implications of our model, we developed a spiking neural network-based agent that learns to navigate through random environments using the SPIN framework. This agent demonstrates exceptional environmental memory and learns to tackle complex tasks, even when confronted with limited resources and simple components. To our knowledge, this work presents the first successful implementation of a spiking neural network using Hebbian principles to learn arbitrary temporal patterns, especially in the presence of corruptions. This research opens up new avenues for developing robust, efficient, and biological learning models that can effectively model temporal patterns using spiking neural networks. Furthermore, our results may also inspire the development of novel hardware architectures, such as neuromorphic chips, that can efficiently learn and retrieve temporal patterns using spiking neural networks. The 2022 Out-of-Category Challenge was an image classification competition hosted by Huawei Technologies. The competition tasked participants with developing algorithms to identify out-of-distribution (OOD) images, i.e., images that do not belong to any of the training categories. The specific goal was to accurately pinpoint "unknown" images among known training categories and distinguish them from "unknown" images that contain noise or other distractions. The evaluation criteria were based on two metrics: the accuracy of in-distribution (ID) classification and the true positive rate of OOD detection. The dataset comprised ImageNet labels, consisting of 220 categories with 120 OOD classes, and included a large collection of natural scenes, artifacts, text, vehicles, construction materials, and other diverse objects. The winning models utilized various ensemble techniques combining pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs), soft-ensemble methods, pseudo-labeling, and input augmentation methods to achieve exceptional performance. The exceptional accuracy of the top models surpassed 0.998, while their detection rates exceeded 0.999 for both ID classification and OOD detection. The best models were designed to operate efficiently on mobile devices, employing reduced computational methods that required minimal memory for processing. The outstanding results were achieved using a Huawei-designed kernel, kernel-ensemble, and mobileOne families of mobile CNN models. The top models also exhibited impressive robustness against various adversarial attacks, both on and off the Malicious Image Challenge. The associated code, models, and dataset are now available for public access at a specified hyperlink. Future research will aim to expand upon the competition's concepts, specifically exploring the incorporation of OOD detection in language models and the utilization of low-resource and real-world datasets for training. The 2022 Out-of-Category Challenge is expected to pave the way for significant advancements in this research area. The study found that the electronic properties of the EuS/InAs interface depend on the configuration of atoms at the interface, with a covalent interface exhibiting a higher energy gap at the Fermi level and thus requiring higher energy inputs to initiate transport above the critical temperature. In contrast, a van der Waals configuration results in a higher density of states at the Fermi level, thus facilitating transport above the critical temperature. A refined hierarchy of Borel Wadge classes is established with the aim of optimizing computation requirements for determining whether a given Borel set belongs to a specific Wadge class. By leveraging an efficient comparison algorithm for Borel Wadge classes introduced by Laskowski and Steinberger, we develop a decision procedure for each class in the hierarchy with a computational complexity bounded by that of a fixed point operator. Specifically, it is demonstrated that whether a Borel set belongs to $\mathcal{W}^n$ can be decided in $n+1$ levels of recursion. This achievement significantly improves upon the previous $2^n$ levels required for determining $\mathcal{W}^n$ membership through the Lightface Wadge test. Additionally, we enhance the computational efficiency of an algorithm for deciding $\mathcal{W}^n$ membership without resorting to an $\alpha$-tree. By incorporating efficient Wadge comparisons on Borel Wadge classes, including those containing only closed sets, we facilitate an accelerated determination of $\mathcal{W}^n$ membership via a more direct analysis of Borel set relations, thereby circumventing the need for an $\alpha$-tree. This breakthrough enables an efficient decision procedure for determining whether a Borel set contains only countably many elements, effectively generalizing a Novikov consistent arithmetic theory. This achievement is also independent of prior research on the Borel Wadge hierarchy and the properties of Borel sets. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm for deciding $\mathcal{W}^n$ membership via an efficient query for an $\mathcal{N}^n$ membership test, which can be accomplished through an optimized search of an $\alpha$-tree. This result is further evidence of the utility of $\alpha$-trees in the analysis of Borel sets. In recent years, there has been a growing need for model compression in deploying
deep learning models. Efforts have focused primarily on the inference stage, despite
the fact that current model compression methods often require cumbersome and time-consuming
processes to transform a fully trained model into a more compact one. We present
a innovative approach called ClickTrain, which efficiently and precisely performs model
compression by decoupling the pruning and optimization stages. ClickTrain iteratively
prunes unnecessary parameters during training, thereby speeding up the process and
enabling direct access to optimally weighted models. We also introduce a dynamic
offset calculator to reposition the values of remaining parameters after pruning, thereby
ensuring accurate computations and preventing gradient noise from being propagated.
By evaluating ClickTrain on six widely used image classification models and four
independent datasets, we demonstrate its capability to surpass state-of-the-art performance
on both tiny and large models, achieving up to 3.56 times faster training times while
achieving comparable or superior accuracy levels. We also find that ClickTrain can be
used to obtain optimal models of fully trained models, enabling seamless and efficient
model compression and deployment. We publicly distribute the code for this research
at https://github.com/hjdw2/ClickTrain. It has been previously released under the
Apache 2.0 License. We hope this research will contribute positively to the deep learning
community. We are happy to report that the paper has been accepted by JMLR and the code has been released on GitHub. In constrained Markov decision processes, an optimal decision maker seeks to maximize long-term rewards while adhering to cost constraints that vary over time. We introduce a new algorithm for solving this problem by transforming it into a sequential optimization task with time-varying side constraints. This reformulation enables applications of a primal-dual algorithm. We prove that under a relatively mild assumption, this method yields an optimal solution with associated dual variables that approximate zero-congestion conditions for the constraints. Furthermore, numerical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing techniques. A demonstration, including source code, is available online at https://github.com/pradhyumshsharma/pd-cmdp. We provide theoretical guarantees that, under certain conditions, the method converges to an optimal solution. We demonstrate that these conditions are met in scenarios with polyhedral, convex, and set-constrained Markov decision processes. We also analyze the algorithm's runtime, revealing a non-uniform rate of convergence. We illustrate the results through numerical simulations, showcasing applications in power management and reinforcement learning with time-varying flow constraints. The proposed algorithm surpasses baseline methods in these scenarios, achieving closer approximations to theoretical performance limits. We demonstrate that dual variables from the algorithm result in optimal solutions with zero-congestion conditions for the constraints. This behavior is observed in numerical evaluations, where the method performs well under various parameter settings. A key aspect of the algorithm is a time-varying potential function, $v_t$, which governs the long-term reward structure. We prove that repeated applications of the method yield a convergent iterative process. Numerical tests confirm that the method converges rapidly, achieving optimal rewards in a sequential power management context. This research introduces an advanced method for recognizing handwritten mathematical equations, using an offline approach, that surpasses the accuracy of contemporary systems relying on real-time input via webcam or touchscreen. By leveraging a comprehensive mathematical expression dataset and applying an annotation framework, we've developed a groundbreaking model that can generate an abstract syntax tree from handwritten equations. This model comprises a novel convolutional neural network, specifically designed to recognize symbols, and a sequential network, responsible for recognizing sub-trees and equation structures. Our innovative approach achieves a 2.7% overall error rate on the Liepedia dataset, outperforming the best available online recognition systems, which typically record error rates of up to 5%. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of distinct sub-trees within an equation and introduces an efficient backtracking strategy to enhance the correction of complex mathematical equations. This research is expected to streamline the development of mathematical equation recognition, enabling more streamlined correction processes. Experimental findings from expert and non-expert users demonstrate that our model facilitates rapid correction of mathematical equations across diverse domains, requiring only minimal training. Specifically, users can achieve an average error rate below 2% after only 10 minutes of training. Notably, although non-expert users may require some initial training, their error rates steadily converge towards those of experts, showcasing the robust versatility of our method. This research is expected to pave the way for innovative applications in software tools, aiming to enhance the user experience through streamlined mathematical equation editing capabilities. This study investigates how the dynamics of systems are influenced by variations in activity patterns occurring throughout the process of interacting with others. To address this, a research approach is proposed that quantifies the extent of temporal instability in systems affected by such activity pattern variability. As a benchmark system, a model for population dynamics that incorporates discrete, irregular network structures is utilized. Findings indicate that a threshold exists beyond which the system's pattern of activity becomes permanently fixed, rendering it incapable of displaying temporal instability. Furthermore, it is observed that this threshold correlates positively with the system's overall flexibility in terms of network topology. To explore the applicability of this research approach in a broader context, a second case study is conducted involving a model for spreading information within networks. Results demonstrate that temporal stability can serve as an accurate limiting factor for the system's ability to undergo multiple waves of spreading. In summary, this research highlights the critical role that activity pattern variability plays in determining the temporal state of a system, thereby constituting a system's inherent characteristic that must be taken into account when developing control strategies tailored to prevent the spread of harmful phenomena. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the record for the longest orbital period, has a non-reflective surface composed of water ice overlying a dark base layer. Spectral analysis of Nereid's near-infrared reflectance reveals the presence of three absorption features, corresponding to bands associated with crystalline water ice. This is the first time such a pattern has been observed in a celestial body's reflectance spectrum. Using a model that simulates the physical properties of Nereid's surface features, we identified a polar temperature of approximately 66 K. The observed absorption sizes in Nereid's near-infrared reflectance spectrum can only be explained by a surface consisting of approximately 60% complex water ice blends. This finding is consistent with theoretical models suggesting that pure water ice crystals cannot occur on Nereid's surface due to the presence of non-ice constituents. As a result, the ice crystals on Nereid are expected to be small and irregular, leading to the observed mixing of ice phases. Nereid's unusual orbit, which takes it from 1.3 to 51 times closer to Neptune than the moon Charon, may be the result of a mechanism that also caused the surface to mix and create the observed ice blend phenomenon. This phenomenon can only be explained by the surface ices on Nereid being quenched, or solidified, below a certain temperature threshold, which is approximately 110 K. This theory is consistent with the observed non-reflective nature of Nereid's surface, as well as its unusual brightness variations, which are not fully understood. The discovery of complex water ice blends on Nereid provides essential insights into the planet's moon composition, which could be useful in future space missions aimed at exploring the Neptune system. This research is the first to analyze Nereid's near-infrared reflectance using data from the New Horizons spacecraft, which flew by the Neptune system in 2007. This discovery demonstrates that more information about the Neptune system could be revealed using (re)analysis of existing data. Furthermore, this research confirms that Nereid's surface can be accurately modeled using physical surface features, which is essential for understanding the moon's physical properties. This method can potentially be used to study other celestial bodies, particularly those with minimal or no atmospheric interference. Using physical surface features to model a moon or planet's reflectance spectrum allows researchers to simulate the moon's surface features and make predictions based on different temperature and polar angle conditions. This study builds upon Pawlikowski's work and introduces a new concept of tukey-order with models, which aligns with his original principles. A comprehensive model theory is developed to establish a complete order with models, and this order satisfies Pawlikowski's basic requirements. Furthermore, the theoretical framework allows for an examination of whether every non-void maximal ideal in the Boolean algebra of all subsets of natural numbers has a countable intersection with the tukey-order, which is shown to be true. To reinforce the coherence of this approach, a formal system is proposed and demonstrated to be complete. In comparison to classical logic, this formal system exhibits unique properties, such as a non-unique valuation and a distribution principle with dependent and independent clauses. Additionally, the study investigates the relationship between the size of infinite cardinalities and their presence in the tukey-order, and shows that a certain cardinality can be present in the order while its power cannot be utilized to construct it. Lastly, the study focuses on the relative size of cardinalities within the tukey-order and establishes that a specific infinite cardinality is larger than another. Based on Pawlikowski's first hypothesis, which asserts that every uncountable cardinality is larger than aleph one, a consistent extension of the formal system is proposed. To verify the coherence of this extension, a model theory is developed that aligns with Pawlikowski's principles, and it is shown that the model satisfies a crucial condition mentioned in Pawlikowski's first hypothesis. Consequently, the study responds affirmatively to Pawlikowski's first hypothesis. On the other hand, based on Cantor's continuum hypothesis, which posits the existence of a specific cardinality, a consistent extension of the formal system is proposed, and a model theory is developed to examine the relationship between this cardinality and the tukey-order. Ultimately, the study shows that neither Pawlikowski's first hypothesis nor Cantor's continuum hypothesis implies each other. To achieve this goal, the study utilizes the tukey-order with models, which provides a novel way to understand these famous problems of mathematics and foundation of set theory. While the study attempts to respond affirmatively to Pawlikowski's second hypothesis, which posits the existence of a specific ordinal, a comprehensive model theory is required to confirm this hypothesis. As a result, the study leaves the resolution of Pawlikowski's second hypothesis for potential future research. In ecological presence-absence data, species presence or absence is typically represented by binary variables at specific locations. These data sets often consist of a small number of observations and a large number of variables, making them multi-dimensional. Identifying clusters within these data based on species presence patterns can aid in understanding ecological communities and managing protected areas. Various clustering methods have been proposed for presence-absence data, but a comprehensive comparison of their effectiveness has been lacking. In this research, we examine nine clustering methods for presence-absence data, including evaluations of their accuracy, robustness, and reliability. Our analysis incorporates data transformations, different types of distance measures, and popular multi-dimensional clustering methods. To illustrate the utility of these clustering methods, we use real-world data from a nature reserve, known as the Cape Breton Highlands, located in Nova Scotia, Canada. Our findings show that the performance of these clustering methods varies depending on the data sets and proposed evaluations, highlighting the importance of testing these algorithms on diverse data sets, as well as their original data of origin. Our results demonstrate that the nonlinear mapping technique and hierarchical clustering methods performed well in our tests. As an added contribution, we make available the code and data used in this study through public repositories, enabling others to replicate our results and explore these clustering methods for presence-absence data. Our ultimate goal is to provide researchers and practitioners with a guide on the best clustering approaches for presence-absence data, as well as empirical comparisons of their performance. Additionally, we aim to facilitate the use of these methods for presence-absence data, as demonstrated by our analysis using the Cape Breton Highands data, and make available the necessary computational resources to replicate our results and evaluate the effectiveness of these clustering methods. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 Aggressive Spreading Task in SemEval-2019 focused on identifying aggressive social media posts in Spanish. Our approach combined rule-based techniques and machine learning methods, including BERT and SVMs. In particular, we used a BERT-based model trained on Spanish data from various sources, as well as custom-built SVM models trained on the provided DataSheet1 dataset with various feature sets. Our strategy involved leveraging BERT's aggressive detection capabilities while complementing it with traditional machine learning methods. Ultimately, our cumulative efforts yielded the highest accuracy in the competition. However, due to a data loading issue, we missed the submission deadline and failed to participate in the evaluation phase. As a result, we could only share our code and results for the baseline dataset. Our results indicate that a combination of machine learning and advanced NLP techniques can effectively improve the identification of aggressive social media posts in Spanish. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. (https://github.com/UM-IU-LING/UM-IU-LING_SemEval-2019_Task6). Vivek S. Agarwal was the lead of this project. Consider the set $\mathbb{N}$ of all natural numbers, a modified version of $\mathbb{N}$ with the digit '0' excluded, and the palindromic numbers within this modified set. We define maps $\varphi$ and $\psi$ such that for any natural number $n$, its image under $\varphi$ is obtained by dividing it by the smallest natural number greater than or equal to $\sqrt{n}$ that is a perfect square, while its image under $\psi$ depends on whether $n$ is a perfect square or not, in which case its image is 1, otherwise its image is 0. We demonstrate that the composition of these maps, $\varphi\circ\psi$, yields a bijection between the exclusion set $A$ of natural numbers containing only palindromic numbers and the set $\mathbb{N}_0$ derived from modifying $\mathbb{N}$ by excluding 0, in addition to also establishing a similar bijection between the exclusion set $B$ of natural numbers not containing palindromic numbers and the set $\mathbb{N}_0$. We compare the quotients of $A$ and $B$ by computing their difference, which gives us the constant 1, consequently proving that the cardinality of $A$ is twice that of $\mathbb{N}_0$. We further extend this result to the set of natural number triplets and provide potential areas of research for further exploration. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in the medical and industrial sectors for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since X-ray sources emit X-rays with distinct wavelengths, which vary according to their energy and atomic number, CT scans necessarily involve multi-energy data. However, current conventional methods either disregard this multi-energy data or make unrealistic assumptions about the subjects being imaged. We will show how a novel mathematical framework can accurately process multi-energy data to produce precise images of the subject's internal structure, along with reliable estimates of X-ray attenuation and density. We will also demonstrate how this framework can be adapted to remove electronic noise from CT sensors and isolate specific materials within subjects. We will support our theoretical findings with experimental results showing that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and stability. We will also provide a detailed analysis of the iterative minimization algorithm we employed to solve the resulting optimization problem, which exhibits non-convex and coupled characteristics, complicating its optimization. We will finally apply our proposed framework to reconstruct human CT scans, analyzing the impact of varying energy intervals and discrete values on reconstruction quality. Additionally, we will investigate how our framework can be used to detect and isolate hazardous materials, such as iodine, in CT scans. We will also demonstrate how our framework can be adapted to process 3D multi-energy CT data, yielding precise volume measurements of subjects and objects. Finally, we will apply our proposed framework to demonstrate its capability in denoising CT data acquired using a CT scanner with built-in pre-filtering technology to reduce electronic noise. We will provide a detailed evaluation of the performance of our approach in comparison to conventional denoising methods, illustrating its ability to produce high-quality denoised images with reduced noise levels, especially at low exposure levels. We will also provide a detailed analysis of the behavior of our iterative minimization algorithm, which exhibits convergent characteristics, despite the non-convex characteristics of the underlying variational problem. We will finally apply our proposed framework to quantify the effective atomic number and density of subjects and objects, yielding accurate estimates in both the linear and non-linear regimes. We will also investigate the performance of our framework under varying levels of measurement error, illustrating its ability to provide stable estimates of interior and surface density, along with the total atomic content and iodine content in subjects and objects. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the absence of comprehensive datasets for script identification and evaluation. This obstacle is exacerbated for rare and historical handwritten scripts where relevant data may not exist or is difficult to acquire. To overcome this issue, we propose an innovative approach to create high-quality datasets from minimal amounts of labeled text images, effectively simulating a full-fledged dataset production method. By incorporating a robust script recognition model and a comprehensive script corpus, we enable accurate identification and labeling of unseen handwritten scripts. The newly developed dataset can serve as a valuable benchmark for HTR tasks involving novel scripts. To demonstrate the efficacy of our solution, we created datasets for three rare scripts: Modhi, Xhos, and Syriac, and achieved remarkable results on the newly established HTR benchmarks for these scripts. Modhi: 4.13% WER, Xhos: 6.34% WER, Syriac: 14.72% WER. The proposed method offers a versatile solution for dataset creation and serves as a flexible tool for script identification and evaluation, potentially extending to other handwritten scripts. The created datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/VlaD-HCR/ScriptBench.

Following an introductory explanation of quantum topology, the model is initially presented with its classic concept of electron transport. Subsequent sections cover more advanced topics, including extra symmetry, charge polarization, Floquet theory, supersymmetry, compactification, Witten index, and related non-Hermitian topology. Each section is self-contained and features illustrative calculations based on the SSH model to support students' understanding of these topological quantum concepts. Predictions based on these ideas are discussed to analyze experimental outcomes. Additionally, the lecture notes address how quantum topology can facilitate the exploration of non-Hermitian topology, making connections along the way. Relevant references are provided for further exploration. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain types of convex regions and analytic circles. Specifically, we investigate the compactness of the composition operator $C_{\varphi}$ for various functions $\varphi$ on the following domains: the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, simply connected bounded convex regions in the plane, and the unit polydisk $\mathbb{D}^2$. We also consider composition operators with symbols from $H^{\infty}$ on the Bergman spaces of certain types of convex regions, establishing a sufficient and necessary condition for compactness in this case. Our results are motivated by a century-old problem initially explored by S. Bernstein and have implications for the theory of analytic functions. This work was partially supported by funds from the Research Fund-University of Memphis. We would like to express our gratitude for this support. Our method of approach is rooted in classical complex variable techniques and the extension of P. L. Doppler's 1928 result, which concerned the compactness of first-order differential operators between Bergman spaces and the convergence of certain infinite product series in $\mathbb{D}$. We have also drawn upon recent research by M. Aziz, M. Ludwig, C. R. Nasar, and B. A. Taylor, as well as established estimates for the means of the derivative of $n$-th degree in $H^2_{\mathbb{D}}$. In addition, we offer an alternative demonstration of a condition for compactness first established by M. Saavedra and M. Storlitz. Our analysis also utilizes a novel technique that involves 'pulling out' weights from symbols, and we investigate the compactness of specific composition operators, such as $C_{z^n}$ and $C_{\log z}$, in various Bergman spaces. We further consider a theorem of A. G. Gorain, which concerned the compactness of a composition operator with a multivariate symbol, and demonstrate that it can be extended to certain types of convex regions in the plane. To overcome these limitations, a parallel memory allocator called DynaSOAr was created, allowing for efficient and contiguous memory access during memory-intensive operations. By leveraging a dynamic memory-scheduling algorithm, DynaSOAr guarantees a high degree of memory coherence, thereby promoting efficient GPU performance. Furthermore, it offers a user-friendly interface to simplify the development of memory-intensive applications on GPUs, demonstrating its potential through successful integration with the SOAr object-based programming platform. The stability of a cylindrical structure, similar to a cane, under internal pressure, is evaluated considering its elastic and nonlinear elastic properties.  A specific geometric feature of the structure leads to a longitudinal axial shortening in response to increased internal pressure.  To determine the optimal balance between resistance to bending and resistance to buckling, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of the structure's mechanical behavior.  This study combines various analytical methods with numerical simulations to provide a thorough understanding of the structure's performance.  Specifically, we have developed a set of design rules and created dimensionless graphs that can be used to identify whether a structure will buckle or deform excessively.  Moreover, we have derived expressions for the tangential modulus of the structure and the critical pressure threshold for buckling.  To confirm the accuracy of our analytical models, we compared them with the results of finite element simulations.  These simulations, coupled with experimental data from physical tests, demonstrate that the structure's mechanical behavior can be accurately predicted using our analytical models.  Consequently, these designs enable the fabrication of structures with the desired mechanical properties and stability.  This knowledge has potential applications in the development of new medical devices, such as stents, and airships. An experimental technique that utilizes ultrasound has been developed to create a moving environment for particles suspended in a liquid by exploiting the acoustic momentum transfer effect. This setup allows for the observation of a oscillatory movement of the particles even when they are not exposed to a standing wave. A theoretical model based on the extended WKB method has been formulated to accurately describe the oscillatory motion of the particles. A comparison between the experimental results and the theoretical findings reveals a high level of agreement, suggesting that this setup could be used to simulate the Bloch oscillation effect in solids. Additionally, the application of this setup to manipulate microscopic particles offers promising avenues for research in fields such as biomedicine and microtechnology. Furthermore, the possibility of simulating an effective force acting on particles has also been investigated. Results show that this effective force can be substantial, reaching values of several millinewtons per gram. The parameters influencing its strength have been identified and discussed. A discussion on the connection between the effective force and the force profile in the system is also presented. To refine the description of the oscillatory motion, an alternative theoretical model based on Floquet engineering has been developed. This approach enables the simultaneous simulation of the oscillatory movement and the movement of the particles' center of mass. A comparison between the two theoretical methods reveals that the Floquet method provides a more precise simulation of the particles' movement. A potential application of the setup has also been explored, specifically its use as a tool to study biological cells and microorganisms in an ultrasound field. A preliminary analysis of the parameters influencing the movement of a specific type of yeast cell has been conducted using the Floquet method. The outcome demonstrates that this setup can serve as a useful tool for simulating the effective force acting on cells, thereby opening up new possibilities for the application of quantum simulation in biomedicine. Furthermore, the quantum nature of the ultrasound has been examined. Both the ultrasound intensity and the wavelength can be varied, allowing for the investigation of the quantum simulation property as a function of either variable. The outcome shows that the quantum nature of the ultrasound must be attributed to the interaction between the particles and the ultrasound rather than the quantum nature of the ultrasound itself. As a result, the setup can be used to simulate an effective quantum force acting on particles in a classical environment. Finally, the feasibility of simulating a quantum momentum distribution has been explored using the setup. Although the ultrasound momentum distribution is not a true quantum momentum distribution, the induced effective force can nonetheless be used to simulate an effective quantum momentum distribution. The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in the Milky Way's bulge region, defined by a bar-like structure approximately 70 parsecs in length, exhibits dynamic and complex star formation behavior. In this research, a two-dimensional analysis of the CMZ's density structure using an anisotropic framework is presented, focusing specifically on Parsec Square Miles per Hypercube kilometer angles (PSMHkA) and related parameters. By examining a high-resolution map of 1.1 mm emission from the CMZ, obtained through the Atacama Large submillimeter/millimeter array (ALMA), the anisotropic density structure is quantified using second-moment statistics. This is further supported by comparing the results to simulated anisotropic distributions using the PHANTOM database, revealing that the CMZ's density structure exhibits certain similarities with giant molecular clusters but differs from more organized, filamentary patterns. Ultimately, this anisotropic analysis demonstrates that the CMZ can be understood as a complex, three-dimensional cloud consisting of multiple anisotropic entities, potentially shaped by the influence of a massive bar potential. This study represents the initial step in leveraging anisotropic analysis to investigate the dynamics and evolution of this critical region of the Milky Way. This technique allowed us to analyze an electron density of approximately 10^16 per cm^3 of impurities, and our results revealed a quasi-particle interaction factor of |1-f| equal to 1.74 x 10^(-8) per cm^3, corresponding to a quasi-particle lifetime of about 420 attoseconds. This value is considered one of the strongest evidence for the existence of long-range kinetic energy generated by correlations in modern many-body theories, specifically in the interaction-driven phase of Fermi-arc liquid in quantum metals with long-lived quasi-particles. Moreover, our study's findings contradict the predictions of Fermi liquid theory, which suggested a interaction factor proportional to 1/m*μ where m* represents the effective mass and μ the chemical potential. This discrepancy may be attributed to the influence of quasi-particle decay to bound Fermi surfaces at extremely low temperatures, and our research indicates that a more detailed analysis of this decay is required to fully comprehend the behavior of sodium at temperatures below 1.5 Kelvin. Lastly, the interaction factor measured in this study is compatible with the existing estimates of electron-phonon coupling strength, suggesting that electron-phonon mediation plays a significant role in the observed quasi-particle interaction effect. In light of our results, we propose conducting similar experiments on potassium, a sister alkali metal with a higher superconducting tendency, to further investigate the interplay between electron-phonon coupling and quasi-particle interactions. Additionally, we suggest that a similar hyperpolarized 75As nuclear magnetic resonance measurement could provide insight into the existence of nodal point states in this material. To minimize interference from nuclear hyperpolarization, it would be beneficial to perform this study using a 75As-doped sodium single crystal rather than using 23Na as the probe element. This could potentially allow for the detection of quasi-particles unaffected by electron-phonon coupling at extremely low temperatures, and we expect that our proposed research will reveal new and significant findings in this field. Building on the Microcanonization technique created by Nakano et al., we develop a new microthermization method to equilibrate the phase space of isolated, non-equilibrium systems. This method generalizes the Microcanonization approach and maintains phase space volume, allowing us to derive a novel Hamiltonian for the free expansion process. We demonstrate that this new Hamiltonian generates trajectories that restore phase space volume, thereby reversing the expansion phenomenon. This outcome provides insights into the dynamics of non-equilibrium systems and offers potential applications in experimental and theoretical physics. In particular, we apply our method to analyze the free expansion of an ideal gas and derive an expanded form of the Boltzmann distribution, which aligns with the observations from causal quantum Stokes parameters. Additionally, we suggest that our method could be employed to counteract the volume change caused by resonance and demonstrate its use to calculate the scattering amplitude of a resonant Breit-Wigner potential. By treating the real part of the potential as a heat bath, we show that our method can restore phase space volume and obtain the scattering amplitude in a topological phase transition. These findings confirm that our method can overcome the volume change and utilize Hamiltonian trajectories for equilibrium and non-equilibrium free evolution processes. In a broader context, we envisions that our method will contribute to bridging the equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics of microscopic and mesoscopic systems. Lastly, we contemplate exploring the applicability of our approach to more intricate systems, such as interacting gases, and suggest that its success could be linked to the observations from causal quantum Stokes parameters. In this regard, we posit that the derived Hamiltonian and the restored phase space volume will facilitate a deeper understanding of the non-equilibrium dynamics of these systems. Furthermore, we propose that our method could be extended to account for correlations in non-equilibrium systems, which would pave the way for equilibrium microthermization across various domains in physics. To realize this potential, we plan to generalize our method to include the effects of non-trivial Hamiltonian action on phase space correlations, which will enable the Scattering of Quantum Information (SQI) technique to be applied in non-equilibrium systems with restored phase space volume. This would allow us to derive a quantum Boltzmann distribution for interacting gases, thereby bridging the gap between equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics of microscopic and mesoscopic systems. In this vision, we anticipate that our method will overcome the longstanding hurdle of phase space volume change and utilize Hamiltonian trajectories for equilibrium and non-equilibrium free evolution processes.

This paper introduces a novel technique for hiding images while maintaining their reversibility, essentially creating an invisible'stealth' mode for image data. In other words, the entire network freezes into a predefined state of unity when triggered, enabling us to derive a universally applicable activation function for the first time. This mechanism is achieved through the use of Bayesian Neural Networks implementing a specific variance constraint, facilitating reliable and consistent triggering. Additionally, the subnetworks within our model exhibit independent behaviors, preventing any cross-interference and thereby improving the reliability of our model as a memory safety feature. Our method is demonstrated through successful applications in deep reinforcement learning and the creation of adversarial examples. Further details are available in our research paper.

which asserts that for any PPT quadrilateral with positive Hilbert Schmidt norm, 
the PPT property holds for all four corners. We find a counterexample to this 
conjecture, specifically for the case of 2x2 matrices, and note that the norm 
condition in the conjecture is the crucial factor determining the PPT property.

In brain tissue, the gradual buildup of substances such as glucose, oxygen, and nutrients can lead to life-threatening conditions known as stroke and head trauma. Understanding how substances move within the brain is essential for uncovering the root causes of these disorders. This process involves the gradual release of substances from blood vessels into the brain, coupled with the removal of waste materials from the brain back into the blood. To model this process, we take a comprehensive approach, combining partial differential equations that describe substance movement with integer variables representing the status of molecules. These variables are governed by an optimization problem with numerous constraints, including equations for neuron activity, substance consumption, and the clearance of waste materials. Due to the vast amount of data available on brain imaging, we also introduce image-based parameters that account for the brain's structure and function. This model is complex to solve because of the nonlinear relationships between variables and the vast amount of data involved. To address this challenge, we develop a series of approximations that ultimately allow us to solve the problem in a reasonable timeframe, demonstrating the model's efficacy with a 3D simulation of brain tissue. This project represents a significant breakthrough in modeling brain substance movement and traffic due to the vast amount of data involved, making it an accessible and solvable problem. This work has the potential to advance our understanding of the optimal design of brain blood flow and waste removal to prevent or treat brain diseases. In particular, the model has applications in targeting critical areas of the brain to deliver therapeutic drugs and genes to prevent or treat strokes, head trauma, and other conditions. Moving forward, we plan to expand the model to include molecule traffic jams, which occur when brain tissue is affected by diseases such as multiple sclerosis, and develop a control strategy to improve brain function and prevent disease progression. This research has the potential to influence various fields beyond just optimization and partial differential equations, including neuroscience, computer science, and medicine, as demonstrated by the ongoing collaborations with neurosurgeons and neurologists involved in the project. In the long term, this model can aid clinicians and researchers in understanding the optimal treatment and prevention of brain diseases at the molecular level. This research focuses on the issue of multiple system failures caused by hidden problems in large network interactions. A thorough investigation is necessary to identify the underlying issue to prevent similar failures in the future. However, detecting these hidden problems across the entire network can be a daunting task. A new method, referred to as NeMo, is introduced to address this challenge. NeMo is an analytical tool that uses network motifs to identify the most common patterns in a given network. By selecting specific nodes and measuring the frequency of associated sub-graph patterns, NeMo can pinpoint hidden problems by comparing typical and abnormal network patterns. This method is successfully implemented and tested on real-world financial data, demonstrating its ability to uncover significant information beyond basic network measures. Additionally, NeMo's results are compared to those obtained from more traditional approaches, highlighting its unique capabilities and applications. Further development of this method could lead to a broader range of usages beyond its current focus on hidden problem detection. Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the Tversky ratio space with parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ that reduce to the Jaccard distance on label sets with sizes $q_\alpha$, $q_\beta$, and $q_\gamma$ satisfying specific conditions. This work builds upon their research by choosing $q_\alpha = q_\beta = 1/2$ and investigating various possibilities for $q_\gamma$. It demonstrates that when $q_\gamma$ takes other values, the resulting metric does not satisfy a balanced ratio property, but rather, it falls into a broader class of consistent Tversky metrics. To date, our study covers the cases for $q_\gamma$ equal to $1/3$, $2/3$, and any value within the open interval $(\frac{1}{2}, 1)$. Importantly, it establishes a connection between the Jaccard distance and a specialized normalized Tversky metric, which can also be viewed as an generalized version of the Lq norms. Furthermore, this research provides evidence suggesting that the Jaccard distance is not only continuous but also has continuous partial derivatives with respect to both its first and second arguments. It resolves an issue raised in the paper by selecting specific values for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that result in a good approximation of the normalized Tversky distance for $q_\gamma = \frac{1}{3}$. Moreover, our research links the Tversky metric to an analogue of the Shannon information distance that is normalized by adding a constant. This constant, which is equal to $-\log q_\gamma$, enables the Tversky metric to be expressed as the difference between two entropy quantities using a logarithmic base. Finally, our investigation relates the Tversky metric to an analogue of the Kent distribution on the real line by demonstrating that it acts as a metric on the sets of probability distributions of a discrete random variable whose support size is limited to $n$. Ultimately, this research is grounded in the broad category of Tversky metrics (Jim\'enez et al., 2013). A particular choice for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is examined in detail, and our results are shown to be cognitively meaningful. They can also be expressed in terms of the widely used normalized Shannon information distance, and our findings provide a connection between our work and that of Arai (2011) on symmetric Tversky spaces. Understanding the working mechanism of graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) is crucial for further improving their performance. Current theories rely on the graph Fourier transform to analyze GCNNs, but this approach is complex and difficult to understand. We propose a new perspective on GCNNs by translating the graph convolution into a matched filtering process on the Fourier domain, and demonstrating the equivalence between GCNNs and traditional filters in the spatial domain. This intuitive matched filtering framework allows us to investigate the effect of GCNNs with varying parameters, and provide a clear explanation for the performance improvement achieved by stacking multiple GCNN layers. We also test the proposed framework by developing a simple, multi-layered GCNN based on Gaussian filters, and evaluating its capabilities in constructing GCNNs with arbitrary dependency graphs and feature dimensions. The proposed framework offers a straightforward method for designing multi-layered GCNNs, and provides a comprehensive understanding of the working mechanism of GCNNs. A recent approach to contextualized models has achieved significant successes
in various NLP tasks.  Despite the benefits, there are still many languages
for which adequate dependency parsing tools do not exist.  To address this
shortcoming, we propose a novel self-learning method that leverages
previously annotated data from related languages to improve parsing performance
in low-resource languages.  Our method builds on recent advances in
transformer models and includes a systematic evaluation of multiple models
and techniques to optimize self-learning performance.  It also offers a
deliberate control system to regulate the influence of external data.
Experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms current state-
of-the-art models for low-resource languages and offers a versatile solution
for languages without fully annotated datasets.  Code and pre-trained models
are available at https://github.com/dure/dplp.

information available at compile-time to eliminate unnecessary options at runtime. By 
doing so, early specialization can substantially reduce the time it takes to set up a system.

into specialized system configurations, enabled by recent advancements in code generation

Our analysis focuses on two aspects: how work is defined and how it behaves. We find that the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle undergoes two types of active work - extending the work done by both quadratic and linear forces. Despite this distinction, we discover that the active work performed on the particle is unaffected by its active motion, leading to the paradoxical result that active work is indistinguishable from passive work. To resolve this anomaly, we investigate the dynamics of the fuel cycle that enables active motion and find that active work is only captured by considering the entire system, not the particle in isolation. Therefore, active work should not be attributed solely to the particle but is instead a manifestation of the interplay between the particle and fuel molecules. In light of this finding, we propose a revised perspective on work that could be generally applicable to other active thermal systems. Our theoretical results are further verified through both numerical simulations and by collecting extensive data in detailed simulations. Moreover, we find that the rate at which active thermal systems convert energy from one form to another is subject to a upper bound, with this maximum rate accurately calculated under both thermal and overdamped conditions. However, issues with the alignment component, such as inaccurate matching of frames and omission of temporal relationships, hinder the quality of the solution. To resolve these problems, a new and improved model, BasicVSR++, has been developed that refines the propagation and alignment components. The updated propagation component now incorporates a cross-scale fusion method that utilizes attention weights to combine different scale networks and reduce spatial and temporal resolution discrepancies. Additionally, a new and improved alignment component, called IndNet, uses an indicator network to accurately match frames and restore a clear video from distorted input. Experimental results demonstrate that BasicVSR++ surpasses the performance of BasicVSR and rival approaches by a considerable margin, as evidenced by notable gains of 0.63, 0.55, and 0.47 dB over the original model in various challenge settings on VIDSRL, NFSD, and VAO in terms of PSNR, FAD, and L1F score. The improved model also achieves superior performance on video decompression, denoising, and interpolation tasks, highlighting its versatility and potential for broad application. The full code and model weights for BasicVSR++ are available at https://github.com/Ingraocheng/BasicVSR++.pdf. Evaluation results for Video Super-Resolution Benchmark are presented in the attached document. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit task acquisition and performance. Despite this, model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning typically employs separate entropy-regularized MDP
constructors and optimal policy evaluators for each task, lacking a shared
representation. Inspired by modular memory designs, we introduce a method to
connect multiple task constructors and evaluators using a shared reinforcement
learning experience buffer. This approach allows for efficient task switching,
eliminating the need for re-construction and re-evaluation, and enables positive
transfer between tasks. Furthermore, it avoids the catastrophic interference
that occurs when introducing new tasks, maintaining high performance on established
tasks. Our method offers a suitable balance of task diversity and experience
repetition. Additionally, it allows for efficient learning of dynamic task
environments. We evaluate its effectiveness in a range of simulated multi-task
scenarios. This research provides a fundamental framework that can be further
improved to facilitate learning across a broad spectrum of diverse tasks. It
also highlights the potential for model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
to outperform existing state-of-the-art single-task methods. The code and data
for this research can be accessed via https://github.com/yarusov-andrey/modular-mbtl.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as modified versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially introduced as a model for chaotic motion with abruptly changing directions. By applying a graph partition approach, we determine that the intrinsic dynamics of these maps consist of a primary component, the Dyck system, alongside additional isolated periodic orbits. Entropy maximization occurs when the Dyck system's measure is taken, yet we have also identified scenarios where this measure is inaccessible due to an inherent discontinuity caused by a 2D map's 'funnel' structure, leading to an imperfect entropy hierarchy. This phenomenon is further explored through analysis of a 3D variant, exhibiting an inherently singular measure that precludes any entropy hierarchy at all. The studies on these modified heterochaos maps provide novel insights into the intrinsic dynamics of 2 and 3 dimensional dissipative systems. Moreover, they generalize the principles of entropy accessibility to settings beyond hyperbolic dynamics, expanding our understanding of this concept. By correlating the intrinsic dynamics of these maps with that of the Dyck system, we establish a significant link between the spectral nature of the Dyck system's transfer operator and the entropic properties of its measures, including the newly introduced singular type. This connection offers a framework for investigating the entropy spectrum of a conservative spectral gap system, a technique that we have initially employed to analyze the entropic characteristics of a 2D area-constraint model. By developing this method, we have obtained a precise entropy hierarchy for the 2D area-constraint model, demonstrating that its measures can be ordered by entropy both conservatively and dissipatively, and thereby extending the principles of entropy accessibility to settings beyond piecewise isometries. Following the successful operation of the Large Hadron Collider, researchers are now looking towards building new, even more powerful colliders like the Future Circular Collider (FCC) or the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC), where scientists aim to discover new physics beyond the standard model. In this investigation, we explore how the standard model's expanded scalar sector appears at the weak scale following the detection of a standard Higgs boson at 125 GeV. We focus on making predictions for the production cross-sections of the heavy scalar states, including the CP-conserving states H and H0, and the CP-varying states A and H±, at upcoming colliders like the 27 and 38 TeV FCC protons, as well as the CLIC e+e- collider operating at 380 GeV, 1.4 TeV, 3 TeV, or 5 TeV. We thoroughly calculate production cross-sections for heavy scalars within two expanded scalar models: a two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) where the Higgs bosons have coupling similarities, and a type-I 2HDM where the Higgs boson's coupling behaves differently than the non-perturbative Higgs boson. The study shows that heavy scalar production can be highly sensitive to the choice of model, indicating a potential breakthrough in differentiating between models through observations of heavy scalar production at 27 and 62 TeV colliders. Specifically, we find that the heavy scalar states in the type-I 2HDM have cross-sections that are generally higher than in the similarity model, with notable variations in how they are produced. We also discover that future colliders offer excellent opportunities to study heavy scalar decays, particularly the Higgs boson's self-coupling, with notable versatility in measuring this coupling at the 27 and 62 TeV FCC protons or the 380 GeV, 1.4 TeV, 3 TeV, or 5 TeV CLIC e+e- collider. In general, we find that heavy scalar production in the standard model expanded with non-perturbative and similarity characteristics exhibits noticeable differences, with notable production cross-sections and heavy scalar interactions that will greatly benefit from observations at the FCC and CLIC. This paper introduces a novel deep generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), built on an autoregressive framework, to generate raw audio signals in real-time. PQNet enhances the standard WaveNet model (WNNet) with two innovative features: 1) Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution Neural Network (PCE-CNN) and 2) Quasi-Periodic Gate (QGate). The PCE-CNN module in PQNet dynamically increases the network's coverage of the frequency spectrum in direct proportion to the pitch of the ground-trtruth signal, thereby optimizing the model's complexity and data requirements. Additionally, the QGate module helps to capture long-term periodic patterns within the signals, thereby improving the model's ability to predict extended periods of time into the future. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed PQNet model surpasses state-of-the-art models in terms of the Perceptual Evaluation of Speech and Music (PESQM) score, while reducing the model size by over 50%. Furthermore, the model exhibits exceptional tolerance to channel noise, demonstrating its significant potential in various raw waveform-based applications. The proposed model's source code will be publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, the model has been designed with real-time generation capabilities, making it suitable for real-world use cases. The deployment of next-generation ground-based telescopes and space-based missions necessitates a deeper comprehension of the spectral impact of solar magnetic activity to ensure accurate and reliable mission planning and execution.
Our research utilizes extensive solar observations from the HARPS-N solar telescope, covering a broad range of magnetic activity levels, to identify potential sources of spectral distortions.
By employing an unbiased and systematic approach, we search for spectral features that can accurately predict and model the spectral variations caused by solar magnetic activity.
The study introduces and evaluates several new indicators that are sensitive to the spectral shifts, which are independent of the fill-in effect.
The most effective indicators are further analyzed to develop a model that explains the spectral variations observed from active to quiet solar states.
The results show that the current solar models are sufficient to account for the spectral variations observed under moderate magnetic activity conditions.
However, these models fail to fully explain the spectral variations observed under strong magnetic activity conditions.
The study provides a baseline for future investigations into the spectral variations caused by solar magnetic activity, and the results can be applied to other stellar objects that exhibit magnetic activity.

This new procedure analyzes the shifted peak by comparing it to a modeled output from the same system but with the electrode's dissipation minimized. Our numerical investigations, utilizing a 1D numerical model of a Majorana island connected to a variety of resistive electrodes, reveal that the technique can distinguish the Majorana peak from others by analyzing the shift in peak position and comparing it to the expected distribution obtained from a 2-term calibration formula. Our simulations demonstrate that the technique can accurately identify the Majorana peak at a wide range of temperatures and dissipation levels. Additionally, our results indicate that the peak's broadening resulting from processes like photon emission, as influenced by the electrode's bandwidth, doesn't hinder the method's ability to distinguish the Majorana peak. Our research shows that the shifted peak positions align closely with the predicted values from the 2-term calibration model, with discrepancies averaging less than 1% for various scenarios. Our simulations demonstrate that the proposed method is capable of differentiating the Majorana peak at a wide temperature range (up to 100mK) and dissipation range (up to 100mOhm), with the method's performance not affected by factors like extra peaks, normal islands, or varying coupling strengths between the island and electrode. These outcomes make the method more robust and versatile in distinguishing the Majorana peak than other peak identification techniques. Based on our research, the method's limitations mainly stem from the same sources of error that affect normal electrode tunneling spectroscopy, such as the inability to distinguish between different zero-energy peaks, the challenge of differentiating the Majorana peak from normal island peaks, and identifying the correct coupling strength between the island and electrode. It's worth noting that these issues can be addressed by developing new electrodes with minimized dissipation and sharpened transitions. In conclusion, our numerical investigations clearly illustrate the potential of the proposed tunneling spectroscopy technique with minimized dissipation and increased electrode dissipation to accurately identify the Majorana peak at a wide range of temperatures and dissipation levels. Furthermore, the technique is expected to play a significant role in distinguishing the Majorana peak at zero energy and understanding the origin of non-Majorana peaks through a thorough analysis of the shifted peak using a 2-term calibration formula. A significant step in creating realistic images involves applying style transfer techniques, but existing methods often produce images with unnatural color tones. This issue is particularly pronounced in portrait global color mapping techniques, where a style image is used to define a color map for multiple subjects. Currently available methods either focus on achieving natural image colors or ensure the color map's consistency, but not both. To address this limitation, we introduce a new neural network that extracts a style profile from paired images and uses it to create natural colors in both directions. This model is based on a novel forward and inverse hue mapping method that ensures a consistent color map and achieves realistic image colors. To train the network efficiently, we develop a distillation method that reduces the requirements for training data, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through a comprehensive set of experiments that compare our natural color preservation approach with other techniques. The validity of our method is confirmed by a user study that shows a strong preference for our natural color method. The source code for our method is available at https://github.com/ImLabUCY/NCP. The demo video is available at https://youtu.be/j_9IpR1K3kY. In snowfall, atmospheric turbulence drives the movement of snowflakes, influencing their patterns of settlement. Despite decades of study, the intricate connections between turbulence, snowflakes, and the resulting ground patterns remain poorly understood. Researchers investigated these relationships by combining data from snowflake observations and wind velocity measurements collected at ground level during a snowstorm in New York. Their analysis reveals that large snowflakes are more likely to follow the direction of the wind's downward extension than smaller ones, demonstrating that atmospheric turbulence can direct solid particles' movement on a large scale. This finding is consistent with previous simulations of similar conditions. Such insights into the interplay between turbulence, snowflakes, and ground patterns offer potential links to other complex systems, like sedimentation and atmospheric phenomena. Furthermore, this research may aid efforts to model and predict snowfall patterns and their impact on transportation and energy industries. Finally, this study underscores the importance of incorporating multiple scales and using selective sweeping to uncover hidden patterns and connections in data, a technique with broad applications across physical sciences. Selective sweeping can be seen as a tool for minimizing noise and revealing meaningful, inherently connected components within a dataset. In this context, it represents a meaningful data transformation that illuminates the snowflake settlement pattern's direction, much like how Helmholtz decomposition reduces velocity gradients to generate meaningful, coherent patterns. Additionally, this study showcases the value of combining small-scale, local observations with large-scale, coherent structures to understand complex systems, as exemplified by the ground-level data and wind velocity measurements. This combination allows researchers to dissect the intricate mechanisms driving snow settlement patterns and offer a new perspective on the development of atmospheric turbulence. It also offers a novel interpretation of the results of previous studies on snowfall and wind interactions, as well as a fresh perspective on the underlying connections between snowflakes, wind, and ground patterns that were previously overlooked. Lastly, this research highlights the practical benefits of reexamining existing findings through the lens of a novel, data-driven approach that incorporates the principles of selective sweeping and Helmholtz decomposition. By doing so, it is possible to uncover the underlying patterns and relationships that underpin complex phenomena, as evidenced by the ground-level snowfall patterns and wind velocity measurements. In multiple-party communication, data compression plays a crucial role in reducing information transmitted between systems. This research targets the efficient reduction of large sensory data from 3D sparse TPC cameras. A novel approach using Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder is proposed, which not only considers the sparse pixel distribution but also incorporates prior knowledge of the underlying scene into the compression model via pre-training. By utilizing the inherent sparsity of TPC pixels, the BCae model achieves significant compression of image sequences, up to 93% in some cases, while also facilitating efficient transmission of compressed data and related head costs. As a result, the reduced data can be accurately reconstructed from the received information, enabling the system to achieve a high overall compression ratio of 94% with minimal distortion. Additionally, the studies conducted using real-world TPC cameras demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in achieving substantial bandwidth savings for video surveillance applications without compromising the quality of the resulting images. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for histological characteristics and abnormalities that can help diagnose adenomas. Given that manual evaluations by pathologists can be time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability, a more reliable method is needed. Advances in histopathological deep learning models have shown potential in assisting this characterization task. However, training an effective model requires a substantial amount of annotated data, which is currently scarce for the task of polyp characterization. To address this challenge, we have created UniToPatho, a large dataset consisting of 192,477 histological images derived from 1,831 tissue samples, along with detailed annotations from expert histopathologists. Airborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images are commonly used due to their ability to penetrate through clouds and provide detailed information about the ground surface. Nevertheless, the inherent speckle noise significantly hinders their enhancement and interpretation. The existing filter-based methods have demonstrated some success but often result in over-smoothed images with lost details. The deep learning-based approaches, on the other hand, produce realistic results; however, their enhanced images lack physical plausibility as they are undifferentiable and uninterpretable. In contrast, the proposed MrSARP model combines a hierarchical prior network with a meta-learning strategy to tackle the SAR image enhancement task. By training the model using multiple pairs of grounded noisy and clean patches, MrSARP learns a suitable filter for each available patch without the need for ground truth enhancement maps. The model achieves notable improvements over current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both objective and perceptual performance. In particular, MrSARP demonstrates an approximately 10 dB improvement in the sparseness metric compared to the least squares optimization method. The model's capabilities are further validated by the addition of various external factors, such as adaptive regression sparsity and curvelet spectral shrinkage, which enhance the filter's coherence and smoothness, respectively. The results show that the augmented MrSARP model achieves a 5% improvement in PSNR comparison to a baseline model without these components. The implementation details and model code are publicly available for others to reproduce and build upon. The proposed MrSARP model sets a new standard for SAR image enhancement, and its generic filter design allows for potential use in other image denoising applications. In addition, the model's embedment of a physical prior results in enhanced images with improved physical plausibility and reduced gradient noise. The success of MrSARP opens up new avenues for its extension to other image enhancement tasks that could benefit from a similar hierarchical deep generative prior framework. The model's focus on SAR image enhancement, however, significantly contributes to the practical achievement of noise reduction in real-world operational conditions. A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical approach, alternating between quantum and classical optimizations to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  Despite its potential, the algorithm's performance often falls short due to suboptimal tuning of its variational parameters.  We propose a straightforward, fully quantum-based method to determine the optimal tuning, replacing the classical process and yielding consistent results across diverse hardware platforms.  The approach leverages a Bayesian technique to determine the optimal tuning parameters, producing a robust and accurate outcome.  We illustrate the method's effectiveness using the Quantum Circuits Based Consistency Problem, a challenging optimization problem suitable for near-term quantum hardware.  Our experiments show that the proposed method yields a 41% improvement in success rate compared to the current state-of-the-art tuning technique.  Additionally, we discovered that the optimal tuning parameters exhibit a normal distribution, facilitating the application of the Bayesian method. Given two ellipses, the number of intersections between them can be determined by examining the signs in a matrix calculated using their respective Gaussian coefficients. Specifically, a positive sign indicates an intersection, also expressed as a point, segment, or complete ellipse. A negative sign denotes the absence of intersection or a void area. This method relies on the use of elliptical coordinate parameters, allowing for the identification of void areas between ellipses and the calculation of their areas via integration in elliptical coordinates. The proposed approach provides an efficient means of estimating these areas, supplementing existing polygon-based methods that may be less efficient for certain applications. The article presents a thorough framework for applying this method in practice. It also addresses potential rounding errors in numerical computations, illustrating the process through a combination of theoretical examples and relevant code. Ultimately, the method is demonstrated to effectively model the visibility of celestial objects, including stars and planets, based on their true shapes and accurate coordinate parameters. The article presents numerical results validating the accuracy of the proposed method in estimating areas, with deviations no greater than 1% from exact values obtained via Monte Carlo sampling. spatiotemporal patterns formed by exciton-polariton condensates using optical
reservoirs. These reservoirs can generate steady-state coherent nonlinear
excitations within the polariton system, even in the presence of significant

sustenance. Firstly, we use a pair of weak and strong optical resonators to create a
protected microcavity receiving exciton-polariton influx from the stronger cavity.
